ecosystem.text: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with their non-living surroundings, linked by flows of energy and nutrients.

biodiversity.text: Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth.

ecosystem service.text: Ecosystem services are the many benefits people get from ecosystems.

natural capital.text: Natural capital is the world's stock of natural resources, including rocks, soils, air, water and all living things.

environmental degradation.text: Environmental degradation is the worsening of the environment through loss of resources such as clean air, water and soil, destruction of ecosystems and habitats, extinction of wildlife, and pollution.

biosphere.text: The biosphere is the sum of all the world's ecosystems: the zone of life on Earth.

anthropocene.text: The Anthropocene is a name for the period in which humanity has become a force that changes the whole planet.

ecosystem service categories.text: The ways ecosystem services are sorted into groups, most famously the four groups of the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.

biodiversity and ecosystem services.text: The link between how varied life is in a place and the benefits that place gives people.

latitudinal diversity gradient.text: The pattern in which the number of species rises from the poles toward the tropics.

cultural services.text: The non-material benefits of nature, such as recreation, beauty, learning and spiritual meaning.

provisioning services.text: The products people obtain from ecosystems, also called ecosystem goods.

ecosystem goods.text: The tangible, material products of ecosystems, such as water, food, fuel, building material and medicinal plants.

regulating services.text: The benefits people get from nature keeping ecosystem processes in check, such as climate, water and pests.

supporting services.text: The background services, such as nutrient cycling and soil formation, that make all other ecosystem services possible.

freshwater depletion.text: The using up and spoiling of Earth's limited fresh water, a major part of environmental degradation.

eco-capitalism.text: Eco-capitalism, or green capitalism, is the view that nature is a form of capital on which all wealth depends, so markets should be used to solve environmental problems.

natural capital protocol.text: A standard framework, released in 2016, that helps organisations identify, measure and value their impacts and dependencies on natural capital.

natural capital declaration.text: A 2012 pledge by finance-sector leaders to build natural capital into their products and reporting.

natural capital valuation debate.text: The argument over whether nature and its free services should be given a money value.

humanity's demand on the biosphere.text: The Dasgupta Review compares humanity's demand for the biosphere's goods and services with the biosphere's regeneration rate: when demand exceeds it, the biosphere depreciates.

system of environmental-economic account.text: The international statistical standard (SEEA) for measuring the environment and how it relates to the economy.

anthropocene start-date debate.text: The disagreement over when the human-shaped era of Earth's history began.

homogenocene.text: A name for the present age in which ecosystems worldwide grow more alike, mainly because people move species around the globe.

produced, human and natural capital.text: The Dasgupta Review sorts capital goods into produced capital, human capital and natural capital.

assimilative capacity.text: Assimilative capacity is how much pollution an environment can absorb without harm to it or to the people who use it.

triple planetary crisis.text: A UN term for three linked global environmental crises: pollution, climate change and biodiversity loss.

short-termism.text: Short-termism is favouring quick profits and short-term results over long-term results and far-sighted action.

ecosystems do not maximise productivity.text: Nature does not maximise net primary production (NPP) or the regeneration rate of its ecosystems, even though a portfolio manager would try to maximise yield.

impact inequality.text: The Dasgupta Review distinguishes inequality in household incomes from inequality in households' impact on the biosphere, which is income corrected for the efficiency of converting nature into income.

invisibility of regulating services.text: Regulating and maintenance services are mostly hidden from view and silent, felt only over the long run or when they are lost.

mobility and silence of nature as a sour.term: Mobility and silence of nature as a source of externalities
mobility and silence of nature as a sour.text: Externalities arise from the biosphere because property rights to large parts of it are weakly defined or enforced, and Nature is mobile, silent and invisible.

economics.text: The social science that studies how goods and services are produced, shared out and used.

externality.text: A cost or benefit that falls on a third party who had no part in the activity that caused it.

own rate of return on assets.term: Own rate of return on assets
own rate of return on assets.text: An asset's yield, or own rate of return, is the growth expected tomorrow if one more unit of it is added to a portfolio today.

sustainability and environmental managem.text: Managing the oceans, fresh water, land and atmosphere at global scale according to sustainability principles.

accommodative capacity.text: The rate at which waste can be added to a body of water while keeping contaminants below levels that cause unacceptable biological harm.

market failure.text: A situation in which a free market's allocation of goods and services is not efficient, so economic value is lost.

environmental economics.text: The branch of economics that studies environmental problems and the economic effects of policies meant to deal with them.

scarcity.text: The basic fact that resources are limited, so only a limited amount of each good can be produced, while human wants have no such limit.

risk assessment.text: A process for identifying hazards and the likelihood they occur, and the actions that can reduce their harmful effects.

negative externality.text: A harmful side effect of producing or consuming something that lands on an unrelated third party and is not counted in the market price.

social cost.text: The full cost of an activity to society: the private cost paid by those involved plus the external costs imposed on others who are not compensated.

externality supply and demand diagram.text: A standard supply and demand graph with an extra curve added to show how an externality pushes the market away from the best quantity for society.

positive externality.text: A beneficial side effect of an activity that helps an unrelated third party, without that party paying for it.

environmental valuation.text: Putting an economic value on the environment and natural resources, many of which have no market price.

environmental versus ecological economic.text: The contrast between environmental economics, which applies standard economics to the environment, and ecological economics, which treats the economy as a part of the ecosystem.

ecological market failure.text: A market failure in which economic activity exhausts vital non-renewable resources, damages fragile ecosystems or overloads nature's ability to absorb waste.

government failure.text: Economic waste caused by government action, when an intervention leaves resources worse allocated than some available alternative.

objections to market failure theory.text: Arguments from several schools of thought that the idea of market failure is misleading, too narrow or does not justify government action.

absolute scarcity.text: A condition in which basic human needs, such as food, exceed the quantities of useful goods available, linked to the ideas of Thomas Malthus.

relative scarcity.text: A condition in which many different wants exceed the available means, which can be put to alternative uses, so people must choose.

causes of externalities.text: The view that externalities come mainly from poorly defined property rights and from the costs of making trades.

marginal social cost.text: The total cost to society of producing one more unit of a good: marginal private cost plus marginal external cost.

ecological critique of externalities.text: The argument from ecological and heterodox economists that treating environmental harm as an occasional 'externality' misreads how the economy works.

inframarginal externality.text: An externality that does not affect the marginal consumer, so it causes no market inefficiency.

positional externality.text: A side effect in which one person's purchase of a status good lowers the value others get from similar goods they already own.

environmentally harmful subsidies.text: Government payments that reward companies more for exploiting natural resources than for protecting them.

unpriced natural capital costs.text: The value of nature that industries use up without paying for it, which would change their profits if it were priced.

failure of competition.text: A market failure in which a firm or small group gains enough market power to block trades that would benefit both sides.

macroeconomic market failures.text: Unemployment, inflation and disequilibrium seen as market failures at the level of the whole economy.

unequal bargaining power.text: A market failure in which one side of a deal, such as an employer, can hold out longer than the other and so sets the terms.

types of scarcity.text: The division of scarcity into demand-induced, supply-induced and structural kinds.

kapp's theory of social costs.text: K. William Kapp's heterodox view that social costs are the share of production costs businesses shift onto society to raise profits.

measuring social costs.text: The difficulty of putting numbers on social costs, especially future, environmental and long-range harms.

biodiversity risk assessment.text: An assessment of risks to biological diversity, especially species extinction or ecosystem collapse.

environmental risk assessment.text: An assessment of the effects of stressors, usually chemicals, on the local environment.

pecuniary externality.text: A side effect that works only by changing market prices, not by changing the real resources available to others.

causes of government failure.text: The main reasons government interventions go wrong, such as missing information, political pressure and short-term thinking.

tyranny of small decisions.text: The way many small decisions, each insignificant on its own, can add up to a large outcome that nobody chose or wanted.

pollution.text: The release into the natural environment of contaminants that cause harm.

market distortion by government.text: The way taxes, subsidies and price controls can change prices artificially and disturb how markets share out scarce resources.

review of environmental economics and po.term: Review of Environmental Economics and Policy
review of environmental economics and po.text: A peer-reviewed environmental economics journal, published twice a year, written to be readable by non-specialists.

pollutant.text: A substance or form of energy put into the environment that has unwanted effects or makes a resource less useful.

air pollution.text: The presence in the air of substances that harm people, other living things or the environment.

persistent organic pollutant.text: Organic compounds that resist chemical, biological and photolytic degradation and are toxic to health and the environment.

noise pollution.text: Sound that can harm the health of people and animals.

economic costs of air pollution.text: The losses air pollution causes to economies through ill health, lost work, lower crop yields and other damage.

health effects of air pollution.text: The diseases and early deaths caused by breathing polluted air.

stock and fund pollutants.text: The division of pollutants by how well the environment can absorb them: stock pollutants build up, fund pollutants are absorbed if emissions stay low enough.

particulate pollution.text: Pollution made of tiny particles suspended in air, water or space.

stockholm convention on persistent organ.term: Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants
stockholm convention on persistent organ.text: The 2001 international agreement to protect human health and the environment from persistent organic pollutants.

history of pollution.text: How pollution grew from prehistoric fires to the industrial age and how societies began to respond.

pollution control.text: The management of emissions and effluents released into air, water or soil.

pollution abatement cost.text: What it costs a firm to cut the pollution it produces, called marginal abatement cost when measured per extra unit cut.

socially optimal level of pollution.text: The amount of pollution at which society's welfare is greatest, where the harm of one more unit equals the benefit of producing it.

air pollution laws and standards.text: Laws that set limits on pollutant concentrations in the air or on emissions from sources such as vehicles.

history of air pollution control.text: The story of how societies came to regulate air pollution, from early anti-smoke groups to international treaties.

primary and secondary air pollutants.text: The division of air pollutants into those released directly by a source and those that form in the air from other pollutants.

smog.text: Smog, or smoke fog, is a type of intense air pollution.

ground-level ozone.text: Ozone near the ground, formed mainly when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight.

air pollution damage to agriculture.text: The losses in crop output and farm productivity caused by polluted air, especially ozone.

unequal exposure to air pollution.text: The pattern in which poorer groups and some racial groups breathe more polluted air than others.

pollutant risk thresholds.text: Concentration levels, such as the no-observed-adverse-effect level, used in risk assessment to decide how much of a chemical is safe.

zones of influence of pollutants.text: A way of grouping pollutants by where they do damage, horizontally (local or regional) and vertically (surface or atmosphere).

health effects of persistent organic pol.term: Health effects of persistent organic pollutants
health effects of persistent organic pol.text: The harms of POP exposure, including developmental defects, chronic illness, endocrine disruption and cancer risk.

health effects of noise.text: The harm that unwanted sound does to people's physical and mental health.

measuring noise.text: Quantifying noise exposure as sound pressure levels in decibels, a logarithmic scale linked to how people hear.

noise control.text: The rules and methods governments and communities use to limit harmful noise exposure.

noise impacts on wildlife.text: The ways human-made noise disrupts animals that rely on sound to communicate, find mates, navigate and avoid predators.

health effects of smog.text: Smog continues to harm human health in many cities.

utility.text: In economics, utility is a measure of how satisfied a person is with a particular state of the world.

goods.text: In economics, goods are things that give someone welfare or satisfaction.

photochemical smog.text: Summer smog formed when sunlight reacts with nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, leaving particles and ground-level ozone.

soundscape ecology.text: The study of the acoustic relationships between living organisms, human and other, and their environment.

pm10 and pm2.5.text: The two main size classes of particulate matter: coarse particles of 10 micrometres and smaller, and fine particles of 2.5 micrometres and smaller.

microeconomics.text: Microeconomics is the branch of economics that studies how individuals and firms decide how to use scarce resources, and how they interact.

economic value.text: Economic value is a measure of the benefit a good or service gives to a person, firm or other economic agent.

incentive.text: An incentive is anything that persuades a person or organisation to change their behaviour toward a desired outcome.

ceteris paribus.text: Ceteris paribus is a Latin phrase meaning 'other things being equal', used to study the effect of one change while assuming everything else stays the same.

economic model.text: An economic model is a simplified, often mathematical, picture of an economic process, built from a set of variables and the relationships between them.

preference.text: In economics, a preference is the order in which a person ranks the options open to them, from most to least wanted.

indifference curve.text: An indifference curve is a line on a graph joining all the combinations of two goods that a consumer likes equally well.

complementary goods.text: Complementary goods are goods used together, so that one becomes more attractive as the other becomes more popular.

ordinal utility.text: Ordinal utility ranks a person's options in order of preference, saying which is better but not by how much.

market structure.text: Market structure describes the features of a market, such as how many firms sell in it, how alike their products are and how easily firms can enter or leave.

positive and normative economics.text: Positive economics describes and explains how the economy works, while normative economics says what people or societies ought to do.

trade-off.text: A trade-off is a choice in which you accept less of one thing in return for more of another.

opportunity cost.text: The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative you give up when limited resources force you to pick one option over others.

rational choice model.text: Rational choice modelling explains economic and social behaviour by imagining how a rational person would act when weighing the same costs and benefits.

budget constraint.text: A budget constraint is the full set of combinations of goods and services a person can afford with their income at current prices.

consumer choice.text: Consumer choice theory is the part of microeconomics that explains how people's preferences shape what they spend and how much they demand.

substitution effect.text: The substitution effect is the change in what a consumer buys caused purely by a change in the relative prices of goods, as they switch toward the one that became cheaper.

utility maximization problem.text: The utility maximization problem describes how a consumer chooses the most preferred bundle of goods they can afford with limited income at given prices.

types of goods.text: Economists sort goods into four types by whether people can be kept from using them (excludability) and whether one person's use leaves less for others (rivalry).

margin.text: In economics, the margin is the current level of consumption or production, and marginal concepts describe what happens with one small change in that quantity rather than with the total.

goods and services.text: Goods are usually tangible items such as pens or pears, while services are activities other people provide, such as teaching or haircuts.

marginal utility.text: Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction a person gets from consuming one more unit of a good or service.

neoclassical economics.text: Neoclassical economics is the approach that explains production, consumption and prices through supply and demand, driven by people maximizing utility and firms maximizing profit.

marginal rate of substitution.text: The marginal rate of substitution is the rate at which a consumer can give up some of one good for another while staying exactly as satisfied.

marginalism.text: Marginalism is the economic theory that explains differences in the value of goods and services by their marginal utility, the extra satisfaction from one more unit.

criticisms of neoclassical economics.text: Many economists and other schools of thought criticize neoclassical economics, especially its assumptions about rational, self-interested, fully informed people.

diminishing marginal utility.text: The law of diminishing marginal utility says that each extra unit of something consumed adds less satisfaction than the one before.

substitute goods.text: Substitute goods are goods that can replace each other, so cheaper prices for one reduce demand for the other.

free good.text: A free good is a good that is not scarce, so it is available in any quantity with no opportunity cost to society.

normal good.text: A normal good is one that people buy more of when their income rises, unlike an inferior good, which they buy less of.

economic problem.text: The economic problem is the set of basic questions every economy must answer: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom.

cardinal utility.text: Cardinal utility treats satisfaction as something that can be measured with numbers, so the size of the differences between options means something.

marshallian demand function.text: A Marshallian demand function gives how much of a good a consumer buys as a function of its price, the consumer's income and the prices of other goods.

bads.text: A bad is the opposite of a good: something with negative value, such as waste, that its owner will pay to be rid of.

convex preferences.text: Convex preferences are preferences in which averages are liked better than extremes, so a person prefers a mix of goods to a lot of just one.

explicit cost.text: An explicit cost is a direct, out-of-pocket cost of an action, paid in cash or by handing over resources.

compensating variation.text: Compensating variation is the amount of money that would leave a person exactly as well off after a price change as before, measured at the new prices.

intertemporal budget constraint.text: An intertemporal budget constraint links what a person can consume in different periods through borrowing and saving at an interest rate.

soft budget constraint.text: A soft budget constraint exists when an organisation expects an outside body, usually a government, to cover its losses if it gets into financial trouble.

expenditure minimization problem.text: The expenditure minimisation problem asks how little money a consumer needs to reach a given level of satisfaction at current prices.

factors of production.text: Factors of production are the inputs used to make goods and services, such as land, labour and capital.

hicksian demand function.text: A Hicksian, or compensated, demand function gives how much of a good a person buys when they keep their satisfaction fixed and spend as little as possible.

equivalent variation.text: Equivalent variation is the change in a person's wealth that would affect their well-being as much as a given price change would.

definitions of economics.text: Economists have offered many definitions of their subject, from the study of wealth to the study of choices under scarcity.

capital (economics).text: Capital means durable goods that people have produced and then use to make further goods and services.

capitalism.text: An economic system built on private ownership of the means of production, run to obtain profit.

land (economics).text: In economics, land means every naturally occurring resource, not just the ground itself.

economic system.text: An economic system is the way a society organizes the production, allocation and distribution of goods and services.

diminishing returns.text: Diminishing returns is the fall in extra output gained as more of one input is added while all other inputs stay fixed.

labour theory of value.text: The labour theory of value holds that a good's economic value is set by the total socially necessary labour needed to produce it.

production-possibility frontier.text: A production-possibility frontier is a graph showing every combination of two outputs an economy can make when all its resources are used fully and efficiently.

institutional economics.text: Institutional economics studies how institutions, such as firms, states, laws and social norms, and their evolution shape economic behaviour.

mixed economy.text: A mixed economy combines features of capitalism, such as private businesses, with features of socialism, such as government-run services.

subjective theory of value.text: The subjective theory of value holds that a good's value is set by the people buying or selling it, not by any property of the good or the labour that went into it.

planned economy.text: An economic system in which investment, production and the allocation of capital goods follow economy-wide plans.

fixed and circulating capital.text: Adam Smith split capital into fixed capital, which is not used up in making a product, and circulating capital, which is.

types of capital.text: Economists divide capital into several kinds, including financial, social, instructional, human, public and natural capital.

ecological factors of production.text: Ecological economics replaces the usual factors of production with matter, energy and design intelligence, so that production obeys physical limits.

entrepreneurship as a factor of producti.term: Entrepreneurship as a factor of production
entrepreneurship as a factor of producti.text: Entrepreneurship, the organising work of combining land, labour and capital to make a profit, is sometimes counted as a fourth factor of production.

marginal revolution.text: The Marginal Revolution was the spread of marginal utility theory in the 1870s through the work of Jevons in England, Menger in Austria and Walras in Switzerland.

absolute advantage.text: Absolute advantage is the ability of a person, firm or country to produce a good or service more efficiently than others.

comparative advantage.text: Comparative advantage is the principle that people, firms and countries can gain from trade even when one of them is better at producing everything.

marginal rate of transformation.text: The marginal rate of transformation is the slope of the production-possibility frontier: how much of one good must be given up to make one more unit of another.

marxist criticism of marginalism.text: Marxist economists rejected marginalism, holding to the labour theory of value and arguing that prices cannot be explained by individual preferences alone.

implicit cost.text: An implicit cost is the opportunity cost of using something you already own, such as income you could have earned by renting it out or selling it.

sunk cost.text: A sunk cost is money, time or effort already spent that cannot be recovered.

economic cost.text: Economic cost is the total value of everything given up for a course of action, including the opportunities passed over.

fixed and variable costs.text: A fixed cost does not change with how much a firm produces, while a variable cost rises or falls with output.

economic profit.text: Economic profit is revenue minus all costs including opportunity costs, whereas accounting profit counts only the measurable costs of running a business.

cost-of-production theory of value.text: The cost-of-production theory of value says a thing's price is set by the total cost of the resources used to make it.

sunk cost fallacy.text: The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to keep going with something because of what has already been invested in it, even when stopping would be better.

inferior good.text: An inferior good is one that people buy less of as their income rises.

income effect.text: The income effect is the change in how much of a good people buy when their real income, or purchasing power, changes.

market.text: Any arrangement that lets buyers and sellers exchange goods, services and information.

price.text: The amount of money buyers are willing and able to pay for a good or service and that sellers are willing to accept.

giffen good.text: A Giffen good is a rare kind of inferior good that people buy more of when its price rises, breaking the usual law of demand.

slutsky equation.text: The Slutsky equation splits the change in demand caused by a price change into a substitution effect and an income effect.

demand.text: The quantity of a good that people are willing and able to buy at various prices over a given period.

willingness to pay.text: The highest price at which a person will definitely buy one unit of something.

supply (economics).text: The amount of something that producers, workers or other sellers are willing and able to offer for sale.

supply and demand.text: The basic economic model of how a market sets prices: the price moves until the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer.

economic equilibrium.text: A state in which the forces of supply and demand balance, so that prices and quantities stop changing.

law of demand.text: The basic rule that, all else being equal, people buy less of a good when its price rises and more when it falls.

free market.text: An economic system in which the prices of goods and services are set by the supply and demand of buyers and sellers, without government steering.

competition.text: Rivalry among firms for customers and limited resources, using price, product, promotion and place.

elasticity.text: A measure of how much one economic variable responds to a change in another, given as the percentage change in one divided by the percentage change in the other.

demand curve.text: A graph showing how much of a good people will buy at each price, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis.

price elasticity of demand.text: A measure of how strongly the quantity people buy responds to a change in its price: the percentage change in quantity for a one percent change in price.

invisible hand.text: Adam Smith's metaphor for the way free markets can lead self-interested people to serve the public good without meaning to.

income elasticity of demand.text: How strongly the quantity of a good people buy responds to a change in their income.

price signal.text: The information a price carries to buyers and sellers, telling them to supply or demand more or less of something.

market economy.text: An economic system in which decisions about investment, production and distribution are guided by prices set through supply and demand.

price controls.text: Government-enforced limits on the prices that may be charged for goods and services in a market.

comparative statics.text: Comparing two economic outcomes, one before and one after a change in some outside factor, once the economy has settled into its new equilibrium.

shifts in supply and demand.text: Changes in conditions other than a good's own price that move a whole supply or demand curve, and so change the equilibrium price and quantity.

marginal cost.text: The extra total cost of producing one more unit of output.

price mechanism.text: The way prices decide how resources are shared out and steer how much of each good is supplied and demanded.

black market.text: A clandestine market or set of transactions with some aspect of illegality within a legal jurisdiction.

total cost.text: The lowest cost of producing a given amount of output, made up of variable costs plus fixed costs.

monopoly.text: A market in which a single person or company is the only supplier of a particular good or service.

profit (economics).text: What a business has left from its revenue after paying the total costs of its inputs, counting both explicit and implicit costs.

perfect competition.text: An idealized market with many buyers and sellers, identical products and full information, so that no one can influence the price.

market power.text: A firm's ability to raise the price of what it sells above its marginal cost, by controlling supply or demand, without losing all its customers.

oligopoly.text: A market in which a few sellers control pricing.

imperfect competition.text: Any market that falls short of at least one of the conditions of a perfectly competitive market.

competitive equilibrium.text: An equilibrium of a market with flexible prices and many traders, each too small to move prices, in which every trader gets the best bundle they can afford and supply equals demand; also called Walrasian equilibrium.

cost curve.text: A graph showing a firm's production costs against the total quantity it produces.

marginal revenue.text: The extra revenue a firm earns by selling one more unit of its product.

barriers to entry.text: A fixed cost a new entrant must bear to enter a market that incumbents do not bear or have not had to bear.

natural monopoly.text: A firm whose average cost of production keeps falling across the whole range of market demand, so one large supplier is cheaper than several small ones.

public utility.text: An organization that maintains the infrastructure for a public service, often also providing the service itself.

effect of taxes and subsidies on price.term: Effect of taxes and subsidies on price
effect of taxes and subsidies on price.text: How taxes and subsidies change the prices buyers pay and sellers receive, and so the quantity bought and sold.

law of supply.text: The basic rule that, all else being equal, a higher price leads sellers to offer more of a good.

market size.text: How big a market is, measured either by its number of buyers and sellers or by the money exchanged in it, usually per year.

negative price.text: A price below zero, where the owner or producer pays the 'buyer' to take an item away.

price elasticity of supply.text: How strongly the quantity sellers offer responds to a change in price: the percentage change in quantity supplied for a 1% change in price.

government-granted monopoly.text: A monopoly created when a government gives one person or company the exclusive right to supply something.

inverse elasticity rule.text: The rule that a monopoly's markup, as a share of its price, is inversely proportional to the price elasticity of demand it faces.

cross elasticity of demand.text: A measure of how the quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of another good.

inverse demand function.text: A formula that gives price as a function of the quantity demanded, so it is also called a price function.

disequilibrium.text: The condition of a market that is not in equilibrium, where the amounts supplied and demanded are out of balance.

dynamic equilibrium.text: An equilibrium in which several quantities keep growing at the same rate, so that the ratios between them stay fixed.

normal profit.text: The return that just makes running a business worthwhile, equal to what the owner's time and capital could earn in their next best use.

shutdown point.text: The price below which a loss-making firm does better to stop producing in the short run: the point where price falls under average variable cost.

laissez-faire.text: The principle that prices and wages should be free of non-market pressure such as government taxes, subsidies, tariffs, regulations or granted monopolies.

spontaneous order.text: The idea, popularised by Friedrich Hayek, that market economies create order through networks no one designed, which arise from many separate individual decisions.

partial equilibrium.text: An analysis of equilibrium in a single market that holds everything else constant except the one change being studied.

general equilibrium theory.text: The branch of economics that studies supply, demand and prices across a whole economy of many linked markets, seeking to show that together they reach an overall equilibrium.

residual demand curve.text: The demand facing one particular firm: the market demand left unmet by other firms at each price.

concentration ratio.text: The combined market share of the largest few firms in a market, such as the top four.

arc elasticity.text: An elasticity measured between two points on a demand curve, using the average of the two prices and the two quantities as the base.

price floor.text: A limit, set by government or another body, on the lowest price that may be charged for a product or service.

excess supply.text: A situation where sellers want to sell more of a good than buyers want to buy, because the price is above its equilibrium level; also called a market surplus or glut.

factor market.text: A market where the inputs to production, such as land, labour and capital, are bought and sold.

monopsony.text: A market with a single dominant buyer, the buying-side mirror of a monopoly; an oligopsony has a few dominant buyers.

derived demand.text: Demand for an input that comes from demand for the final product it helps make.

herfindahl index.text: A measure of how concentrated a market is, found by adding up the squares of every firm's market share.

walrasian auction.text: An ascending auction that finds a competitive equilibrium by raising the price of any item more than one buyer wants until each item is wanted by at most one buyer.

lerner index.text: A measure of market power: the gap between price and marginal cost as a share of price, named after economist Abba Lerner.

veblen good.text: A luxury good whose demand rises as its price rises, because a high price signals status.

economic surplus.text: The total gain that buyers and sellers get from trading in a market, made up of consumer surplus and producer surplus; also called total or social welfare.

minimum wage.text: A price floor for labour: the lowest hourly rate an employer is allowed by law to pay.

market mechanism.text: The way buyers and sellers exchanging money for goods, at prices that reflect value and scarcity, tends to share out goods and services well.

utility rate regulation.text: Ways regulators set the prices a utility may charge, such as average-cost pricing, rate-of-return limits and price caps.

zero-profit condition.text: The state an industry reaches when firms can enter or leave it almost freely, so that competition pushes each firm's economic profit to zero.

deadweight loss.text: The loss of society's welfare when a good is produced or consumed at a quantity where its benefit to society does not equal its cost to society.

gains from trade.text: The net benefits people or economies get when they are allowed to trade more freely with each other.

consumer surplus.text: The gap between the most a buyer would be willing to pay for something and the price they actually pay.

price discrimination.text: A pricing strategy in which the same seller charges different buyers different prices for the same or nearly the same good, according to which group they seem to belong to.

producer surplus.text: The gain sellers get when the market price is higher than the least they would accept to supply a good.

market clearing.text: The process by which a market's price settles where the amount supplied equals the amount demanded, leaving neither a surplus nor a shortage.

shortage.text: A situation in which people want to buy more of a product than is available at the going price; also called excess demand.

rule of one-half.text: A shortcut that estimates the change in consumer surplus from a small change in supply when the demand curve stays the same.

harberger's triangle.text: The triangle on a supply and demand graph that shows the deadweight loss from government intervention in an otherwise perfect market.

profit maximization.text: The process by which a firm chooses the price, inputs and output that give it the highest possible total profit.

production function.text: A technical relation showing how much output can be made from given quantities of physical inputs.

price ceiling.text: A limit, set by government or another body, on the highest price that may be charged for a product or service.

fixed cost.text: A business cost, also called overhead, that does not change with how much the business produces.

rent control.text: A price ceiling on housing rents, such as the US rent controls of the 1940s brought in under Franklin D. Roosevelt's Office of Price Administration.

long run and short run.text: In economics the short run is a period when some inputs or prices cannot yet change, while the long run is long enough for everything to adjust fully.

returns to scale.text: How much a firm's output rises, in proportion, when it increases all its inputs together in the long run.

product differentiation.text: The process of distinguishing a product from competitors' and from a firm's other products to make it more attractive to a target market.

monopolistic competition.text: A market with many producers selling products that are differentiated, for example by brand or quality, so they are not perfect substitutes.

cartel.text: A group of independent firms that agree not to compete with each other so as to raise their profits and dominate a market.

marginal product.text: The extra output gained by using one more unit of an input, such as one more worker, while other inputs stay the same.

theory of the firm.text: A set of economic theories that explain and predict the nature of firms such as businesses and corporations.

collusion.text: An agreement or secret cooperation among firms or individuals to limit competition, for example by dividing a market, fixing prices or limiting output.

cournot competition.text: An economic model of an oligopoly in which firms compete by each choosing, at the same time, how much to produce.

vertical integration.text: An arrangement in which a company owns and controls several stages of its supply chain.

technological change.text: The overall process of inventing, innovating and spreading new technologies or processes.

variable cost.text: A cost that changes as the quantity a business produces changes.

average cost.text: Average cost, or unit cost, is total cost divided by the number of units produced.

bertrand competition.text: A model of oligopoly in which firms selling identical goods compete by setting prices, while buyers choose the quantities.

natural resources in production function.text: The debate over how, or whether, standard production functions should include natural resources such as energy.

diffusion of innovations.text: A theory that explains how, why and how fast new ideas and technologies spread through a social system.

economies of scale.text: The cost advantages a business gains from operating on a larger scale, so that each unit of output costs less.

isoquant.text: A curve joining all the combinations of two or more inputs that produce the same quantity of output.

transaction cost theory of the firm.term: Transaction cost theory of the firm
transaction cost theory of the firm.text: Ronald Coase's explanation that firms exist because organising some production inside a firm costs less than coordinating it through market exchange.

long-run average cost.text: The unit cost of producing a given output when every input, including buildings and machinery, can be changed.

cournot's dilemma.text: The puzzle that strong economies of scale should logically lead to monopoly, yet many industries keep numerous firms of different sizes.

external economies of scale.text: Cost savings that come from the growth of a whole industry and benefit most or all of its firms, not just one.

learning and growth economies.text: Dynamic economies of scale that come from the process of growing and from experience, rather than from size itself.

marginal revenue product rule.text: The rule that a firm maximises profit by using more of an input until the extra revenue it brings equals the input's extra cost.

stages of production.text: The three ranges into which a production function is divided according to how output per unit of the variable input changes.

marginal revenue productivity theory of.term: Marginal revenue productivity theory of wages
marginal revenue productivity theory of.text: A neoclassical model in which wages equal the marginal revenue product of labour, the extra revenue an added unit of labour brings.

asset specificity.text: Oliver Williamson's idea that firms exist because some assets are tied to each other and worth much less in any other use.

behavioural theory of the firm.text: An approach, developed by Cyert and March, that explains how decisions are actually made inside firms, going beyond neoclassical economics.

property rights theory of the firm.term: Property rights theory of the firm
property rights theory of the firm.text: The approach of Grossman, Hart and Moore that explains firm boundaries through ownership of assets when contracts are incomplete.

resource-based view of the firm.text: The view that a firm's lasting competitive advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and not substitutable.

stackelberg competition.text: A sequential game in which a leader firm chooses its quantity first and follower firms then respond, competing on quantity.

induced technological change.text: The hypothesis that policymakers can steer the direction of technical progress by changing relative input prices.

economic efficiency.text: An economy or market is efficient when it gets the most of what people want, such as well-being, out of the resources it has; economists usually mean allocative (Pareto) or productive efficiency.

neutral technical change.text: Ways of classifying technical progress by which input's productivity it raises.

technology diffusion.text: The spread of a technology through a society or industry.

shutdown rule.text: The short-run rule that a firm should keep producing as long as its revenue covers its variable costs, and shut down if it does not.

pareto efficiency.text: A situation is Pareto efficient when there is no longer any way to make one person better off without making someone else worse off.

welfare economics.text: The branch of economics that uses the tools of microeconomics to judge how well off a society is as a whole.

utilitarianism.text: A family of ethical theories holding that the right action is the one that produces the most happiness and well-being for everyone affected.

income distribution.text: How a country's total income, or GDP, is shared among its population.

social welfare function.text: A rule that ranks possible states of society from more to less desirable by combining the preferences of everyone in it.

social choice theory.text: The branch of welfare economics that studies how individual preferences can be combined into good collective decisions.

progressive tax.text: A tax whose rate rises as the taxable amount rises, so a taxpayer's average rate is lower than the marginal rate.

market distortion.text: Any departure from perfect competition that makes a market settle at a price clearly different from the competitive one, so that people pursuing their own good no longer maximize society's welfare.

distributive justice.text: The question of how a society's resources, goods and opportunities should be shared out fairly among its members.

allocative efficiency.text: A state of the economy in which the mix of goods produced matches what people want, so that society's welfare is as high as it can be.

distribution (economics).text: The way an economy's total output, income or wealth is shared out among people or among the factors of production such as labour, land and capital.

equity (economics).text: Fairness in economics: the idea of justice in how wealth, resources and taxes are shared within a society.

fundamental theorems of welfare economic.text: Two results linking markets and efficiency: competitive markets reach a Pareto efficient outcome, and any Pareto efficient outcome can be reached by a competitive market from suitable starting endowments.

productive efficiency.text: A situation in which an economy, using today's technology, cannot make more of one good without making less of another.

kaldor–hicks efficiency.text: A change counts as a Kaldor–Hicks improvement if the people who gain could, in principle, fully compensate the people who lose, even if they never actually do.

theory of the second best.text: The result that when one condition for an ideal economy cannot be met, the best remaining option may require moving other conditions away from their ideal values too.

arrow's impossibility theorem.text: Kenneth Arrow's proof that no way of combining people's rankings of options into a group ranking can meet all the basic requirements of rational choice.

capability approach.text: A way of judging human welfare by what people are actually able to do and be in leading lives they value, not just by their rights or income.

equity–efficiency trade-off.text: The conflict that arises because policies making the economy fairer usually cost some efficiency, so society must choose between the two.

excess burden of taxation.text: The economic loss a society suffers, beyond the money collected, because taxes or subsidies change how people behave; also called the deadweight loss of taxation.

cardinal social welfare functions.text: A social welfare function that takes numerical measures of each person's well-being, often income, and turns them into one number for the whole society's welfare.

constrained pareto efficiency.text: A weaker form of Pareto efficiency that recognises a planner such as a government may be unable to improve on an inefficient market outcome because it faces the same limits as everyone else.

pareto efficiency and welfare maximizati.text: The link showing that maximizing a weighted sum of everyone's utility, with positive weights, always gives a Pareto efficient allocation, and under some assumptions every efficient allocation can be found that way.

weak pareto efficiency.text: A situation is weakly Pareto efficient if no change could make every single person strictly better off.

x-inefficiency.text: The gap between a firm's actual cost of production and the minimum cost for a given output, caused by internal inefficiency.

edgeworth box.text: A diagram of a tiny market with just two goods and two consumers, where each point in the box is one way of splitting the goods between them.

lump-sum tax.text: A tax of a fixed amount that does not depend on the taxpayer's circumstances, so nothing they do can change what they owe.

causes of economic inefficiency.text: The conditions, such as monopoly, hidden information or poorly designed regulation, that keep an economy from reaching Pareto efficiency.

conditions for pareto efficiency.text: The four marginal conditions on consumption and production that must all hold for an economy to be Pareto efficient.

old (cardinal) welfare economics.text: The early neoclassical approach to welfare, built by Edgeworth, Sidgwick, Marshall and Pigou, which treated utility as measurable and added it up across people.

new welfare economics.text: The ordinal approach to welfare, based on the work of Pareto, Kaldor, Hicks and Scitovsky, which judges efficiency without measuring or comparing people's utility.

compensation principle.text: A rule in welfare economics that favours a change if those who gain from it could compensate those who lose and still leave nobody worse off.

contract curve.text: The set of final splits of two goods between two people that they could reach by trading to mutual benefit from their starting holdings; every point on it is Pareto efficient.

inequity aversion.text: People's preference for fairness and their dislike of unequal outcomes, even when it costs them.

missing market.text: A situation where a competitive market for some good would make everyone better off, yet no such market exists.

harsanyi's utilitarian theorem.text: The result that if society's choices follow the rules of rational choice under risk, the social welfare function must be the utilitarian sum of individual utilities.

condorcet paradox.text: The finding that majority voting over three or more options can go round in a circle: A beats B, B beats C, yet C beats A.

interpersonal utility comparison.text: The disputed question of whether one person's gain or loss in well-being can be measured and weighed against another's.

negative income tax.text: A system in which tax flows are inverted for incomes below a threshold, so low earners receive payments while those above pay tax.

distributive norms.text: The different rules a group can use to share out rewards and costs, such as equal shares, shares by contribution, or shares by need.

egalitarianism.text: The view, based on the equal worth of all people, that citizens should be treated equally in respect and concern by the state and by one another.

justice as fairness.text: John Rawls's theory, set out in A Theory of Justice, that a just society gives equal rights and liberties, equal opportunity, and arranges inequalities to benefit the least advantaged.

horizontal and vertical equity.text: Two fairness principles for taxes and public services: treat people in similar situations alike (horizontal), and treat people with more ability to pay differently (vertical).

greenwald–stiglitz theorem.text: Bruce Greenwald and Joseph Stiglitz's 1986 result that the welfare theorems fail when markets are incomplete or information is imperfect.

social planner.text: An imaginary decision-maker used in economic models who chooses everyone's allocations to maximize a social welfare function.

atkinson index.text: A measure of income inequality, developed by the British economist Anthony Atkinson, that lets the user choose how much to care about inequality.

dynamic efficiency.text: An economy is dynamically efficient when it invests less than the return to capital, so that no generation can be made better off without making another worse off.

prioritarianism.text: The ethical view that judgements of social welfare should give extra weight to benefits for people who are worse off.

independence of irrelevant alternatives.text: The principle that a choice between two options, A and B, should not depend on how anyone feels about some third, unrelated option C.

scitovsky paradox.text: The finding that the Kaldor compensation test can judge allocation A better than B and also, by the same test, B better than A.

original position.text: A thought experiment in which people choose the rules of their society from behind a 'veil of ignorance', not knowing what place they will occupy in it.

tax wedge.text: The gap a tax opens between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive for a good.

marginal cost of public funds.text: A measure of how much society loses, because taxes distort behaviour, for each extra unit of money the government raises.

non-convexity (economics).text: A breach of the convexity assumptions of basic economics, such as consumers preferring extremes over mixtures or firms with increasing returns to scale.

nuisance.text: A common-law wrong where someone's activity causes offence, annoyance or harm to others, such as a smoking chimney or loud noise.

the problem of social cost.text: Ronald Coase's 1960 law review article on the economic problem of externalities, such as pollution harming neighbours.

utility–possibility frontier.text: A curve showing the most utility one person can have for each level of utility the others have, given society's resources; the welfare counterpart of the production possibility frontier.

tax incidence.text: Who actually bears the cost of a tax, which may differ from who legally hands the money to the government.

strict liability.text: A legal rule that makes a person responsible for harm caused by their activity even when they were not at fault.

negligence.text: A failure to take the care that would be expected in similar circumstances, which makes a person liable in tort for the harm it causes.

cheapest cost avoider.text: The party able to prevent a harm at the lowest cost, to whom liability can efficiently be assigned when bargaining is hard.

coming to the nuisance.text: The question of whether someone who moves next to an existing nuisance can still complain about it.

nuisance remedies: damages and injunctio.text: The two ways courts deal with a nuisance: ordering payment of damages, or issuing an injunction to stop the activity.

internalizing externalities.text: Making those who cause an external cost bear it themselves, so their private costs line up with the costs to society.

marginal damage.text: The extra harm done to others by one more unit of a polluting activity, also called the marginal external cost.

property rules and liability rules.text: Legal rules, described by Calabresi and Melamed, under which a liability rule is a form of legalized private expropriation that can be used when transaction costs block voluntary trade.

transboundary pollution.text: Pollution produced in one country that crosses borders and harms other places.

public good.text: A good or service that no one can be kept from using and that one person's use does not reduce for others, usually supplied by government and paid for by taxes.

transaction cost.text: A cost of making a trade in a market, over and above the price of the thing traded.

excludability.text: How far the supplier of a good can stop people who have not paid from using it.

rivalry (economics).text: A good is rival when one person's use of it stops or reduces others' use of it at the same time.

common-pool resource.text: A natural or human-made resource system, such as fishing grounds or an irrigation system, that is costly but not impossible to keep people from using.

tragedy of the commons.text: The idea that when people share a resource that benefits each user at a cost to everyone, each person has a reason to overuse it, so together they use it up.

free-rider problem.text: A market failure that happens when people who benefit from a shared resource or public good pay nothing, or too little, for it.

private good.text: A useful good that its owner can keep others from using and that one person's use uses up for others.

property rights.text: The rules that decide who owns a resource or good and how it may be used.

public economics.text: The study of government policy in terms of efficiency and fairness, asking whether and how far government should take part in markets.

four types of goods.text: A grid that sorts goods by two questions, whether people can be kept from using them and whether one person's use leaves less for others.

club good.text: A good that people can be kept from using, usually by charging them, but that one person's use does not reduce for others until it gets crowded.

property.text: A system of rights that gives people legal control over valuable things, and also the valuable things themselves.

land tenure.text: The system that decides who may use land, for how long and on what conditions.

private property.text: Ownership of property by people or organizations other than the government.

georgism.text: The economic idea that people should own what they produce, but the income that comes from land and natural resources should belong equally to everyone in society.

common property regime.text: A social arrangement by which a community regulates how a shared resource is kept up, maintained and used.

solutions to the tragedy of the commons.term: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons
solutions to the tragedy of the commons.text: The range of ways, from local self-organized rules to government action, proposed for stopping people from overusing a shared resource.

open access resource.text: A resource that no one owns and that anyone can use, where what one person takes leaves less for others.

ostrom's design principles for the commo.term: Ostrom's design principles for the commons
ostrom's design principles for the commo.text: Eight conditions that Elinor Ostrom found in long-lasting community arrangements for managing shared resources.

types of property regimes.text: The main ways a resource can be held, open access, public, private or common property, sorted by whether others can be kept out and whether use leaves less for others.

bargaining.text: A kind of negotiation in which a buyer and a seller argue over the price or terms of a deal.

coase theorem.text: The claim that when one party's activity harms or helps another, the two can bargain their way to an efficient outcome, whoever starts with the property rights, provided bargaining costs are low enough.

digital public goods.text: Open-source software, data sets, AI models, standards and content that anyone can use, treated as public goods.

local public goods.text: Public goods whose benefits fall mainly on the people nearby, such as a clean office or a neighborhood crime watch, rather than equally on everyone.

lotteries for public goods.text: Funding a public good by selling lottery tickets, with all ticket money going to the good and the prize paid from outside funds.

environmental good.text: A usually unpriced good from nature or green infrastructure, such as clean air and water, landscapes, parks, rivers, forests and beaches.

public bad.text: The mirror image of a public good: something harmful that no one can avoid and that harms everyone at once, such as air pollution.

nonprofits and public goods.text: The Weisbrod model's idea that nonprofit organizations supply public goods that government leaves unprovided.

quasi-public goods and classification pr.text: Goods such as streets, libraries and education that share some traits of public goods but from which people can be excluded, and are therefore often misclassified.

global public good.text: A public good available more or less worldwide, which no one can be kept from and whose use by one does not reduce it for others.

common good (economics).text: In economics, a good that is rival (one person's use leaves less for others) but non-excludable (people cannot be kept from using it).

new institutional economics.text: A school of economics that studies the institutions, meaning the legal rules and social norms, that underlie economic activity.

adaptive governance of common-pool resou.text: A way of managing shared resources that Ostrom recommended for problems that are complex, uncertain and fragmented.

samuelson condition.text: Paul Samuelson's rule for the best amount of a public good: provide more as long as the total of everyone's extra benefit is at least the extra cost of providing it.

resource stock and flow.text: The split of a shared resource into a core stock that must be protected and a flow of units, such as fish or grass, that can be harvested from it.

transaction cost economics.text: Oliver Williamson's approach that studies the transaction itself and treats firms as structures for governing deals rather than just production machines.

assurance contract.text: An agreement in which people pledge money toward a public good only if enough others also pledge; otherwise the good is not built and the money is returned.

intellectual property as an exclusion me.term: Intellectual property as an exclusion mechanism
intellectual property as an exclusion me.text: Using laws such as copyright and patents to stop people copying an information good, turning a public good into a club good.

social sanctions against free riders.text: Punishments that group members impose on those who use a shared resource without contributing, as a way to keep cooperation going without the state.

traditional land tenure.text: Indigenous ways of holding land, which in North America rested on stewardship rather than the control at the heart of European ownership.

coasean bargaining failures.text: The practical reasons why private bargaining over harms such as pollution often fails to reach the efficient outcome the Coase theorem predicts.

efficiency and invariance versions of th.term: Efficiency and invariance versions of the Coase theorem
efficiency and invariance versions of th.text: The two separate claims inside the Coase theorem: that bargaining gives an efficient result, and that it gives the same result whoever starts with the rights.

anti-rival good.text: A good that becomes more valuable to each user the more other people use it.

comedy of the commons.text: The case where a shared resource becomes more valuable to each user the more people use it, so 'the more the merrier'.

georgism and environmental economics.text: The Georgist view that pollution is a taking from the commons, so its value should be captured for the public through taxes or quotas.

lockean labor theory of property.text: John Locke's idea that a person who mixes their labor with an unowned resource comes to own the result, as long as enough of as good quality is left for others.

social trap.text: A situation where people act for short-term personal gain in a way that, in the long run, leaves the whole group worse off.

diamond-mirrlees efficiency theorem.text: The 1971 result by Peter Diamond and James Mirrlees that production efficiency is still desirable even when a government cannot use lump-sum taxes.

nash bargaining solution.text: John Nash's answer to how two parties should split the gains from agreeing: the deal that maximizes the product of what each gains over failing to agree.

lindahl tax.text: A tax, proposed by Swedish economist Erik Lindahl, in which each person pays for a public good according to the extra benefit they get from one more unit of it.

club theory.text: The branch of economics, founded by James M. Buchanan in 1965, that studies how big a group sharing a good should be and how it should share the costs.

social dilemma.text: A situation where each person does better by acting selfishly whatever others do, yet everyone would do best if all cooperated.

commons dilemma.text: A kind of social dilemma in which people's short-term selfish interests clash with the long-term interests of the group and the common good.

res communis.text: A Roman law idea of things common to all humankind, such as air, running water, the sea and its shores, that came before modern ideas of the commons.

public trust doctrine.text: The principle that the state holds certain resources, such as the shore between high and low tide, in trust for public use, whoever owns the land beside them.

bundle of rights.text: A way of picturing property ownership as a set of separate rights, like sticks in a bundle, that can be split among different people and put back together.

usufruct.text: The right to use someone else's property, often land, and to take its fruits or profits, without owning it or being allowed to damage it.

preference revelation.text: The problem of finding out how much the public really wants a public good, when there is no market to make people show what it is worth to them.

vickrey-clarke-groves mechanism.text: One of the best-studied procedures for deciding how much of a public good to fund and who pays, based on what each person reports it is worth to them.

quadratic funding.text: A recent way to fund public goods, developed by Buterin, Hitzig and Weyl from quadratic voting, in which each contributor gives a single amount and a subsidy tops up the total.

information asymmetry.text: A situation in which one side of a deal has more or better information than the other.

moral hazard.text: A situation in which someone has a reason to take more risk because they will not bear the full cost if things go wrong.

environmental goods agreement.text: Talks among 18 World Trade Organization members, begun in 2015, to cut tariffs on goods used to protect the environment.

impure public good.text: A good that is non-rival and non-excludable only partly or only some of the time.

tragedy of the anticommons.text: The mirror image of the tragedy of the commons: when a resource has many owners who can each block its use, it ends up underused.

principal–agent problem.text: The clash of interests that arises when one party, the agent, acts on behalf of another, the principal, and may pursue its own goals instead.

adverse selection.text: A market problem in which one side of a deal knows something the other does not, and uses that hidden information to get a better bargain.

contract theory.text: The study of how people and firms design agreements with each other, usually when one side knows more than the other.

mandatory information disclosure.text: Rules that require the better-informed party to reveal information, used when voluntary disclosure does not happen.

signalling (economics).text: A way for the better-informed side to show its type believably to the other side and so reduce an information gap.

job-market signalling.text: Michael Spence's model in which job seekers show employers their hidden ability by earning education credentials.

screening (economics).text: A way for the less-informed side to get the other side to reveal private information, for example by offering a menu of choices.

the market for lemons.text: George Akerlof's 1970 paper showing how markets behave when buyers cannot judge quality, using the used-car market.

absolute and relative performance pay.text: Two ways to reward workers: in proportion to what each achieves (absolute) or by ranking workers against each other (relative).

incomplete contracts.text: Contracts that cannot spell out what happens in every possible situation, because writing a complete one would be too hard or too costly.

mechanism design.text: A branch of economics and game theory that designs rules, called mechanisms, so that good outcomes result even when the designer cannot see people's true preferences or information.

brands as quality signals.text: The use of brand reputation by firms to signal quality and reliability to buyers who cannot judge them directly.

screening in insurance markets.text: Insurers' efforts to find out how risky each customer is, and so how likely a claim is, before offering cover.

screening models in contract theory.text: Models in which a principal, facing an agent with private information about its type, offers a menu of contracts designed so different types pick different ones.

incentive compatibility.text: A property of a mechanism or set of rules under which every participant does best for themselves by reporting their true preferences.

gibbard–satterthwaite theorem.text: An impossibility result showing that, with three or more options, any rule that makes truthful reporting always worthwhile must be dictatorial.

myerson–satterthwaite theorem.text: The 1983 result that two parties who each privately know how much a good is worth to them cannot always trade it efficiently without risking a loss for one side.

standard moral hazard model.text: The basic contract-theory model in which a principal who cannot observe an agent's effort chooses a pay scheme tied to output to maximize expected profit.

revelation principle.text: The result that any outcome that can be achieved by some strategic mechanism can also be achieved by an incentive-compatible one, in which everyone simply tells the truth.

vickrey auction.text: A sealed-bid auction for a single item in which the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid.

inflation.text: Inflation is a rise in the average price of goods and services measured in money, which means each unit of money buys less.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty describes situations where information is imperfect or unknown.

expected value.text: The expected value of an uncertain quantity is the average of its possible values, each weighted by how likely it is.

expected utility hypothesis.text: The expected utility hypothesis holds that people choose between risky options by comparing the probability-weighted average of the utility of each outcome.

interest.text: Interest is the extra money a borrower pays a lender, on top of paying back the amount borrowed, at a set rate.

interest rate.text: An interest rate is the interest charged or paid each period, expressed as a share of the amount lent, deposited or borrowed.

real and nominal value.text: A nominal value is measured in plain money amounts, while a real value is measured by the goods and services that money can actually buy.

time preference.text: Time preference, also called time or delay discounting, is how much more a person values getting something sooner rather than later.

time value of money.text: The time value of money is the idea that receiving a sum of money now is generally better than receiving the same sum later.

present value.text: Present value is what a stream of expected future payments is worth as of today.

discounting.text: Discounting is the arrangement in which someone who owes money pays a charge for the right to delay the payment for a set time.

decision theory.text: Decision theory, or the theory of rational choice, uses expected utility and probability to model how people would act rationally under uncertainty.

compound interest.text: Compound interest is interest earned on both the original sum and on interest already added to it.

von neumann–morgenstern utility theorem.text: The von Neumann–Morgenstern theorem shows that rational choice under uncertainty amounts to maximising the expected value of some utility function.

intertemporal choice.text: Intertemporal choice is the study of how people value payoffs that arrive at different times, usually simplified to now versus some future date.

minimax.text: Minimax is a decision rule that picks the option whose worst possible outcome is least bad; for gains it is called maximin, maximising the minimum gain.

real interest rate.text: The real interest rate is the interest rate after allowing for inflation, while the nominal rate is the rate before that adjustment.

risk and uncertainty.text: Risk is uncertainty that has been quantified: the possible outcomes have known probabilities and some of them involve losses.

insurance.text: Insurance is protection from financial loss: for a fee, one party promises to pay another if a particular loss, damage or injury happens.

risk aversion.text: Risk aversion is the tendency to prefer a more certain outcome to a riskier one, even when the risky option pays the same or more on average.

risk premium.text: A risk premium is the extra return a person demands to accept more risk, generally the expected risky return minus the risk-free return.

cost of capital.text: The cost of capital is what a company pays for its funds, both borrowed and from shareholders, or the return investors require for providing them.

discounted cash flow.text: Discounted cash flow analysis values a security, project, company or asset by allowing for the time value of money in its expected cash flows.

internal rate of return.text: The internal rate of return (IRR) is the yearly rate of return at which the net present value of all of an investment's cash flows equals zero.

knightian uncertainty.text: Knightian uncertainty is uncertainty that cannot be measured or turned into probabilities, as distinct from measurable risk.

ambiguity aversion.text: Ambiguity aversion is a preference for risks whose odds are known over risks whose odds are unknown.

risk pooling.text: Risk pooling is gathering money from many insured people or firms so that it can pay the losses that only some of them will suffer.

determinants of market interest rates.text: Market interest rates are set in markets such as the money market, bond market and banks, and each loan's rate reflects several factors.

social discount rate.text: The social discount rate is the discount rate used to value money spent on public or social projects.

annuity.text: An annuity is a series of equal payments made at regular intervals, usually for a limited term.

stochastic dominance.text: Stochastic dominance is a way of ranking risky options so that one is preferred by every decision maker in a broad class, even when their exact utility function is unknown.

discount rate.text: The discount rate is the rate at which the charge for delaying a payment must grow as the delay gets longer.

bayesian probability.text: An interpretation of probability as a reasonable expectation or personal belief representing a state of knowledge, rather than a frequency.

capital asset pricing model.text: The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) gives the return an asset should be expected to earn, given how much it moves with the overall market.

pure time preference debate.text: Pure time preference is the assumption that an experience, or a life, is intrinsically worth more the sooner it occurs, and whether society should use it is disputed.

discounting in climate economics.text: The choice of discount rate for the benefits of cutting greenhouse gas emissions is a highly controversial question in climate economics.

real options valuation.text: Real options valuation applies the methods used to price financial options to decisions about investing in real projects.

risk neutrality.text: Risk neutral preferences are neither risk averse nor risk seeking: the person cares only about the expected payoff, not how uncertain it is.

climateflation.text: Climateflation is inflation driven by climate change, through its effects on food production and supply chains.

inflation targeting.text: Inflation targeting is a monetary policy in which the central bank keeps adjusting its interest rate to steer inflation towards an official target.

theories of inflation.text: Economists have long debated what causes inflation, with competing theories such as the quantity theory of money and the real bills doctrine.

interest rates and monetary policy.text: Central banks set target interest rates as a main tool for influencing investment, inflation and unemployment.

exponential discounting.text: Exponential discounting is a discount function in which value falls by the same proportion for each extra unit of delay.

hyperbolic discounting.text: Hyperbolic discounting is a model of how people devalue delayed rewards in which their choices are not consistent over time.

liquidity preference.text: Liquidity preference is the tendency of people and firms to prefer holding cash or easily sold assets over harder-to-convert investments.

negative interest rate.text: A negative interest rate charges savers for holding money and has been described as a tax on holding money.

discount function.text: A discount function gives the weights an economic model places on rewards received at different times.

dynamic inconsistency.text: A situation in which a decision-maker's preferences change over time so that a plan made earlier becomes inconsistent with what the person wants later.

radical uncertainty.text: Radical uncertainty is uncertainty that no available means of gaining knowledge could resolve.

uncertainty in science communication.text: Scientific uncertainty is often understood differently by the public than by scientists, and can be misread as ignorance or lack of consensus.

heuristics in decision-making.text: Heuristics are shortcuts for making a decision without working out the consequences of every option.

limits of probabilistic decision theory.text: Whether probability can be replaced by something else in decision theory is a highly controversial question.

normative and descriptive decision theor.text: Decision theory splits into a normative branch about how an ideal rational decision-maker should choose and a descriptive branch about how people actually choose.

preference reversal over lotteries.text: A preference reversal occurs when people value one lottery more when pricing it but choose the other when comparing them directly.

st. petersburg paradox.text: The St. Petersburg paradox is a coin-flipping game with an infinite expected payoff that people will nonetheless pay only a little to play.
