fen.text: A fen is a peat-building wetland fed by mineral-rich groundwater or surface water.

wetland products.text: Wetlands naturally produce plants, fish and other goods that people harvest for their own use and for sale.

wetland water purification.text: Wetlands clean water by taking up nutrients and trapping sediment and the pollutants attached to it.

urban ecosystem.text: An urban ecosystem is the ecosystem of a city, town or industrial area, a complex patchwork of buildings, roads, parks and gardens created and maintained by people.

wetlands for wastewater treatment.text: Natural and specially built (constructed) wetlands can be used to treat sewage and other wastewater.

thermogenic and biogenic methane.text: Methane is generated by geological, biological or industrial routes.

wetland methane feedback.text: Wetlands are the largest natural source of atmospheric methane, about 20-30% of the total.

forest ecosystem services.text: Forests provide many benefits to the planet and to people, from oxygen and carbon storage to water regulation, soil protection, habitat and products.

mangrove adaptations to salt and floodin.term: Mangrove adaptations to salt and flooding
mangrove adaptations to salt and floodin.text: Mangroves have evolved special roots, leaves and seeds that let them cope with salty water, waterlogged mud and tides.

mangrove carbon storage.text: Mangrove forests take up carbon and lock it away in their wood and sediments, making them an important store of coastal 'blue carbon'.

mangroves as fish nurseries.text: The tangle of mangrove roots forms a sheltered underwater habitat where young fish and other sea animals grow up.

threats to forest ecology.text: Forests are threatened mainly by clearing for timber, land, mining, cities and farming, and by climate change.

sediment and coral reef stress.text: Coastal development in a watershed is a primary cause of sediment-related stress on coral reefs.

sediment transport.text: Sediment transport is the movement of sediment by flowing water, wind or ice, set by the strength of the flow and the particle's size, volume, density and shape.

hydrological models.text: Hydrological models are simplified conceptual representations of part of the hydrologic cycle, used for prediction and for understanding processes.

remote sensing in hydrology.text: Remote sensing gives information on hydrologic processes where in situ sensors are sparse, and over large spatial extents.

statistical hydrology.text: Statistical hydrology provides statistical methods to analyse and model parts of the hydrological cycle.

abiotic factors in aquatic ecosystems.text: The non-living conditions that shape aquatic life, such as substrate, depth, nutrients, temperature, salinity and flow.

lake ecosystem.text: A still-water (lentic) freshwater ecosystem of a lake or pond, with its living things and physical and chemical conditions.

marine coastal ecosystem.text: A marine ecosystem where the land meets the ocean.

coral reef.text: A coral reef is an underwater ecosystem built by reef-building corals, colonies of tiny animals called polyps held together by calcium carbonate.

seagrass.text: Seagrasses are the only flowering land-plant group that grows in the sea, usually forming meadows in shallow, sheltered coastal waters.

salt marsh.text: A salt marsh is a coastal wetland between land and sea that is regularly flooded by tides and covered with dense salt-tolerant herbs, grasses or low shrubs.

kelp forest.text: A kelp forest is an underwater area densely grown with kelp, a large brown seaweed; smaller patches are called kelp beds.

coral reef ecosystem services.text: Coral reefs give people valuable services, chiefly tourism, fisheries and protection of coastlines.

seagrass meadow.text: An underwater ecosystem made up of seagrasses, flowering plants that grow in shallow coastal and estuary waters.

coral reef shoreline protection.text: Coral reefs protect coastlines by absorbing wave energy before it reaches the shore.

threats to coral reefs.text: Coral reefs are threatened by nutrient pollution, warming and acidifying oceans, overfishing and destructive land and sea uses.

coral reef protection.text: Coral reefs are protected mainly through marine protected areas and limits on fishing, pollution and coastal development.

human impacts on salt marshes.text: Salt marshes have been heavily damaged by people, who long treated them as coastal wastelands to be drained, built on or polluted.

salt marshes and sea level rise.term: Salt marshes and sea level rise
salt marshes and sea level rise.text: Rising seas threaten to flood and erode salt marshes, but marshes can sometimes build themselves up fast enough to keep pace.

kelp forest ecosystem services.text: Kelp forests give people food, materials, recreation and other benefits, which are ecosystem services specific to these forests.

kelp forest trophic cascade.text: In a kelp forest trophic cascade, the loss of predators such as sea otters lets sea urchins multiply and graze away the kelp.

threats to kelp forests.text: Kelp forests are threatened mainly by overfishing, pollution, kelp harvesting, invasive species and climate change.

seagrass decline and threats.text: The worldwide loss of seagrass meadows, driven mostly by human activity.

seagrass ecosystem services.text: The goods and services seagrass meadows give coastal areas, such as cleaner water, oxygen, food and shelter.

coral farming.text: Coral farming, or coral gardening, grows coral fragments in nurseries and then replants them on damaged reefs.

coral–algae symbiosis.text: Coral polyps cannot photosynthesize themselves but live in partnership with tiny algae, called zooxanthellae, inside their tissues.

coral bleaching.text: Coral bleaching is the stress response in which corals expel the colourful symbiotic algae living in their tissues.

marine heatwave.text: A period of abnormally high sea surface temperatures compared with typical temperatures for a given season and place.

types of coral reef.text: Coral reefs are classed by shape and setting, classically as fringing reefs, barrier reefs and atolls, with platform reefs often added.

marine surface ecosystem.text: The community of organisms (neuston) that live at the ocean's surface, such as Sargassum seaweed and floating snails.

river ecosystem.text: A flowing-water (lotic) ecosystem that drains the landscape, with its living things and physical and chemical conditions.

riparian zone.text: The strip where land meets a river or stream, with its own water-loving vegetation.

floodplain.text: A floodplain is the land beside a river, from its banks to the edges of the valley, that floods when the river runs high.

wetland flood control.text: Floodplains and other wetlands act as natural storage reservoirs that soak up excess water and so reduce flooding downstream.

floodplain ecology.text: Floodplain ecology centres on the flood pulse: the yearly cycle of flooding and drying that brings nutrients and shapes life on the floodplain.

threats to aquatic ecosystems.text: The stresses that degrade aquatic ecosystems once they exceed what the ecosystem can absorb.

estuary types by landform.text: The classes of estuary by how they formed: drowned river valleys, bar-built, fjord-type and tectonic estuaries.

estuary types by water circulation.text: The classes of estuary by how fresh and salt water mix: salt wedge, partially mixed, well-mixed, inverse and intermittent.

eutrophication of estuaries.text: Nutrient overloading of estuaries, mostly by nitrogen, that fuels algal blooms and harms plants, animals and fisheries.

human impact on estuaries.text: How pollution, overfishing, development, dams and diversions degrade estuaries.

afforestation of grasslands.text: Planting trees on grasslands, often to store carbon, can damage grasslands and the services they provide.

grassland management by fire and grazing.term: Grassland management by fire and grazing
grassland management by fire and grazing.text: Many grasslands depend on disturbances such as fire and grazing to stay open, so how they are managed can make them persist or vanish.

semi-natural grassland.text: A semi-natural grassland has wild, unsown plant communities but is kept open by human activities such as grazing and mowing.

types of grassland.text: Grasslands are grouped into broad types by climate and setting: tropical, temperate, flooded, montane, tundra and desert grasslands.

free trade and infant industry debate.term: Free trade and infant industry debate
free trade and infant industry debate.text: Economists dispute whether forced economic liberalism helps or harms industrialization in the Global South.

large marine ecosystem.text: A large marine ecosystem is an ocean region of roughly 200,000 km2 or more, defined by its seabed shape, water movement, productivity and linked food webs.

peat swamp forest.text: Peat swamp forests are tropical moist forests whose waterlogged soil stops dead leaves and wood from fully rotting, building a thick layer of acidic peat.

rainforest layers.text: Rainforests are organised into vertical layers, from forest floor and understory to canopy and emergent layer, each with its own community of plants and animals.

positive feedback in socioeconomic syste.text: Self-reinforcing loops in markets, populations and institutions, where an outcome strengthens its own cause.

riparian zone ecosystem services.text: The benefits riparian zones provide, from slowing floods and filtering runoff to wildlife habitat and recreation.

riparian buffers in logging.text: Leaving riparian strips undisturbed during timber harvesting so they keep protecting the stream.

riparian zone restoration.text: Repairing damaged riverbanks through removing human structures, active rehabilitation, or simply giving them time.

boreal fire regime.text: Fire is the main disturbance that renews boreal forest stands, and an area's fire regime describes the type, size and frequency of its fires.

floodplain flood control.text: Floodplain flood control covers the rules, maps, insurance and works used to limit flood damage to people living on floodplains.

floodplain formation.text: Most floodplains are built by rivers depositing sediment, both on the inside of their bends and when floods spill over the banks.

floodplain phosphorus retention.text: Floodplains can store phosphorus in their soils and plants, keeping it from overloading rivers downstream.

detritus cycle.text: The detritus cycle is a food chain linking detritivores, detritus and the microorganisms that multiply on it.

mosquito ditching of salt marshes.text: In the early 20th century people dug straight ditches through salt marshes, believing that draining them would reduce mosquitoes.

salt marsh restoration.text: Salt marsh restoration brings damaged or reclaimed marshes back toward their natural state, a practice that has grown since the 1980s.

nitrogen loading in salt marshes.text: Nitrogen loading is the extra nitrogen from sewage, urban runoff and farm and industrial waste that flows into salt marshes and changes their plant life.

salt marsh formation.text: A salt marsh forms when mudflats build up with sediment until tides flood them less often, letting plants take root.

salt marsh land reclamation.text: Land reclamation turned salt marsh into dry farmland, often by building dikes that kept the tide out.

salt marsh microbes.text: Microbes do most of the nutrient cycling and chemical processing in salt marshes, thriving in their salty, low-oxygen mud.

biological desert.text: A biological desert is a place defined by lack of life rather than lack of water.

desert dust storms.text: Sand and dust storms are natural events in arid regions where the land lacks a covering of vegetation.

desert farming.text: Traditional desert farming has long existed in North Africa, with irrigation the key where water stress limits growth.

desert solar energy.text: Deserts are increasingly seen as sources of solar energy, partly because of low cloud cover.

polar desert.text: Polar deserts are cold deserts where low precipitation and marginal evaporation, not lack of water, make them dry.

kelp carbon sequestration.text: Kelp takes up carbon as it grows, and when it sinks to the deep ocean floor that carbon can stay stored away from human disturbance.

kelp forest structure.text: A kelp forest is built in layers, from tall canopy kelps reaching the surface down to kelps and algae on the sea floor, and this structure decides which species live there.

forest stand development stages.text: In forest dynamics, a stand passes through stand-replacing disturbance, stand initiation, stem exclusion and understory reinitiation before reaching old growth.

old growth in logging economics.text: In logging terms, an old-growth stand is one past the economic optimum age for harvesting, usually 80 to 150 years depending on species.

mire, bog and fen.text: A mire is a peatland still forming peat; its two types are bogs, fed only by rain, and fens, fed by groundwater.

palm oil plantations on peatland.text: In Southeast Asia, large areas of peatland forest have been drained and cleared for palm oil, trading economic gains against carbon, fire and biodiversity losses.

tropical peatland fires.text: Drained and cleared tropical peatlands, especially in Southeast Asia, burn increasingly often, releasing huge amounts of carbon dioxide.

peat extraction.text: Cutting peat from bogs to burn as fuel or to sell as a garden soil improver.

threats to bogs.text: The drying, drainage and warming that are degrading bogs, which take thousands of years to form and are very hard to recover.

types of bog.text: The classes of bog defined by landscape position, water source and nutrient supply, such as valley, raised, blanket and quaking bogs.

methane hydrate feedback.text: Methane hydrates are frozen compounds in which a large amount of methane is trapped in a water crystal structure, usually beneath ocean-floor sediments.

planck response.text: The Planck response is the extra thermal radiation objects emit as they warm, the most fundamental stabilizing feedback in the climate system.

seagrass coastal protection.text: How seagrass leaves and roots calm waves and hold sediment, protecting coasts from erosion and storm surge.

seagrass nursery habitat for fisheries.text: The role of seagrass meadows as sheltered nurseries for young fish and shellfish that later support fisheries.

seagrass restoration.text: Re-establishing lost seagrass beds by transplanting plants or sowing seeds and other propagules.

seagrass wasting disease.text: A disease of eelgrass, the most widespread seagrass, caused by the marine slime mold Labyrinthula zosterae.

pelagic depth zones.text: The open ocean is divided by depth into five layers: epipelagic, mesopelagic, bathypelagic, abyssopelagic and hadopelagic.

biomagnification.text: Biomagnification is the rise in the concentration of a chemical or metal as it moves up from one trophic level to the next.

hyperaccumulator plants.text: Hyperaccumulators are plants that concentrate certain elements or their ions far above neighbouring plants.

mangrove forest.text: Mangrove forests are productive wetlands of salt-tolerant trees growing in tropical and subtropical intertidal zones.

permafrost thaw feedback.text: As warming thaws permafrost, stored carbon is released as greenhouse gases that cause more warming and more thaw, a positive feedback.

muirburn.text: Muirburn is the burning of large areas of grouse moor in northern Great Britain.

savanna burning for emissions abatement.text: Controlled burns on Australian savannas can produce a long-term cumulative reduction in greenhouse gas emissions.

intertidal zone.text: The intertidal zone is the shore area exposed to air at low tide and covered by seawater at high tide.

vegetated coastal ecosystems.text: Vegetated coastal ecosystems are plant-dominated shore habitats, chiefly seagrass beds, mangrove forests and tidal marshes.

seagrass blue carbon.text: The carbon dioxide seagrass meadows pull from the air and bury in seabed sediment, part of coastal blue carbon.

mudflat.text: Mudflats, or tidal flats, are coastal wetlands formed in intertidal areas where tides or rivers have deposited sediment.

outwelling hypothesis.text: The outwelling hypothesis holds that carbon exported from mangroves as organic matter feeds detritus-based food webs in nearby coastal habitats.

coral–seagrass–mangrove connectivity.text: Coral reefs, seagrasses and mangroves are linked systems that shield one another and exchange fish and invertebrates.

criticism of fsc certification.text: FSC has been criticized since its founding, including by NGOs that withdrew their support.

fsc certification labels.text: FSC offers forest management certification and chain of custody certification, and only chain of custody holders may use FSC labels.

non-state market driven governance.text: Non-state market driven governance is environmental governance outside state regulation that uses the market to drive sustainable management; FSC is a leading example.

effects of ocean deoxygenation on fisher.term: Effects of ocean deoxygenation on fisheries
effects of ocean deoxygenation on fisher.text: How shrinking oxygen habitat changes where fish live and how fisheries perform.

oxygen minimum zones.text: Parts of the open ocean with naturally low oxygen because biological use outpaces oxygen supply.

anaerobic oxidation of methane.text: Anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM), or reverse methanogenesis, is the oxidation of methane by some organisms, functionally reversing methanogenesis.

enteric methane from ruminants.text: In the rumen, methanogens help digest cellulose, and methane leaves the animal mainly by belching.

cobra effect.text: A perverse result in which an apparent solution makes the problem worse, named for a bounty on cobras.

animal and plant biomonitors.text: Plants and animals serve as biomonitors because their tissues or populations change measurably with pollution.

benthic macroinvertebrate indicators.text: Macroinvertebrates are convenient indicators of the ecological health of water bodies and terrestrial ecosystems.

microbial indicators of contamination.text: Indicator bacteria may not be pathogenic themselves, but their presence in waste may signal other pathogens.

bush control.text: Actions that manage the density and composition of bushes and shrubs, to cut risks such as wildfire or rehabilitate land.

bog–rich-fen gradient.text: The bog–rich-fen gradient arranges peatlands from species-poor bogs, through poor fens, to species-rich fens.

river continuum concept.text: The river continuum concept is a framework describing how temperate river ecosystems change in function from small headwaters to large rivers.

allochthonous and autochthonous carbon.text: Allochthonous carbon and nutrients come from outside an aquatic system, while autochthonous carbon comes from within it, such as algae.

aquatic metabolism and dissolved oxygen.text: Dissolved oxygen in water is raised by photosynthesis and wind mixing and lowered by aerobic respiration.

lake trophic classification.text: Lakes can be classified by a trophic state index according to their nutrient levels and primary production.

nutrient limitation in freshwater.text: Phosphorus is a limiting factor for phytoplankton growth because its concentration in water is generally low.

tropical limnology.text: Tropical limnology studies the physical, chemical, biological and cultural aspects of freshwater systems in tropical regions.

dryland restoration.text: Deliberate work to help degraded drylands recover, either by restoring their former function or by preventing further decline.

desertification narrative debate.text: The dispute over whether the dominant story of spreading deserts, especially in the Sahel, is accurate.

dryland ecosystem services.text: The food, livelihoods, carbon storage and biodiversity that drylands provide to local people and the world.

dryland sub-types.text: The four classes of dryland by aridity: dry sub-humid, semi-arid, arid and hyper-arid lands.

drylands and climate change.text: How climate change and human activity degrade drylands, bringing more drought, desertification and erosion.

indigenous knowledge in dryland restorat.text: Using local and indigenous knowledge and community involvement to protect and restore drylands.

restoration islands.text: A restoration method that plants small, well-placed patches which then spread into the land around them.

sustainable rangeland management.text: Managing and restoring grazing lands so they keep producing while storing carbon and resisting desertification.

controls on wetland methane flux.text: The factors that set how much methane a wetland releases, such as water table, temperature, soil and plants.

wetland drainage and greenhouse gases.text: How draining wetlands for development, housing and farming changes their methane emissions.

wetland methane emission pathways.text: The three main routes by which wetland methane reaches the air: diffusion, transport through plant tissue, and bubbling (ebullition).

intact forest landscape.text: An intact forest landscape is a large, unbroken natural forest area with no sign of significant human activity or fragmentation.

aridity index.text: An aridity index is a numerical indicator of how dry the climate is at a given place.

seascape ecology.text: The study of the causes and ecological consequences of spatial pattern in the marine environment, using landscape ecology frameworks.

lake zones.text: Lakes are commonly divided into a shallow shoreline (littoral) zone, an open sunlit water zone and a dark deep-water zone.

lake stratification and turnover.text: In large lakes, summer warming splits the water into a warm upper layer and a cold lower layer that stay apart until autumn cooling mixes them again.

coarse woody debris.text: Coarse woody debris is dead wood such as fallen trunks and branches, which decays slowly on the forest floor.

forest biomass.text: Forests build up large amounts of living plant material, or biomass, and many do so quickly, making them highly productive.

mycorrhizal networks in forests.text: A mycorrhizal network is a partnership in which fungi and plants share resources through connections in the soil.

deep-sea zones.text: The depth bands of the deep ocean: the bathyal, abyssal and hadal zones.

hydrothermal vent communities.text: Deep-sea communities around hydrothermal vents that are powered by chemosynthetic bacteria rather than sunlight.

boreal ecosystem services.text: The services boreal ecosystems provide, led by timber and climate regulation through carbon cycling.

climate change in boreal ecosystems.text: How warming changes boreal ecosystems and how their changes feed back on the climate.

environmental problems of urban ecosyste.text: Growing cities face pollution, loss of green space, habitat fragmentation, invasive species, urban heat and disease.

green and blue infrastructure.text: Green and blue infrastructure means building in ways that weave natural systems such as vegetation and water into human-made structures.

urban ecosystem services research.text: Urban ecology, including the study of the services that urban nature provides, is a young field whose research is still limited and unevenly spread.

millennium ecosystem assessment.text: A major United Nations-backed study of how people affect the environment, called for in 2000, launched in 2001 and published in 2005.

economics of ecosystem services.text: The effort to express what ecosystem services are worth in economic terms, so that their value can be weighed in decisions.

history of the ecosystem services idea.term: History of the ecosystem services idea
history of the ecosystem services idea.text: How the idea that ecosystems provide services to people grew from ancient observations into a standard scientific term.

managing ecosystem services.text: Efforts to protect ecosystem services through policy, institutions and management, which face large practical hurdles even where services have money values.

nature's contributions to people.text: The IPBES term for all the ways nature benefits people, adopted in place of 'nature's benefits to people'.

ecological goods and services.text: The economic benefits, in goods and services, that come from the natural workings of ecosystems.

ecosystem service trade-offs.text: Cases where using or boosting one ecosystem service reduces others or harms some people, as opposed to synergies, where services rise together.

ecosystem services in life-cycle assessm.text: Using life-cycle assessment, which tracks the environmental pressures of making products, to estimate how human activities change ecosystem services.

nutrient cycle.text: A nutrient cycle is the movement of living and non-living matter back into the making of new living matter: nature's recycling system.

pollination.text: Pollination is the moving of pollen from the male part of a flower to the female part, which lets the plant make seeds.

ecosystem service decision-making.text: Making land-use choices that affect ecosystem services, which means weighing ecology, technology, society and the economy together.

beneficiaries of ecosystem services.text: The people who gain from a given ecosystem service, whether they live beside the ecosystem or feel its effects only indirectly.

nature's services (1997).text: Gretchen Daily's edited book Nature's Services: Societal Dependence on Natural Ecosystems, published in 1997, which laid out the framework widely used for understanding nature's benefits to people.

food security.text: Food security means having reliable access to enough affordable, healthy food.

groundwater recharge.text: Groundwater recharge is the downward movement of water from the surface into underground water stores.

storm surge.text: A storm surge is a coastal flood of rising seawater pushed ashore by a storm, usually a low-pressure system such as a tropical cyclone.

biological pest control.text: Biological pest control is the use of living organisms to control pests, whether animals, weeds or disease-causing organisms.

microclimate.text: A microclimate is the local set of air, soil and water conditions near the ground that differs measurably from the surrounding area.

water purification.text: Water purification is the removal of unwanted chemicals, germs, suspended solids and gases from water so it is fit for a given use.

soil formation.text: Soil formation, or pedogenesis, is the slow making of soil, shaped by place, environment and history.

bioprospecting.text: Bioprospecting is the search through living things for molecules and genetic information that could become valuable products such as drugs, cosmetics or farm inputs.

medicinal plants.text: Medicinal plants are plants used to keep people healthy or treat illness, in traditional medicine since prehistoric times and in modern medicine today.

pollinator decline.text: Pollinator decline is the drop in numbers of insect and other animal pollinators in many ecosystems around the world, recorded since the end of the 20th century.

economics of commercial honeybee pollina.text: Beekeepers rent their honeybee colonies to farmers for a fee, turning crop pollination into a service sold in a market.

firewood.text: Firewood is any wood used for fuel, usually as recognizable logs or branches rather than processed products such as pellets.

pillars of food security.text: Food security is usually broken into pillars: whether food is available, whether people can get it, how well they use it, and whether this stays stable over time.

complete recycling debate.text: A dispute over whether matter can be recycled completely, with 100% of waste rebuilt into new material without end.

ecological versus technological recyclin.text: Recycling in human industry differs from recycling in ecosystems in scale, complexity and organization.

managed aquifer recharge.text: Managed aquifer recharge means deliberately putting water back into aquifers, for example through altered streambeds, bank filtration, water spreading or recharge wells.

biotic and abiotic pollination.text: Biotic pollination uses living animals to carry pollen, while abiotic pollination relies on wind, water or rain.

pollination in agriculture.text: Many farm crops depend on pollinators, while the main staple grains such as wheat, maize and rice are pollinated by wind or by themselves.

storm surge defences.text: Communities can adapt to storm surges with hard infrastructure such as flood barriers, soft infrastructure such as dunes or mangroves, better building and social measures.

biological control strategies.text: Biological control comes in three basic strategies: importation, augmentation and conservation of natural enemies.

conservation biological control.text: Conservation biological control protects and encourages the natural enemies of pests that already live in an area.

side effects of biological control.text: An introduced control agent can harm biodiversity by attacking native species as well as the pest it was meant for.

types of seed dispersal.text: Seed dispersal is split into autochory, where the plant moves its own seeds, and allochory, where an outside agent carries them.

nursery habitat.text: A nursery habitat is a place where young marine animals live that contributes more young to the adult population per unit area than other places they use.

soil-forming factors.text: Five classic factors shape every soil: climate, organisms, relief (topography), parent material and time, remembered as CLORPT.

jenny's state equation.text: Hans Jenny's 1941 state equation describes a soil as a function of climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, with room for more factors.

bioprospecting contracts.text: Bioprospecting contracts set the rules for sharing benefits between researchers and the countries whose genetic resources they use.

causes of pollinator decline.text: Proposed causes of pollinator decline include pesticides, parasites and diseases, habitat destruction, climate change, market forces and competition with invasive species.

nutritional effects of pollinator declin.text: Losing pollinators could cut the supply of vitamins and other nutrients that come mainly from animal-pollinated crops.

ecological values of mangroves.text: Mangrove forests are a form of natural capital that yields many goods and services to coasts, local communities and society at large.

climate regulation.text: Climate regulation is the regulating ecosystem service by which nature dampens environmental change, for example by storing carbon and moderating local temperatures.

pollination management.text: Pollination management is the farming practice of ensuring or improving a crop's pollination by managing pollinators, pollen-supplying plants and conditions.

mangrove water filtration.text: Mangroves keep coastal water clean by trapping, removing and recycling nutrients, pollutants and particles from land before they reach reefs and seagrass.

watershed services.text: Watershed (hydrological) services are the water-related benefits a healthy catchment gives, such as less soil erosion, lower landslide risk and milder floods and droughts.

well-being.text: What is good for a person in itself: a measure of how well their life is going for them.

recreation.text: Leisure activity done for enjoyment, amusement or pleasure.

outdoor recreation.text: Leisure activity done outdoors, usually in natural settings.

biophilia hypothesis.text: The idea that humans have an inborn urge to seek connection with nature and other living things.

subjective well-being.text: Well-being, or happiness, as judged by the people whose lives are being assessed rather than from an outside, objective view.

aesthetics of nature.text: The branch of philosophy that studies natural things for their beauty and other aesthetic qualities.

nature connectedness.text: How far a person counts nature as part of who they are.

nature tourism.text: Travel to enjoy an area's natural attractions, including its plants and animals.

sustainable tourism.text: Tourism that attends to its economic, social and environmental effects while improving visitors' experiences and meeting the needs of host communities.

ecotourism.text: Travel to natural places that aims to do little harm and to support conservation and environmental education.

nature exposure and mental health.text: The link between spending time in natural surroundings and a person's mental health.

attention restoration theory.text: The theory that time in nature, or even views of it, helps people recover from the mental tiredness caused by sustained deliberate focus.

underdevelopment tourism.text: The idea that multinational companies control ecotourism development and take most of its gains, leaving local communities without ownership.

theories of well-being.text: The main philosophical accounts of what well-being consists of: hedonism, desire theories and objective list theories.

nature therapy.text: A broad group of treatments, also called ecotherapy, that use time in nature to improve mental or physical health.

sense of place.text: The many-sided relationship between people and places, covering what makes a place special and the attachment people feel to it.

cultural landscape.text: A landscape shaped by the long interplay of human activity and the natural environment.

therapeutic recreation.text: A profession that uses recreation's health benefits as a form of therapy.

nature positive tourism.text: Tourism that aims not just to leave no trace but to leave positive benefits for the natural world.

sacred natural site.text: A natural feature or area of land or water that holds special spiritual meaning for a people or community.

tourism carrying capacity.text: The largest number of visitors a destination can take at once without damaging its environment, economy or community or spoiling the visitor experience.

responsible tourism.text: The behaviours and practices of travellers and providers that can lead to sustainable tourism.

fractal fluency.text: A neuroscience model holding that human vision has adapted to process nature's fractal patterns, those that repeat at different scales, with ease.

indigenous kinship with nature.text: The view, common in many Indigenous cultures, that humans are part of the natural world and bound to it by kinship and reciprocity.

ecotourism management tools.text: The rules and measures used to stop ecotourism operations from damaging the places they sell, from visitor limits to certification labels.

set point theory of happiness.text: The idea that each person has an inherited baseline level of subjective well-being to which they tend to return.

beautiful, sublime and picturesque.text: Three classic ways of appreciating nature: the tame beauty of gardens, the awe of wild and threatening nature, and nature seen as picture-like scenes.

decline in nature experience.text: The probable fall in people's direct contact with nature, which earlier studies link to effects on health and on care for the environment.

nature prescriptions.text: Health-system programmes in which doctors or public agencies formally send people to spend time in nature.

nature relatedness scale.text: A 21-item questionnaire that measures how connected to nature a person feels as a lasting trait.

city parks and mental health.text: The benefit that parks inside cities bring to the mental health of the people living near them.

placelessness.text: The quality of places that lack a sense of place and feel as if they could be anywhere.

stress recovery theory.text: The idea that contact with nature helps the body and emotions recover from stress, lowering cortisol and heart rate.

limits of acceptable change.text: A visitor-management framework that monitors a site against set objectives instead of relying on a single maximum visitor number.

remote sensing.text: Gathering information about an object or area from a distance, without touching it, usually by observing Earth from satellites or aircraft.

geographic information system.text: A GIS is a combination of computer hardware and software that stores, manages, analyses, edits and displays geographic data.

landscape ecology.text: The science that studies how ecological processes relate to particular ecosystems across whole landscapes, and how to improve those relationships.

system dynamics.text: An approach to understanding how complex systems behave over time by modelling their stocks, flows, feedback loops and time delays.

ecosystem model.text: An abstract, usually mathematical, representation of an ecological system, from one population to a whole biome, studied to understand the real system.

agent-based model.text: A computer model that simulates the actions and interactions of autonomous agents, such as individuals or organisations, to understand how a whole system behaves.

land cover.text: The physical material at Earth's land surface, such as plants, concrete, buildings, bare ground or water.

normalized difference vegetation index.text: NDVI is a widely used number, calculated from red and near-infrared sensor readings, that measures how dense and healthy vegetation is.

scenario planning.text: A strategic planning method in which organizations imagine several plausible futures in order to make flexible long-term plans.

spatial analysis.text: The set of formal techniques that study things through their location, shape and geographic arrangement, drawing especially on spatial statistics.

species distribution modelling.text: Using ecological models and environmental data, most often climate, to predict where a species lives across space and time.

land change modeling.text: Land change models describe, project and explain how land use and land cover change over time.

active and passive sensors.text: The two classes of remote sensing: passive sensors record energy an object reflects or emits, while active sensors send out their own energy and measure what comes back.

lidar.text: A way of measuring distance by shining a laser at a surface and timing how long the reflected light takes to return.

false-color composite.text: An image in which wavelengths are assigned to display colours other than their true ones, to reveal patterns the eye cannot normally see.

raster and vector data.text: The two traditional ways a GIS stores geographic data: as raster images made of cells, or as vector points, lines and polygons.

remote sensing resolution.text: The quality of remote sensing data, described by its spatial, spectral, radiometric and temporal resolution.

map overlay.text: Combining several spatial datasets of the same area into a new one, like stacking maps of one region on top of each other.

gis multi-criteria decision analysis.text: Using GIS to compare alternative places, such as candidate habitat for restoration, against several criteria at once.

spatial interpolation.text: Building a continuous surface, usually a raster, by predicting values between a set of measured sample points.

bayesian network.text: A probability model that shows a set of variables and how they depend on one another as a diagram of arrows with no loops.

causal loop diagram.text: A simple map of a system's parts and how they affect each other, drawn to reveal its feedback loops.

edges and ecotones.text: An ecotone is the transition zone where two ecological communities meet, such as forest giving way to grassland.

landscape patches, corridors and matrix.text: A patch is a fairly uniform area that differs from its surroundings; patches, corridors and the background matrix together make up a landscape's mosaic.

landscape fragmentation.text: The breaking up of a habitat, ecosystem or land-use type into smaller separate pieces.

lotka–volterra predator–prey model.text: One of the earliest ecological models: a pair of equations, one for a prey species and one for its predator, describing how their numbers rise and fall together.

invest model.text: InVEST (Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Trade-offs) is free, open-source software from the Natural Capital Project for mapping and valuing ecosystem services.

i-tree.text: A suite of US Forest Service software tools that measure and value the ecosystem services trees provide in cities and the countryside.

participatory gis.text: A participatory approach to spatial planning that puts mapping tools in the hands of local people so their own knowledge shapes decisions.

modifiable areal unit problem.text: A source of statistical bias that arises because results change depending on how point data are grouped into areas such as districts or regions.

spatial autocorrelation.text: The tendency for values at nearby locations to be related to one another, either positively or negatively.

use value.text: The usefulness of a thing: the features that let it satisfy a human want or need, a concept from classical and Marxist economics.

exchange value.text: In political economy, especially Marxian economics, the proportion in which a commodity can be traded for other goods.

environmental philosophy.text: The branch of philosophy concerned with the natural environment and humans' place in it.

land change model validation.text: Checking a land change model by comparing its processes or its predicted maps with what really happened.

runoff curve number.text: An empirical number used in hydrology to predict how much rainfall runs straight off the land rather than soaking in.

anthropocentrism.text: The belief that human beings are the central or most important beings on the planet.

paradox of value.text: The puzzle, also called the diamond–water paradox, that water is far more useful for survival than diamonds, yet diamonds cost much more.

intrinsic value.text: In ethics, the value something has in itself, for its own sake, rather than as a means to something else.

instrumental and intrinsic value.text: The philosophical distinction between what is good as a means to an end and what is good as an end in itself.

deep ecology.text: An environmental philosophy holding that all living beings have worth regardless of their usefulness to people, and that society should be reshaped to match.

ecocentrism.text: A nature-centred rather than human-centred system of values.

biocentrism.text: The environmental ethic that gives equal inherent value to all living things.

values of nature.text: The ways societies see importance in the non-human world, grouped as extrinsic (instrumental), intrinsic and relational values.

technocentrism.text: A set of values centred on technology, holding that humans can control nature and solve environmental problems through science.

direct damage-cost valuation.text: Valuing environmental improvement as the reduction in the monetary damage costs of pollution.

social ecology.text: Murray Bookchin's 1982 philosophy linking how humans treat nature to how they treat each other.

rights of nature.text: The legal recognition of nature as having rights of its own, an application of biocentric values in law.

total economic value.text: The full value people get from a natural resource, heritage site or infrastructure compared with not having it, built up from several kinds of value.

non-use value.text: The value people place on a good, often a natural resource, even if they never have used it and never will.

existence value.text: The benefit people get simply from knowing that something, such as Antarctica, the Grand Canyon or an endangered species, exists.

non-market goods.text: Goods that are not bought and sold in markets, such as most environmental goods: clean air, clean water, landscapes, parks, rivers and forests.

revealed preference.text: A way of working out what people prefer from the choices they actually make, pioneered by Paul Samuelson in 1938.

option value.text: What people are willing to pay to keep a public asset or service available even if they are unlikely ever to use it.

bequest value.text: The satisfaction people get from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations.

direct and indirect use value.text: The split of use value into direct use, from goods taken from nature, and indirect use, from benefits nature provides without anything being removed.

relational values.text: Values arising from the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature.

ecosystem valuation.text: The process of assigning a value, in money, physical units or other terms, to an ecosystem or the services it provides.

hedonic regression.text: A revealed preference method that estimates the value of each characteristic of a good, such as a house, by breaking its price into contributions from its features.

willingness to accept.text: The smallest amount of money a person would take to sell a good or service, or to put up with a harm such as pollution.

travel cost analysis.text: A revealed preference method that values a place without a market price, such as a national park or beach, from what visitors spend in time and money to get there.

weak axiom of revealed preference.text: A consistency rule saying that if a consumer picks a over b when both are affordable, they will never pick b over a when both are affordable.

contingent valuation.text: A survey-based technique for putting a money value on things that are not sold in markets, such as a protected environment or the harm done by pollution.

stated preference methods.text: Valuation methods that measure what people value by asking them directly in surveys, rather than watching what they buy.

afriat's theorem.text: A 1967 result by Sydney Afriat proving that a finite set of observed choices satisfying GARP can be explained by a utility function.

benefit transfer.text: A valuation method that estimates a project's benefits by borrowing the data, models and results of earlier studies of similar projects or sites.

replacement cost.text: The amount one would have to pay at today's prices to replace an asset with an undamaged equivalent.

choice modelling.text: A family of methods that model how a person or group decides, using either their real choices or choices they state in a set context.

noaa panel on contingent valuation.text: A panel of leading economists, chaired by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow, convened by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to judge whether contingent valuation surveys could be trusted.

embedding effect.text: A bias in contingent valuation where people struggle to put a value on one public good that is part of a larger set of similar goods.

wta–wtp gap.text: The finding that people ask far more to give something up than they would pay to get it, even though standard theory predicts the two amounts should match.

compensating differential.text: The extra pay a worker must be offered to take an unpleasant or risky job instead of other jobs they could do.

discrete choice.text: Models that describe and predict choices between separate alternatives, such as which mode of transport to take, rather than how much of something to buy.

normal distribution.text: The bell-shaped probability distribution defined by a mean, which sets its location, and a variance, which sets its squared scale.

central limit theorem.text: Under fairly common conditions, the sum of many random variables is approximately normally distributed.

random utility model.text: A random utility model describes a person's preferences when their choices are not fixed but depend on a random, unobserved state.

conjoint analysis.text: A survey-based statistical technique, mainly from market research, that works out how much people value each attribute that makes up a product or service.

multinomial logistic regression.text: Multinomial logistic regression is a statistical method that predicts the probabilities of more than two unordered outcomes from a set of explanatory variables.

exxon valdez oil spill.text: The Exxon Valdez oil spill was a major environmental disaster in Prince William Sound, Alaska, on March 24, 1989.

probit model.text: A probit model is a regression model for a dependent variable that can take only two values, built on the normal distribution.

mixed logit.text: Mixed logit is a fully general statistical model for analysing discrete choices, in which tastes are allowed to vary randomly between people.

best–worst scaling.text: Best–worst scaling is a survey choice method in which respondents pick the best and the worst item from a subset of a longer list.

scope neglect.text: Scope neglect is a cognitive bias in which the value people place on a problem does not grow in proportion to its size.

cheap talk.text: In game theory, cheap talk is costless communication between players whose messages do not directly change the game's payoffs.

hypothetical bias.text: Hypothetical bias is the distortion in values people state in surveys about goods they do not actually have to pay for or give up.

latent class model.text: A latent class model is a statistical model that sorts multivariate discrete data into hidden groups, or classes.

meta-regression.text: Meta-regression is a meta-analysis that uses regression to combine and compare findings from many studies while adjusting for study characteristics.

cost–benefit analysis.text: A systematic way of judging alternatives by estimating and comparing their benefits and their costs.

regulation.text: Regulation is the management of complex systems according to a set of rules and trends.

net present value.text: A way to judge an investment by turning all its future gains and costs into today's money and adding them up.

cost-effectiveness analysis.text: A form of economic analysis that compares the costs and the outcomes of different courses of action without putting a money value on the outcomes.

shadow price.text: A money value given to something that is not traded in a market, or a market price corrected for distortions and social effects.

value of a statistical life.text: A money value for avoiding one death on average, based on what people will pay for small reductions in their risk of dying.

quality-adjusted life year.text: A measure of health that combines how long and how well people live, where one unit equals one year in perfect health.

discounting in cost–benefit analysis.text: Putting costs and benefits that occur at different times on a common footing by converting them to present values with a discount rate.

criticisms of cost–benefit analysis.text: Objections that cost–benefit analysis ignores who gains and who loses, discounts the future too heavily and leaves out values that cannot be priced.

multiple-criteria decision analysis.text: A field of decision science that explicitly weighs several conflicting criteria, such as cost and quality, when choosing among options.

disability-adjusted life year.text: A measure of disease burden in which one unit equals one year of healthy life lost to illness, disability or early death.

regulatory impact analysis.text: A document prepared before a new government regulation is introduced that systematically appraises its likely impacts.

cost–benefit analysis in us regulation.text: The rise of mandatory cost–benefit review of federal rules in the United States from 1981 onward.

distributional weights in cost–benefit a.text: Weights applied to gains and losses so that a dollar to a poor person counts for more than a dollar to a rich one.

history of cost–benefit analysis.text: The development of cost–benefit analysis from a nineteenth-century engineering idea into a standard tool of government.

risk and uncertainty in cost–benefit ana.term: Risk and uncertainty in cost–benefit analysis
risk and uncertainty in cost–benefit ana.text: The ways a cost–benefit analysis handles uncertain outcomes, chiefly with probability, sensitivity analysis and simulation.

deregulation.text: Deregulation is the process of removing or reducing state regulations, typically in the economic sphere.

pitfalls in cost estimation.text: Careful cost estimates for a policy must avoid several common mistakes: ignoring opportunity costs, using the wrong counterfactual, counting non-additional costs and ignoring market changes.

regulatory state.text: The regulatory state is the expansion in the state's use of rulemaking, monitoring and enforcement techniques and institutions.

mild and wild risk.text: Mandelbrot distinguished mild risk, which follows normal or near-normal distributions, from wild risk, which follows fat-tailed distributions.

risk society.text: Giddens and Beck argued that modern societies face manufactured risks, such as pollution, produced by modernization itself, not only external risks from non-human forces.

payback period.text: The time an investment takes to earn back the money spent on it, or to reach the break-even point.

cost-effectiveness of energy efficiency.text: Using cost-effectiveness analysis to price the energy saved by an efficiency investment, in dollars per kilowatt-hour.

shadow price in constrained optimization.text: The change in the best achievable value of an objective when a constraint is relaxed by one small unit.

dose–response relationship.text: How strongly an organism or biological system responds as a function of how much of a substance or stressor it is exposed to.

multiple-criteria evaluation and design.text: The main split of multi-criteria problems, according to whether the options are listed in advance or only implicitly defined.

nondominated solution.text: An option that cannot be improved on one criterion without being made worse on another.

benefit–cost ratio.text: A summary indicator in cost–benefit analysis: a project's discounted benefits divided by its discounted costs, both in money.

risk–benefit ratio.text: The ratio of the risks of an action to its potential benefits.

project appraisal.text: A structured assessment of whether a project or proposal should go ahead, or whether it is viable.

transfers versus real costs.text: A cost total should count only real changes in behavior or resource use, not transfers of money from one party to another.

incremental cost-effectiveness ratio.text: The extra cost of one option over another divided by the extra effect it delivers.

environmental ethics.text: The branch of practical philosophy that sets out the kinds of argument that can be made for protecting nature and using natural resources sustainably.

commodification of nature.text: A critical field of research on how natural things and processes are made tradable in markets, and what follows from that.

animal rights.text: The philosophy that many or all sentient animals have moral worth apart from their usefulness to people, and that their basic interests, such as avoiding suffering, deserve the same consideration as similar human interests.

lexicographic preferences.text: Preferences in which a person prefers any amount of one good to any amount of another, looking at the second good only to break ties.

land ethic.text: A framework for how, ethically, people should regard the land.

critiques of commodifying nature.text: The objections to turning nature into commodities, which fall into practical, moral and consequential problems.

market environmentalism.text: The view, prominent in environmental policy since the late 1980s, that environmental damage comes from nature lacking prices and that markets can fix it.

value pluralism.text: The idea that there are several basic values that can all be right and yet conflict with one another.

commensurability.text: Whether two values share a common measure; incommensurable values have no common standard or cannot be compared in a certain way.

fictitious commodities.text: Karl Polanyi's term for things treated as market commodities though not made for sale: land, labour and money.

ecological modernization.text: A school of thought arguing that the state and the market can work together to protect the environment.

value of earth.text: The net worth of the planet, a disputed idea both in what 'value' means and in what counts as 'Earth'.

conservation ethics.text: Valuing the environment only for its usefulness to people, and protecting it as a means to human welfare.

ecologic extension.text: An approach to environmental ethics that stresses the interdependence and diversity of living things and gives intrinsic value to whole ecosystems.

ethical theories applied to nature.text: How the main theories of right action, consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics, are used to reason about the environment.

utilitarian and libertarian land ethics.text: Land ethics that judge land use by the greatest good for people, or by individual property rights and freedom.

accumulation by dispossession.text: David Harvey's term for a new wave of enclosing the commons in which natural assets are released to capital at very low or no cost.

second contradiction of capitalism.text: James O'Connor's idea that capitalism degrades the environmental 'conditions of production' it depends on but cannot produce itself.

deliberative monetary valuation.text: A set of approaches that combine individual willingness-to-pay valuation of environmental damage or protection with group discussion methods.

social ecological economics.text: A proposed paradigm shift in ecological economics that integrates social, ecological and economic knowledge.

small-improvement argument.text: An argument that two options are incomparable: if a tiny gain to one does not make it better than the other, they cannot have been exactly equal.

beyond gdp.text: Beyond GDP is the push to develop broad measures of economic well-being that go further than GDP and other national income figures.

gross national happiness.text: Gross National Happiness (GNH) is a philosophy followed by Bhutan's government, with an index measuring a population's collective happiness and well-being.

human development (economics).text: Human development is a view of progress that widens economic development to include social, political and even ethical dimensions.

human development index.text: The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite score of life expectancy, schooling and income per person, used to rank countries into four tiers of human development.

green gross domestic product.text: Green GDP is a measure of economic growth that subtracts the environmental consequences of that growth from a country's ordinary GDP.

stiglitz-sen-fitoussi commission.text: The Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress, known as the Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission, was an inquiry set up by the French government in 2008.

inclusive wealth.text: Inclusive wealth is the total value of all capital assets in a place, including human, social, public and natural capital.

wellbeing economy.text: A wellbeing economy is a public policy framework in which the economy is designed to serve social, health, cultural, fairness and nature outcomes.

happiness economics.text: Happiness economics is the study of happiness, well-being, life satisfaction and quality of life, linking economics with psychology, sociology and health.

adjusted net saving.text: Adjusted net saving, or genuine savings, is ordinary net saving minus the value of resource depletion and environmental damage plus investment in human capital.

world happiness report.text: An annual publication that ranks national happiness from people's own ratings of their lives and correlates them with quality-of-life factors.

oecd better life index.text: The OECD Better Life Index, launched in May 2011, is an OECD tool that measures several dimensions of economic and social progress beyond GDP.

social progress index.text: The Social Progress Index, created by the Social Progress Imperative, measures the real-life outcomes people experience across many social and environmental indicators.

green gdp in china.text: China's green GDP experiment was a national attempt, announced in 2004, to replace GDP with green GDP as a performance measure for top officials.

beyond gdp conference and eu actions.term: Beyond GDP conference and EU actions
beyond gdp conference and eu actions.text: The 'Beyond GDP' conference of 2007, hosted by the European Commission, European Parliament, Club of Rome, OECD and WWF, sought wider measures of progress to guide policy.

uk measuring national well-being program.text: The Measuring National Well-being programme, launched in the UK in 2010 and led by the Office for National Statistics, aims to build trusted measures of the nation's well-being.

new zealand wellbeing budget.text: New Zealand's Wellbeing Budget, launched in May 2019, was the country's first budget built around people's wellbeing and the environment rather than GDP alone.

environmental functions.text: Environmental functions are the possible uses of our non-human-made physical surroundings, on which people depend for producing, consuming, breathing and recreation.

sustainable national income.text: Sustainable national income (SNI) estimates the highest production level at which, with that year's technology, vital environmental functions stay available for ever.

easterlin paradox.text: The Easterlin paradox is the finding that richer people in a country report more happiness than poorer ones, yet average happiness does not rise as the nation's average income grows.

inequality-adjusted human development in.text: The inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI), introduced in the 2010 Human Development Report, discounts the HDI for inequality to show the actual level of human development.

measure of economic welfare.text: The Measure of Economic Welfare (MEW), introduced by William Nordhaus and James Tobin in 1972, was the first model to estimate households' real yearly consumption as a welfare measure.

index of sustainable economic welfare.text: The Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW) is an economic indicator proposed as a replacement for GDP, the main headline figure of national accounts.

genuine progress indicator.text: The genuine progress indicator (GPI) is a measure proposed to replace or supplement GDP by counting environmental and social factors that GDP leaves out.

green national product.text: The green national product is a measure that folds environmental degradation and resource depletion into a country's national product.

defensive expenditures.text: In environmental accounting, defensive expenditures are spending meant to limit possible damage to oneself.

environmental accounting.text: A branch of accounting that measures, analyses and reports money and non-money information about environmental impacts.

natural capital accounting.text: The process of calculating the total stocks and flows of natural resources and services in an ecosystem or region.

asset.text: In financial accounting, any resource a business or other economic entity owns or controls.

triple bottom line.text: An accounting framework that judges an organisation on three results: social, environmental and economic.

green accounting.text: Accounting that tries to bring environmental costs into the financial results of an activity.

environmental full-cost accounting.text: A cost-accounting method that gathers the possible environmental costs and benefits of each option under consideration, tracing direct costs and allocating indirect ones.

sustainability accounting.text: Accounting, also called social and environmental accounting or non-financial reporting, that discloses information about a firm's social and environmental performance to outsiders such as investors and creditors.

true cost accounting.text: An accounting approach that measures and puts values on the hidden effects of economic activity on the environment, society and health.

material flow accounting.text: The measurement of material flows through a national or regional economy, also called economy-wide material flow analysis.

net domestic product.text: Net domestic product (NDP) is gross domestic product minus the depreciation of a country's capital goods.

integrated reporting.text: Corporate reporting that produces a periodic integrated report on how a firm's strategy, governance, performance and prospects create value over time.

seea ecosystem accounting.text: SEEA EA is a statistical framework that gives a consistent accounting approach for measuring ecosystems.

depletion (accounting).text: An accounting and tax method that records the gradual using up of natural resources such as minerals, oil and timber as an expense over time.

gross ecosystem product.text: A statistic giving the money value of the ecosystem services produced in an area over an accounting period, usually a year.

wasting asset.text: An asset that loses value irreversibly over time.

environmental management accounting.text: The branch of corporate environmental accounting that supports a firm's internal decisions with physical and money data on its environmental use and costs.

environmental reporting.text: The disclosure of an organisation's environmental impacts and performance.

environmentally adjusted net domestic pr.text: A 'green' version of net domestic product that subtracts the using up of natural assets, also called EDP or Green NDP.

true cost accounting in food and farming.term: True cost accounting in food and farming
true cost accounting in food and farming.text: The use of full or true cost accounting to price the hidden environmental and social costs of food production and waste.

residence principle in emission accounts.text: The SEEA rule that counts all emissions caused by a country's economy, wherever they happen, rather than those released inside its borders.

hidden costs of global agrifood systems.term: Hidden costs of global agrifood systems
hidden costs of global agrifood systems.text: Estimates of the environmental, health and social costs of the world's food systems that market prices leave out.

repetto's green accounts for indonesia.text: A 1990 World Resources Institute study that adjusted Indonesia's national accounts for the depletion of its natural resources.

environmental profit and loss account.text: A company's money valuation of its environmental impacts across its own operations and its supply chain, from raw materials to the factory gate.

wealth accounting and valuation of ecosy.term: Wealth Accounting and Valuation of Ecosystem Services
wealth accounting and valuation of ecosy.text: WAVES is a World Bank-led global partnership that helps countries put the value of natural capital into their national accounts.

material flow indicators.text: Standard indicators calculated from material flow accounts to summarise an economy's material use.

seea-water.text: The UN's framework for organising physical and economic information about water with the same concepts and classifications as the System of National Accounts.

el serafy depletion cost method.text: Salah El Serafy's method for valuing the depletion cost of natural resources, one of several alternatives for estimating resource rent in national accounts.

biocapacity.text: An estimate of how much an ecosystem can produce of useful biological materials and how much waste such as carbon dioxide it can absorb.

ecological footprint.text: A measure of how much nature, counted as biologically productive land and sea, people need to support their way of life and their economies.

emission intensity.text: The amount of a pollutant released per unit of an activity, such as grams of CO2 per megajoule of energy or greenhouse gases per unit of GDP; also called carbon intensity.

iucn red list.text: The global inventory, founded in 1964, of the conservation status and extinction risk of the world's species.

carbon footprint.text: The total amount of greenhouse gases that an activity, product, company or country adds to the atmosphere, expressed as one comparable number.

environmental indicator.text: A simple measure, tracked over time, that tells us what is happening in the environment.

water footprint.text: The total volume of fresh water used to produce the goods and services that a person, community or business consumes or produces.

sustainability measurement.text: The frameworks and indicators used to measure how sustainable a process, product, service or business is.

supply chain.text: A supply chain is the system of facilities that turn raw materials into finished products and distribute them to end customers.

life-cycle assessment.text: A method for adding up the environmental impacts of a product, process or service across every stage of its life, from raw materials to disposal.

input–output model.text: A quantitative economic model that shows how the sectors of an economy depend on one another, with each sector's output becoming other sectors' inputs.

embedded emissions.text: The greenhouse gases released in making a good, counted as belonging to whoever consumes it; also called embodied emissions or embodied carbon.

consumption-based emission accounting.text: A way of counting a country's emissions that assigns all the emissions along a global supply chain to the place where the goods are finally consumed.

scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions.text: The Greenhouse Gas Protocol's three-way split of an organization's emissions into direct ones, those from bought energy, and all other indirect ones in its value chain.

earth overshoot day.text: The calculated date each year on which humanity's use of resources passes what Earth can regenerate in that whole year.

phases of life-cycle assessment.text: The four phases in which the ISO 14040 and 14044 standards say a life-cycle assessment is carried out: goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment and interpretation.

iucn red list of ecosystems.text: The IUCN's global framework for assessing and recording how close ecosystems are to collapse, the ecosystem-level counterpart of the Red List of species.

ecological indicator.text: A measure that sums up the state of an ecosystem, or the human impact on it, in simple terms for the public and policy makers.

living planet index.text: An indicator of the state of global biodiversity built from population trends of vertebrate species around the world.

iucn red list categories.text: The nine groups into which the IUCN Red List sorts species, from Extinct to Not Evaluated, based on criteria such as rate of decline, population size and range.

red list index.text: An indicator, built from the IUCN Red List, that tracks how the extinction risk of whole groups of species changes over time.

blue, green and grey water footprints.term: Blue, green and grey water footprints
blue, green and grey water footprints.text: The three parts of a water footprint: blue for surface and groundwater, green for rainwater, and grey for water needed to dilute pollution.

sustainability metrics and indices.text: Numerical measures that try to quantify the environmental, social and economic sides of sustainability.

sustainability indicator.text: A measure that tracks some part of the interplay between the environment and social and economic activity, mainly to inform public policy.

environmentally extended input–output an.text: An environmental accounting tool that attaches resource use and emissions to an economy's input-output tables, so they can be traced through production to final consumption.

happy planet index.text: An index, introduced by the New Economics Foundation in 2006, that measures how efficiently countries turn environmental impact into long, satisfied lives.

environmental performance index.text: A score that ranks countries on the environmental performance of their policies.

dpsir framework.text: A cause-and-effect framework that sorts information about a society–environment problem into drivers, pressures, state, impacts and responses.

ecological footprint by country.text: Comparisons of national footprints that show how unequally countries use the planet's resources.

ecological footprint critiques.text: The scholarly argument over whether the ecological footprint is a reliable and fair measure of human demand on nature.

carbon footprint of food.text: The greenhouse gas emissions caused by producing a food, which differ greatly between plant-based foods and meat or dairy.

personal carbon footprint debate.text: The dispute over whether promoting personal carbon footprints shifts responsibility for climate change from fossil fuel companies to individuals.

economic input–output life-cycle assessm.text: A form of life-cycle assessment that uses sector-level data on each industry's environmental impact and its purchases from other industries.

lca system boundaries.text: The variants of life-cycle assessment that differ in which stretch of a product's life they cover, such as cradle-to-grave, cradle-to-gate and gate-to-gate.

life cycle energy analysis.text: An approach that counts all the energy a product needs, including the energy used to make its components, materials and services.

emission factor.text: A fixed rate linking an activity to the emissions it causes, so that emissions equal activity multiplied by the emission factor.

emission inventory.text: An account of how much of one or more pollutants or greenhouse gases all sources in an area release over a set period, usually a year.

daly rules.text: Herman Daly's three operating rules for ecological sustainability, covering renewable resources, nonrenewable resources and pollution.

lifecycle emissions of electricity sourc.text: The total greenhouse gases released per unit of electricity over the whole life of each kind of power plant, as compiled by the IPCC in 2011.

circles of sustainability.text: A framework for choosing sustainability indicators, organized around four domains: economics, ecology, politics and culture.

national water footprint.text: The water used to produce the goods and services consumed by a nation's inhabitants, wherever that water is used.

hubbert peak as a depletion metric.term: Hubbert peak as a depletion metric
hubbert peak as a depletion metric.text: The use of the Hubbert production curve, which rises to a peak and then declines, as a measure of how far a non-renewable resource has been depleted.

leontief inverse.text: The matrix (I−A)^−1 that turns final demand into the total output every sector must produce, counting all direct and indirect inputs.

physical input-output table.text: An input-output table measured in physical units instead of money, built to estimate environmental impacts more faithfully.

embodied carbon in buildings.text: The emissions from extracting, making, transporting and installing a building's materials, and from its repair and end-of-life treatment, as opposed to the emissions from running it.

biocapacity deficit.text: The gap that opens when a population's ecological footprint is larger than the biocapacity of the area it lives in.

top-down and bottom-up carbon accounting.text: The three main ways to quantify embodied carbon: bottom-up process-based LCA, top-down environmentally extended input-output models, and hybrids of the two.

material input per unit of service.term: Material input per unit of service
material input per unit of service.text: A measure of eco-efficiency, developed at the Wuppertal Institute in the 1990s, that divides the total material input of a product over its life by the units of service it provides.

red list of ecosystems categories and cr.term: Red List of Ecosystems categories and criteria
red list of ecosystems categories and cr.text: The eight risk categories and five criteria (A to E) the IUCN Red List of Ecosystems uses to rate an ecosystem's risk of collapse.

emission inventory quality criteria.text: The standards the UNFCCC and LRTAP conventions require of a national emission inventory: transparent, consistent, comparable, complete and accurate.

emergy sustainability index.text: An index proposed by M.T. Brown and S. Ulgiati in 1997 that divides the emergy yield ratio by the environmental loading ratio.

environmental sustainability index.text: A country index of environmental sustainability built by Yale and Columbia University centres with the World Economic Forum and released in 2005.

natural step framework.text: A science-based definition of sustainability, built by consensus after the Brundtland report, that sets out system conditions a sustainable society must meet.

consumer and producer responsibility.text: The choice of whether environmental impacts in input-output accounts are assigned to final consumers, to producers, or shared between them.

material footprint.text: A consumption-based indicator of material use: all the raw materials needed along the supply chain to make the goods a country consumes, also called raw material equivalents.

waste input-output model.text: An extension of environmentally extended input-output analysis by Nakamura and Kondo that tracks physical waste flows and their treatment alongside money flows.

ecological backpack.text: The hidden material flows behind a product: its total material input minus the product's own weight.

factor x.text: Friedrich Schmidt-Bleek's idea of setting targets, such as Factor Four or Factor Ten, for dematerializing economies by raising resource productivity.

global hectare.text: The adjusted unit of footprint accounting: a hectare with the world's average biological productivity in a given year.

human appropriation of net primary produ.term: Human appropriation of net primary production
human appropriation of net primary produ.text: An indicator, abbreviated HANPP, of how much of the plant growth that ecosystems produce each year is taken or prevented by human use, used as a proxy for human impact on nature.

particulate matter.text: Particulate matter is microscopic solid or liquid particles suspended in the air.

acid rain.text: Acid rain is rain, snow or other precipitation that is unusually acidic, with a low pH.

municipal solid waste.text: Municipal solid waste is everyday rubbish, the trash or garbage of items thrown away by the public.

landfill.text: A landfill is a site for disposing of waste, including household rubbish.

hazardous waste.text: Hazardous waste is waste that can damage human health or the environment.

nonpoint source pollution.text: Nonpoint source pollution is diffuse contamination of water or air that does not come from a single identifiable source.

waste incineration.text: Incineration is a waste treatment process that burns the substances in waste, turning it into ash, flue gas and heat.

black carbon.text: Black carbon is the light-absorbing form of elemental carbon left by pyrolysis or produced by incomplete combustion, as in soot.

brownfield land.text: Brownfield land is previously developed land, abandoned or underused, that may be polluted from past industrial use.

environmental remediation.text: Environmental remediation is the cleanup of hazardous substances: removing, treating or containing pollution in soil, groundwater and sediment.

health effects of particulate matter.text: Breathing particulate matter is linked to disease throughout the body and to large numbers of early deaths.

effects of acid rain.text: Acid rain harms forests, fresh waters and soils, kills plants and animals, damages buildings and affects human health.
