damage function.text: A relationship used in cost-benefit analysis that estimates the economic damage caused by an environmental change such as warming.

climate effects of aerosols.text: Aerosols change Earth's climate by altering how much incoming sunlight and outgoing heat the planet keeps.

particle size classes (pm10 and pm2.5).text: Particles are grouped by diameter: coarse PM10 (10 micrometres or less), fine PM2.5 (2.5 micrometres or less) and ultrafine particles.

particulate control technologies.text: Industries control particle emissions with dust collection systems such as cyclones, fabric filters, wet scrubbers and electrostatic precipitators.

unequal exposure to particulate pollutio.text: The burden of particle pollution falls more heavily on non-White people and those living in poverty.

who air quality guidelines.text: The World Health Organization sets guideline limits for particle exposure, above which health risks rise.

alternatives to landfill.text: Alternatives to landfill include waste reduction and recycling, waste-to-energy incineration, anaerobic digestion, composting and other treatments.

landfill gas.text: Landfill gas is the mix of mainly methane and carbon dioxide produced when microbes digest organic waste without oxygen.

landfill leachate.text: Leachate is the contaminated liquid formed when water seeps through landfill waste, picking up organic matter, heavy metals and other pollutants.

landfill aftercare.text: Aftercare is the long period after a landfill is full and capped, when liners, gas capture and leachate treatment continue to limit harm.

sanitary landfill life cycle.text: A sanitary landfill works as a biological reactor in which microbes break organic waste down into simpler, less toxic compounds over several phases.

acid deposition.text: Acid deposition is the delivery of acids from the air to the ground, either washed down by precipitation (wet) or settling without it (dry).

controlling acid rain.text: Acid rain has been reduced by scrubbing sulfur from power-station exhaust, international treaties and emissions trading.

reuse.text: Reuse means using items again, by repairing, gifting, refurbishing or lending them, instead of throwing them away.

source separation of waste.text: Source separation means sorting waste into types, such as biodegradable, recyclable, residual and hazardous, where it is produced.

waste-to-energy.text: Waste-to-energy is the generation of power from municipal waste, by burning it or by capturing landfill gas, pyrolysis or gasification.

hazardous waste disposal.text: Hazardous waste is disposed of by treating and stabilising it for secure landfills, burning it, or recycling it.

international trade in hazardous waste.text: Hazardous waste has been shipped from rich countries to poorer ones with weaker rules, prompting the Basel Convention to curb the trade.

unequal exposure to hazardous waste.text: Poorer people and social minorities face a higher risk of exposure to hazardous waste and its pollution.

controlling nonpoint source pollution.text: Nonpoint pollution is controlled by land practices that slow runoff and trap pollutants before they reach water.

regulating nonpoint source pollution.text: Nonpoint pollution is hard to regulate because it has no single discharge point; US federal law leaves it largely to states and voluntary programs.

types of nonpoint water pollutants.text: The main nonpoint water pollutants are sediment, nutrients, toxic chemicals and disease-causing pathogens.

debate over waste incineration.text: The use of incinerators for waste management is controversial, weighing the economic appeal of local industry against health and environmental risk.

black carbon and climate.text: Black carbon warms the climate by absorbing sunlight, altering clouds and darkening snow and ice.

black carbon mitigation.text: Black carbon can be cut with existing technology and national laws on particulate emissions.

barriers to brownfield redevelopment.text: Many contaminated brownfields sit unused for decades because cleaning them costs more than the land would then be worth.

brownfield remediation.text: Brownfield remediation is cleaning contaminated former industrial land so it can be reused.

brownfield valuation.text: Valuing a brownfield needs specialised appraisal, because contamination changes a site's best use and value before and after cleanup.

incremental health risk.text: Incremental health risk is the added risk a nearby person faces from a remediation project or from the lack of one.

remediation technologies.text: Remediation technologies fall into ex-situ methods, which excavate or extract contaminated soil and groundwater for surface treatment, and in-situ methods, which treat contamination in place.

greenfield land.text: Greenfield land is undeveloped land, farmed, landscaped or left natural, in an urban or rural area.

environmental law.text: The body of treaties, statutes, regulations and policies meant to protect the natural environment and manage how human activity affects ecosystems and natural resources.

environmental impact assessment.text: A study of the likely environmental effects of a project, plan or policy, done before anyone decides whether to go ahead with it.

biofuel.text: A fuel made over a short time span from biomass, rather than by the very slow natural processes that form fossil fuels.

endangered species act of 1973.text: The main United States law for protecting imperilled species, signed in 1973 to stop extinctions caused by economic growth that ignored conservation.

zoning.text: A way for a local government to divide land into zones, each with its own rules on what may be built and how the land may be used.

urban sprawl.text: The rapid spread of cities and towns, often with low-density housing, single-use zoning and heavy reliance on the private car.

national environmental policy act.text: The 1969 United States law, in force from 1970, that requires federal agencies to weigh environmental effects before acting and created the Council on Environmental Quality.

point source pollution.text: Pollution of air, water, heat, noise or light that comes from a single identifiable source, such as a factory outlet or smokestack.

natura 2000.text: The European Union's network of protected nature areas on land and at sea, designated under the Birds and Habitats Directives.

regulatory economics.text: The study and use of government rules to achieve economic aims, such as correcting market failures and protecting the environment.

food vs fuel debate.text: The dispute over whether growing crops for biofuel competes with food production.

international environmental law.text: The part of international law dealing with global and regional environmental problems, made up of treaties, customary rules and the decisions of international courts.

principles of environmental law.text: A set of guiding ideas, not universally accepted, that run through environmental law, such as sustainable development, equity, prevention, precaution and polluter pays.

perverse incentives of endangered specie.term: Perverse incentives of endangered species protection
perverse incentives of endangered specie.text: The problem that strict species-protection rules can make an endangered species a financial burden for landowners, tempting them to destroy habitat before the species arrives.

indirect land use change from biofuels.term: Indirect land use change from biofuels
indirect land use change from biofuels.text: The unintended extra carbon emissions from land-use change elsewhere, caused by cropland expanding to meet global demand for biofuels.

strategic environmental assessment.text: A systematic process for making sure environmental, and sometimes wider sustainability, effects are considered when policies, plans and programmes are made.

environmental standard.text: A rule, regulation or practice, usually set by government, that says how the environment must be treated and kept, such as a pollution limit or a permit requirement.

command and control regulation.text: Direct regulation by law that states what an industry or activity may and may not do, backed by penalties for breaking the rules.

clean water act.text: The main United States federal law controlling pollution of surface waters, adopted as the Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments of 1972.

emission standard.text: A legal limit on how much of a given air pollutant a particular source may release over a set period.

renewable portfolio standard.text: A rule requiring electricity suppliers to get a set share of their power from renewable sources such as wind, solar, biomass and geothermal.

best available technology.text: The technology or techniques that regulators approve as the standard for meeting a process's output limits, such as for pollution control.

command and control versus economic ince.term: Command and control versus economic incentives
command and control versus economic ince.text: The long-running argument over whether direct rules or price-based tools such as taxes and tradable permits protect the environment at lower cost.

corporate average fuel economy.text: United States rules, first enacted in 1975 after the 1973-74 oil embargo, requiring the cars and light trucks each maker sells to meet an average fuel economy.

porter hypothesis.text: The idea that strict environmental regulation can push firms to become more efficient and innovative, improving their competitiveness.

aviation biofuel.text: A biofuel for aircraft, also called bio-jet fuel or sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

biodiesel.text: A liquid fuel made from oils or fats by transesterification, similar in composition to fossil diesel and made mostly of fatty acid methyl or ethyl esters.

biogas.text: A gas mixture of mainly methane and carbon dioxide, produced by microorganisms digesting organic material without oxygen.

ethanol fuel.text: Alcohol, most commonly ethanol, made by fermenting sugars or starches (or harder, cellulose) with microorganisms and enzymes for use as fuel.

clean air act (united states).text: The main United States federal law for preventing and reducing air pollution, first passed in 1963 and greatly expanded by later amendments.

environmental cleanup law.text: Laws governing the removal of pollution from soil, sediment, surface water or groundwater after contamination has happened.

environmental impact statement.text: In United States law, a document required under the National Environmental Policy Act for federal actions that significantly affect the quality of the human environment.

air quality law.text: Laws that govern the release of air pollutants into the atmosphere, mostly to protect human health.

clean water act section 404 permits.text: Permits required under the US Clean Water Act before dredged or fill material may be placed in streams, wetlands and other regulated waters.

smart growth.text: A planning approach that favors mixed-use, closely spaced development over sprawl.

urban sprawl debate.text: The argument over whether sprawl is a market-efficient settlement pattern or a problem that planning should regulate.

criticisms of environmental impact asses.text: Objections that environmental impact assessments are too narrow in scope, handle uncertainty poorly, have little influence on decisions and can delay projects.

meat tax.text: A tax on meat or other animal products meant to cover the health and environmental costs of using animals for food.

transboundary environmental impact asses.text: Assessing the environmental effects of a project that cross national borders, such as pollution reaching another country.

performance and incentive zoning.text: Flexible zoning approaches that judge projects by their effects or let developers build more in return for public benefits such as open space.

command and control and global environme.term: Command and control and global environmental problems
command and control and global environme.text: The question of how well direct regulation, built for national governments, can work for problems that cross borders, such as ozone depletion and climate change.

types of command-and-control standards.text: The kinds of standards direct regulation uses: general environmental standards, target standards about the receiving environment, and performance standards on releases.

performance and technology standards.text: The two main forms of direct pollution rules: a performance standard sets a numerical emission limit for each polluter, while a technology standard dictates the equipment it must use.

national ambient air quality standards.text: United States limits on the concentration in outdoor air of six pollutants that cause smog, acid rain and other health hazards.

positive and normative theories of regul.term: Positive and normative theories of regulation
positive and normative theories of regul.text: Two families of theory: positive theories explain why regulation happens, normative theories say how regulators should act.

critical habitat.text: A legal designation under the US Endangered Species Act of areas essential to conserving a listed species, even if the species does not occupy them yet.

european emission standards.text: The European Union's set of emission limits that all new road vehicles must meet, graded in stages such as Euro 4, Euro 5 and Euro 6.

technology-based and water-quality-based.text: Two layers of discharge limits under the Clean Water Act: a national floor based on what control technology can achieve, topped up by stricter limits where a water body stays polluted.

emission performance standard.text: A limit on emissions above which a different type of emission-control technology may be needed.

low-emission zone.text: An area, usually in a city, where polluting vehicles are barred or charged for entering, to improve air quality.

minimum energy performance standard.text: A mandatory specification that caps how much energy an appliance or other device may use to do a given task.

low-carbon fuel standard.text: A tradable-credit rule that requires the average carbon intensity of a region's transport fuels to fall below that of petrol and diesel.

regulation and monitoring of pollution.text: The laws and agencies that limit pollution and reduce its harm, together with the measurement of pollution levels.

voluntary corporate environmental standa.text: Environmental standards that companies adopt for themselves, beyond what the law requires, usually to satisfy customers, governments and industry partners.

pollution prevention.text: A strategy of cutting the amount of waste created in the first place, rather than treating it after release, especially by industry, farms and consumers.

environmental enforcement and compliance.text: The work of checking whether polluters and other regulated parties follow environmental rules, and of penalising those who do not.

harrington paradox.text: The puzzle that firms mostly obey environmental rules even though inspections are rare, violators are seldom punished and expected fines are small next to compliance costs.

superfund.text: The common name for the 1980 US law (CERCLA) and its trust fund that pay for cleaning up abandoned hazardous waste sites and make polluters liable for the costs.

economics of crime and optimal enforceme.term: Economics of crime and optimal enforcement
economics of crime and optimal enforceme.text: Gary Becker's approach of treating rule-breaking as a rational choice: a profit-maximising firm complies only if the expected fine exceeds the cost of complying.

environmental liability.text: The legal responsibility of a polluter to pay for preventing and repairing the environmental damage it causes.

pigouvian tax.text: A Pigouvian tax is a tax on a market activity that imposes costs on third parties, known as negative externalities.

environmental tax.text: An environmental tax, also called an ecotax or green tax, is a tax on activities that harm the environment, meant to steer people toward cleaner alternatives.

natural resource damage assessment.text: A legal process in which public trustees measure the harm done to natural resources by pollution, so the polluter can be made to pay for restoring them.

global warming taxes.text: Taxes proposed or imposed to raise money for dealing with global warming, or to discourage the activities that cause it.

carbon tax.text: A carbon tax is a tax charged on the carbon released when goods and services are produced.

polluter pays principle.text: The polluter pays principle says that whoever causes pollution should pay for the damage it does to the environment.

congestion pricing.text: Congestion pricing charges users of crowded public goods, such as busy roads, higher prices at peak times to reduce overuse.

excise.text: An excise is a tax on a particular category of goods, usually charged when they are made for sale at home.

regressive tax.text: A regressive tax is one whose rate falls as the amount being taxed rises, so poorer people pay a larger share of what they have.

eco-tariff.text: An eco-tariff, or environmental tariff, is a trade barrier such as an import or export tax used to reduce pollution.

fuel tax.text: A fuel tax, also called a gas tax or fuel duty, is an excise tax charged on the sale of fuel, usually transport fuel.

carbon tariff.text: A carbon tariff, or border carbon adjustment, is a charge on imports according to the carbon emitted in making them.

categories of environmental taxes.text: Environmental taxes are usually sorted into four categories: energy, transport, pollution and resource taxes.

energy tax.text: An energy tax is a tax that raises the price of energy, usually charged on the fuels themselves.

optimal tax.text: Optimal tax theory studies how to design taxes that do the most for overall social welfare within economic limits.

emissions tax.text: An emissions tax makes each emitter pay a charge for every tonne of greenhouse gas it releases, while an energy tax is charged on the fuels themselves.

environmental pricing reform.text: Environmental pricing reform, or ecological fiscal reform, adjusts market prices through taxes or subsidies so they reflect environmental costs and benefits.

tax shift.text: A tax shift, or tax swap, cuts some taxes and raises others while keeping total revenue the same.

effluent.text: Effluent is wastewater from sewers or industrial outlets that flows into rivers, lakes or the sea, either treated or untreated.

sin tax.text: A sin tax is an excise on goods and services seen as harmful, such as alcohol, tobacco, sugar, gambling or polluting vehicles.

double dividend hypothesis.text: The double dividend hypothesis holds that swapping environmental taxes for other taxes, without changing total revenue, could deliver two benefits at once.

measurement problem of pigouvian taxes.text: The measurement problem is the criticism that governments cannot know the true social cost of an externality, so they cannot set the right Pigouvian tax.

noise tax.text: A noise tax is a charge meant to limit noise pollution that disturbs nearby communities or wildlife.

plastic tax.text: A plastic tax charges for plastic use or plastic waste to cut waste and encourage recycling.

second-best pigouvian taxation.text: Second-best Pigouvian taxation taxes a product linked to a harm when the harm itself cannot be taxed directly.

deposit-refund system.text: A deposit-refund system adds a surcharge when a product is bought and pays it back when the product or its packaging is returned.

prices versus quantities.text: Price-based instruments such as taxes fix the price of pollution and let the amount vary, while quantity-based instruments such as cap-and-trade fix the amount and let the price vary.

revenue recycling.text: Revenue recycling means using the money raised by an environmental tax to cut other taxes or return it to people, rather than adding it to general spending.

tax interaction effect.text: The tax interaction effect is the idea that an environmental tax, by raising prices, worsens the distortions already caused by income taxes.

road pricing.text: Road pricing means charging drivers directly for road use, through tolls, distance or time fees, congestion charges or charges on more polluting vehicles.

carbon fee and dividend.text: Carbon fee and dividend taxes fossil fuels for their carbon and pays the money back to everyone in equal per-person payments.

british columbia carbon tax.text: The British Columbia carbon tax, in force from 2008 until its repeal on 1 April 2025, taxed fossil fuels while cutting income and corporate taxes by about the same amount.

landfill tax.text: A landfill tax is a charge per tonne or per unit of volume that raises the cost of dumping waste in landfill.

hypothecated tax.text: A hypothecated, or earmarked, tax is one whose revenue is set aside for a particular kind of spending.

per unit tax.text: A per unit, or specific, tax is a fixed amount charged on each unit of a good sold, such as cents per kilogram, whatever its price.

steering tax.text: A steering tax, or ecological incentive tax, is meant to change taxpayers' behaviour rather than to raise revenue.

stormwater fee.text: A stormwater fee charges property owners for polluted rainwater runoff from their hard, waterproof surfaces.

cost pass-through.text: Cost pass-through is the extent to which a business changes its prices when its own costs change.

feebate.text: A feebate charges a fee on products with harmful side effects and uses the money to give rebates on cleaner alternatives.

user fee.text: A user fee is a payment charged to people for using a facility or service, such as a park, toll road or parking space.

pollution pricing reform.text: Pollution pricing reform adjusts market prices to include directly measurable pollution, such as dust and exhaust from road vehicles.

plastic bag charges and bans.text: A plastic bag ban or charge is a law that restricts or puts a price on the lightweight plastic bags handed out by shops.

fossil fuel subsidy reform.text: Fossil fuel subsidy reform removes subsidies that keep fossil fuel prices below their supply cost or below their full environmental cost.

carbon pricing on shipping.text: Carbon pricing on shipping charges ships for the greenhouse gases they emit.

emissions trading.text: A market-based way of controlling pollution in which a government caps total emissions and issues permits that polluters can buy and sell.

carbon pricing.text: A government policy that puts a money cost on greenhouse gas emissions so that polluters burn less fossil fuel.

carbon emission trading.text: Emissions trading applied to carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases: a market with a limited number of allowances to emit, created to limit climate change.

carbon leakage.text: A rise in greenhouse gas emissions in one country caused by another country cutting its own emissions under stricter climate policies.

chinese national carbon trading scheme.text: China's national emissions trading system for carbon dioxide, which caps emissions per unit of output rather than in total, and began operating in 2021.

least-cost abatement under emissions tra.text: The idea that trading permits makes pollution cuts happen first wherever they are cheapest, so a target is met at the lowest total cost.

allocation of emission permits.text: How a trading scheme hands out its permits: either free to existing emitters or sold at auction.

european union emissions trading system.text: The European Union's cap-and-trade scheme for greenhouse gases, begun in 2005, in which each allowance permits its holder to emit 1 ton of CO2.

criticisms of carbon trading.text: The arguments that carbon emissions trading is ineffective, unfair or open to abuse.

carbon tax versus emissions trading.text: The policy choice between a carbon tax, which fixes the price of each tonne emitted, and emissions trading, which fixes the total amount emitted and lets the price adjust.

internal carbon pricing.text: A carbon price that a company sets on its own greenhouse gas emissions, voluntarily and on top of any price a government imposes.

flexible mechanisms.text: The three Kyoto Protocol tools, emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation, that let countries meet emission targets more cheaply by acting in other countries.

acid rain program.text: A US Environmental Protection Agency emissions trading programme that cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, the gases that cause acid rain, from power plants.

eu carbon border adjustment mechanism.text: A European Union carbon tariff on carbon-intensive imports such as steel, cement and some electricity.

joint implementation.text: A Kyoto Protocol mechanism letting one developed (Annex I) country invest in an emission-cutting project in another and count the cuts towards its own target.

baseline and credit.text: A trading scheme in which polluters earn credits, or offsets, by cutting emissions below a baseline, often their historical emissions.

history of emissions trading.text: The development of cap and trade from computer studies of air pollution costs in the late 1960s to national and global carbon markets.

linked emissions trading systems.text: Separate cap-and-trade systems joined together by recognising each other's allowances for compliance.

monitoring, reporting and verification.text: The checks that make an emissions market credible: measuring or calculating emissions, reporting them, and having them verified by government or third-party auditors.

safety valve (emissions trading).text: A hybrid of a cap and a tax: a cap-and-trade system in which the permit price is held below a maximum, or above a minimum.

auctioning of emission permits.text: Selling emission permits to firms at auction, so that the government receives their value.

carbon trading and environmental justice.text: The question of whether carbon trading helps poorer countries and communities or leaves them bearing more of the pollution.

global carbon market.text: A proposed worldwide market in emission allowances, for which the Paris Agreement provides a legal basis.

grandfathering of emission permits.text: Giving out emission permits for free according to how much each firm emitted in the past.

over-allocation of emission permits.text: The risk that a regulator issues too many emission permits, pushing their price so low that firms have little reason to cut emissions.

certified emission reduction.text: A carbon credit issued by the Clean Development Mechanism for verified emission cuts made by its projects under the Kyoto Protocol.

carbon revenue recycling.text: The choices governments make about how to spend the money raised by a carbon tax or by selling emission permits.

overlapping policies under an emissions.term: Overlapping policies under an emissions cap
overlapping policies under an emissions.text: The way a carbon tax or an emissions cap changes what other climate policies, such as renewable energy subsidies, can achieve.

economic spillover.text: An impact, positive or more often negative, felt in one region or across the world because of an independent event elsewhere.

assigned amount unit.text: A tradable Kyoto Protocol unit allowing a country to emit one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent.

auction theory.text: The branch of applied economics that studies how bidders behave in auctions and how auction features lead to predictable outcomes.

emission reduction unit.text: A Kyoto Protocol credit for one tonne of CO2 equivalent cut by a Joint Implementation project.

eu ets2.text: A second EU emissions trading system for carbon dioxide from buildings, road transport and other sectors outside the original ETS.

water trading.text: Buying and selling water access entitlements, often called water rights, between willing sellers and buyers.

market stability reserve.text: An EU ETS mechanism that changes how many permits are auctioned each year according to how many surplus permits are in circulation.

corsia.text: The Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, which makes airlines buy carbon credits to offset growth in emissions from international flights.

personal carbon trading.text: Proposed schemes that would give each adult an equal share of emission credits within a national carbon budget, to be surrendered when buying fuel or electricity.

market design.text: The branch of economics that sets the rules of exchange, who gets what and by what procedure, to build or repair markets so that they give efficient and fair outcomes.

cap and dividend.text: A cap-and-trade system in which all permits are sold and the money is paid back to citizens to offset higher energy prices.

voluntary emission reduction.text: A carbon offset, also called a Verified Emission Reduction, traded in the voluntary market and usually certified outside the Kyoto Protocol.

revenue equivalence theorem.text: Vickrey's 1961 result that, under certain conditions, a large class of auctions all give the seller the same expected revenue, the best the seller can get.

windfall gain.text: A sudden, usually unexpected addition to income well above the norm, arising from luck or circumstance rather than planning.

measuring international spillovers.text: Three families of methods, input-output analysis, life-cycle assessment and material-flow analysis, used to assess trade-related spillovers.

simultaneous multiple-round auction.text: An auction format invented by Milgrom and Wilson that combines the benefits of open English-style bidding and sealed bids.

transferable development rights.text: A land-use tool that lets developers buy the building rights of land in a protected sending area and use them to build more densely in a receiving area.

green certificate.text: A tradable certificate proving that a certain amount of electricity, typically one megawatthour, was generated from renewable sources.

renewable energy certificate (united sta.text: A tradable, non-tangible certificate in the United States proving that one megawatt-hour of electricity came from an eligible renewable source and was fed into the grid.

pollution hot spots.text: The problem that a regional pollutant traded under a cap can pile up in some places, since the same amount does far more harm in some locations than others.

ambient pollution permit markets.text: Markets in licences that give the right to raise pollution at a given location by no more than a set amount, rather than the right to emit a set amount.

water quality trading.text: A market-based approach, run at watershed scale, in which sources that can cut water pollution cheaply sell pollution-reduction credits to sources for whom cuts are costly.

white certificates.text: Tradable certificates proving that a certain amount of energy saving has been achieved, usually tied to an obligation on energy suppliers to save energy.

carbon retirement.text: Permanently removing emission allowances or carbon credits from circulation so they can never be sold or used again.

subsidy.text: A form of government spending that passes money from taxpayers to individuals, households or businesses to support them or encourage some activity.

precautionary principle.text: An approach to new activities or technologies that might cause harm when scientific knowledge about them is still incomplete, favouring caution and review first.

perverse incentive.text: An incentive structure that produces undesirable results, especially effects that are unexpected and contrary to what its designers intended.

ecolabel.text: A labelling system on food and consumer products that tells shoppers about the product's environmental impact.

fossil fuel subsidies.text: Energy subsidies for coal, oil and gas: any government action that lowers the cost of producing fossil fuel energy, raises producers' prices or lowers consumers' prices.

sustainability standards and certificati.text: Voluntary guidelines that producers, traders and retailers follow to show they use good environmental, social, ethical and food-safety practices.

fair trade.text: A trade arrangement meant to help producers in developing countries get sustainable and fair conditions, by paying higher prices and raising social and environmental standards.

energy subsidy.text: A government measure that keeps energy prices below market levels for customers, keeps them above market levels for suppliers, or cuts their costs.

extended producer responsibility.text: A policy that makes manufacturers responsible for the environmental costs of their products across the whole life cycle, mainly the costs of dealing with them as waste.

sustainable procurement.text: Buying goods, services and works in a way that gives value for money over the whole life cycle while also benefiting society and staying within the environment's limits.

common agricultural policy.text: The European Union's farm policy, which runs a system of agricultural subsidies, risk management tools and other programmes.

nudge theory.text: The idea from behavioural science that changing how choices are presented (choice architecture) can steer people's behaviour without forcing them.

economic effects of subsidies.text: How a subsidy changes a market: it shifts the supply or demand curve to the right by the amount of the subsidy.

perverse subsidies.text: Subsidies whose effects are clearly and significantly harmful both to the economy and to the environment.

feed-in tariff.text: A policy that speeds up investment in renewable energy by giving producers long-term contracts at a guaranteed, usually above-market price for the electricity they supply.

tax incentive.text: Part of a government's tax policy that encourages a particular economic activity by lowering the tax owed.

forest certification.text: A voluntary system that certifies wood and paper products as coming from forests managed responsibly under a particular standard.

pollutant release and transfer register.text: A system that collects and publishes information on releases and transfers of hazardous substances from industrial and other facilities.

environmental certification.text: A voluntary form of environmental regulation in which a company chooses to meet processes or goals set by a certification service.

iso 14000 family.text: A set of international standards for environmental management systems, first issued by the International Organization for Standardization in 1996.

toxics release inventory.text: A public US database of toxic chemical releases and waste management activities reported by industrial and federal facilities.

fishing subsidies.text: Government support for fishing, such as direct aid to fishers, loans, tax breaks, infrastructure and price support.

green industrial policy.text: Government strategy to speed the growth of green industries, correcting market failures and moving toward a low-carbon economy.

ways of classifying subsidies.text: Subsidies are sorted as direct or indirect, production or consumption, and broad or narrow.

eco-management and audit scheme.text: A standard for environmental management systems, developed by the European Commission in 1993, that helps organisations assess, manage and keep improving their environmental performance.

inflation reduction act.text: A 2022 United States law that is the largest federal legislation ever to address climate change, mainly through tax credits and grants for clean energy.

measuring fossil fuel subsidies.text: Ways of estimating fossil fuel subsidies by adding up government payments, comparing domestic prices with world prices, and sometimes counting health and climate damage.

precautionary approach (rio principle 15.text: A softer form of the precautionary principle, set out in Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration, that takes local capabilities and costs into account.

strong and weak precaution.text: Two versions of the precautionary principle: the strong one requires regulation whenever harm is possible, the weak one only permits action without full proof.

precautionary dilemma.text: The common objection that weak versions of the precautionary principle are trivial and strong versions are incoherent.

plan-do-check-act cycle in iso 14001.text: The four-step management cycle of Plan, Do, Check and Act on which ISO 14001 environmental management is based.

voluntary consensus versus private stand.text: Sustainability standards fall into two groups: voluntary consensus standards and private standards.

ecolabeling innovation cycle.text: A repeating process in which consumers, firms, governments and institutions interact through ecolabels to produce eco-innovation.

ecolabelling as market governance.text: The idea that ecolabelling is a self-regulating, market-based policy tool that partly takes over from government command and control.

ecolabels as non-tariff trade barriers.text: The concern that the spread of ecolabels creates obstacles to international trade other than tariffs.

energy labels.text: Labels on consumer appliances that show whether they use energy efficiently compared with similar products.

energy star.text: A voluntary energy-efficiency labelling program set up by the US Environmental Protection Agency in 1992.

iso types of environmental labels.text: The International Organization for Standardization sorts environmental labels into three types by what they cover and how strictly they are checked.

criticism of fair trade.text: The debate over whether fair trade actually benefits poor producers, given studies that find both gains and little effect.

fair trade social premium.text: Extra money that buyers of fair trade goods pay to producer groups, who decide democratically how to spend it.

arguments for and against energy subsidi.term: Arguments for and against energy subsidies
arguments for and against energy subsidi.text: The debate over whether governments should support energy prices or producers, weighing supply security and social aims against waste and environmental harm.

extended producer responsibility for ele.text: The use of producer responsibility rules to deal with e-waste, used electronic equipment that cannot safely go out with household trash.

take-back programs.text: Waste policies that require manufacturers to take back their products at the end of their useful life, or to help pay for collection and recycling.

green public procurement.text: The part of sustainable public procurement that uses government buying power to reach environmental goals.

cap rural development pillar.text: The second pillar of the EU farm policy, in effect since 2000, which funds the economic, social and environmental development of the countryside.

decoupling and cross compliance.text: The 2003 reform of EU farm support that cut the link between subsidies and particular crops and tied payments to environmental and other conditions.

voluntary environmental agreements.text: Policy tools in which firms or other actors agree, without being forced, to take environmental action, often in a deal with government.

environmental effects of the common agri.term: Environmental effects of the Common Agricultural Policy
environmental effects of the common agri.text: The criticism that EU farm subsidies drove a large expansion of production using fertilisers and pesticides, with serious environmental harm.

grid parity.text: The point at which electricity from an alternative technology costs the same as the average grid electricity price in an area.

chain-of-custody certification.text: Certification that tracks certified material through every stage of processing and distribution, from the forest to the consumer.

carbon emission label.text: A label stating the carbon dioxide emitted in making, transporting or disposing of a consumer product.

right to know.text: The right of people to know about hazards and substances that may harm them, often framed around environmental and workplace exposure to chemicals.

sustainable seafood advisory lists and c.term: Sustainable seafood advisory lists and certification
sustainable seafood advisory lists and c.text: Guides and certification schemes meant to make seafood supply chains transparent and help shoppers choose seafood from well-managed stocks.

limits of environmental certification.text: The drawbacks of voluntary environmental certification, including high costs, weak incentives for poor performers and gaps in what it covers.

local content requirements.text: Rules requiring producers to source a minimum share of goods, labour or services locally.

risks of green industrial policy.text: The concerns that governments may back the wrong firms or industries and that support invites rent-seeking and regulatory capture.

environmental policy.text: A commitment by a government or organization to adopt laws, rules and other measures that deal with environmental problems.

market-based environmental policy instru.text: Policy tools that use markets, prices and other economic signals to give polluters a reason to cut harmful side effects such as pollution.

public choice.text: The use of economic tools such as rational choice and game theory to study how politicians, officials and voters behave and interact.

environmental policy instruments.text: The main families of tools governments use to carry out environmental policy: regulation, economic instruments and persuasion.

choosing between policy instruments.text: The debate over whether regulation, taxes, tradable permits or other tools work best for a given environmental problem.

taxes versus tradable permits.text: The trade-off between a pollution tax, which fixes the cost of cutting pollution, and a tradable permit system, which fixes the total amount allowed.

induced innovation.text: The idea that when one input becomes relatively more expensive, firms are spurred to invent ways of using less of it.

environmental policy analysis.text: The academic study of how environmental policies are made, how well they work and how they could be improved.

implicit carbon price.text: A cost placed on greenhouse gas emissions indirectly, by measures that change the cost of emitting without targeting carbon itself.

environmental policy integration.text: The idea that policies in every area should take account of their effects on the environment and on other areas.

constitutional economics.text: A research programme that applies public choice and political economy to the design of constitutional rules.

rational ignorance.text: The theory that a self-interested voter may sensibly choose not to vote or get informed, because one vote almost never decides an election.

lobbying.text: Lobbying is legal advocacy that tries to influence decisions made by legislators, regulators or sometimes judges.

market-based instruments versus command.term: Market-based instruments versus command and control
market-based instruments versus command.text: The comparison between flexible market-based tools and prescriptive rules such as emission standards and equipment requirements.

policy mix.text: A combination of several policy instruments used together; in macroeconomics, the combination of a country's monetary and fiscal policy.

gossen's second law.text: The principle that a person gets the most from a budget by spending so that the extra satisfaction per unit of money is equal across all goods.

rent-seeking.text: Rent-seeking is increasing one's wealth by manipulating public policy or economic conditions, without creating new wealth.

climate change denial.text: Climate change denial is a form of science denial that rejects, disputes or fights the extensive evidence for human-caused global warming and the scientific consensus on it.

advocacy group.text: Advocacy groups, also called lobby groups, interest groups or pressure groups, use advocacy or lobbying to influence political and social systems.

path dependence.text: Path dependence is when past events or decisions constrain later ones, so that 'history matters' for where a system ends up.

regulatory capture.text: Regulatory capture is when a regulator or policymaker is co-opted to serve the interests of a small group, such as an industry, instead of the public.

median voter theorem.text: The median voter theorem says that when voters and candidates line up along one left-right spectrum, majority-rule voting elects the candidate the middle (median) voter prefers.

fossil fuels lobby.text: The fossil fuels lobby is the paid representatives of oil, gas and coal companies and related industries such as chemicals, plastics and aviation.

logic of collective action.text: Mancur Olson's 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action argues that small groups with concentrated interests win out over large groups with diffuse interests, because large groups suffer worse free-riding.

network effect.text: A network effect is when the value a user gets from a good or service depends on how many users of compatible products there are.

tullock paradox.text: The Tullock paradox is the puzzle that rent-seekers can buy political favours for far less than the favours are worth to them.

psychology of climate change denial.text: The psychology of climate change denial studies why people deny climate change despite the scientific consensus.

incentives to join interest groups.text: Because members must be enticed to join an interest group, groups rely on a mix of free-rider-limiting benefits: selective, solidarity and expressive incentives.

critical juncture.text: A critical juncture is a moment when contingent choices set an institution on a path of development that is hard to reverse.

international trade.text: The exchange of capital, goods and services across national borders to meet a need or demand.

bootleggers and baptists.text: Bootleggers and Baptists is Bruce Yandle's idea that regulations win support both from groups that want their stated purpose and from groups that profit from undermining it.

types of regulatory capture.text: Regulatory capture comes in two basic types: materialist (financial) capture driven by the regulator's self-interest, and non-materialist (cognitive) capture driven by biased views.

market tipping.text: Market tipping is the tendency of one system to pull away from its rivals in popularity once it has gained an initial edge.

hotelling–downs model.text: The Hotelling–Downs model predicts that politicians who care only about winning will move to the median voter's position.

world trade organization.text: The intergovernmental organization, formed in 1995, that regulates and eases trade between countries.

tariff.text: A duty imposed by a national government or union on imported goods, paid by the importer.

foreign direct investment.text: A controlling ownership stake in a company or asset in one country held by an investor, firm or government from another country.

global waste trade.text: The international trade in waste, shipped between countries for treatment, disposal or recycling.

trade versus local production.text: The debate over whether goods, especially food, should be produced locally or imported, weighing environmental, economic and security effects.

non-tariff barriers to trade.text: Restrictions on imports or exports other than tariffs, such as quotas, licences, subsidies, customs delays and technical standards.

environmental exceptions in trade rules.text: Provisions in WTO agreements that let countries restrict trade to protect the environment and health, as long as the measures are not disguised protectionism.

criticism of the wto.text: Arguments that WTO-led trade liberalisation has not delivered the promised growth, poverty reduction and fair sharing of gains.

most-favoured-nation and national treatm.text: The WTO's non-discrimination rule: a member must offer all other members equal terms and treat imports no worse than its own goods.

environmental dumping argument.text: The argument for tariffs where firms gain unfair competition from weaker environmental regulation elsewhere.

infant industry argument.text: The claim that emerging industries, especially in less-developed countries, need temporary protection from established foreign competitors.

optimal tariff.text: A tariff set to maximise the welfare of the country imposing it.

environmental standards as trade barrier.text: Product standards on labelling, testing and composition that protect health and the environment but can also keep out foreign goods.

pollution haven hypothesis.text: The idea that firms investing abroad move to countries with cheap resources and weak environmental rules, making those countries havens for pollution.

types of foreign direct investment.text: FDI is classified from the investor's view as horizontal, vertical or conglomerate, and from the host country's view by its purpose.

bamako convention.text: A 1991 treaty in which African nations, unhappy with the Basel Convention, banned imports of hazardous waste.

economic case for the waste trade.term: Economic case for the waste trade
economic case for the waste trade.text: The argument that sending hazardous waste to low-wage, less polluted countries makes economic sense, famously made in a 1991 memo by Lawrence Summers.

electronic waste trade.text: The shipment of discarded electrical and electronic devices, mostly from rich countries, to developing countries for processing and recycling.

plastic waste trade.text: The international trade in waste plastics, identified as the main cause of marine litter.

shipbreaking.text: Dismantling old ships, which industrialised countries increasingly send to Asia because it is cheaper there.

toxic colonialism.text: The use of poorer countries as cheap places to export or dump the hazardous waste of developed countries.

import quota.text: A limit, by value or quantity, on how much of a good may be imported or exported over a period.

payment for ecosystem services.text: Payments offered to farmers or landowners in return for managing their land so that it provides an ecological service.

additionality.text: Whether an intervention, such as a payment or credit, actually causes an outcome that would not have happened anyway, judged against a baseline.

watershed management.text: The planning and running of programmes that sustain a watershed's functions and share its resources sustainably among its plant, animal and human communities.

conservation reserve program.text: A US Department of Agriculture programme that pays farmers to take cropland out of production and plant protective cover such as grass, trees or buffer strips.

theoretical perspectives on pes.text: The three main ways of viewing PES: environmental economics, ecological economics, and the rejection of ecosystem services altogether.

reverse auction.text: An auction with one buyer and many sellers, in which sellers compete by underbidding each other.

grain for green.text: A Chinese programme launched in 1999 that pays farmers to convert erosion-prone farmland back to vegetation to curb flooding and soil erosion.

conditional cash transfer.text: Programmes that fight poverty by paying cash only to people who meet conditions, such as sending children to school or getting vaccinations.

baselines and counterfactuals in pes.text: The predicted outcome without a payment or project, against which its real effect is measured.

conditionality in pes.text: The rule that a payment for ecosystem services is made only if the service is delivered or the agreed land use is kept up.

costa rica's pes programme.text: Costa Rica's Pagos por servicios ambientales, set up in 1997 as the first PES programme run on a national scale.

hoima and kibaale pes trial.text: A 2010 to 2013 PES scheme in Uganda that was the first set up as a randomized controlled trial to measure its effect on deforestation.

vittel pes arrangement.text: A negotiated deal in which the Vittel mineral-water brand paid nearby farmers to adopt practices that protect its groundwater.

results-based payments.text: Payments made only for measured, verified environmental results, such as emission reductions, rather than for planned actions.

new york city water supply system.term: New York City water supply system
new york city water supply system.text: The network of reservoirs, aqueducts and tunnels that supplies New York City with fresh water, kept clean largely by protecting its upstate watersheds.

spatial targeting of payments.text: Directing conservation payments to the places where they buy the most environmental benefit for the money.

environmental management scheme.text: A mechanism that gives landowners and land managers incentives to look after the environment.

no net loss.text: An environmental policy approach that aims to balance out a development's harm to the environment through mitigation measures.

biodiversity offsetting.text: A system, used mainly by planning authorities and developers, for fully compensating the harm a development does to biodiversity.

environmental mitigation.text: The process of applying measures to avoid, minimise or compensate for harm to the environment.

mitigation hierarchy.text: A sequence of steps (avoid, minimise, restore, then offset) applied in order to reduce a project's harm to the environment until none remains.

biodiversity banking.text: A market-based form of biodiversity offsetting in which conservation gains are turned into credits that developers can buy to offset their damage.

mitigation banking.text: A market-based system of debits and credits, used mainly in the United States, in which wetlands are restored, created or enhanced to make up for unavoidable damage to wetlands elsewhere.

conservation banking.text: A market-based method of offsetting harm to threatened or endangered species protected under the US Endangered Species Act by creating conservation banks.

safe harbor agreement.text: A voluntary US agreement in which a landowner improves land for a listed species and in return is allowed some future harm to that species.

biodiversity impact credit.text: A transferable biodiversity credit designed to reduce the global risk of species extinction.

averted loss offset.text: A biodiversity offset that prevents ecological damage that would almost certainly have happened, rather than restoring or creating habitat.

conservation credit.text: A unit representing the cost of re-creating a piece of damaged habitat, which developers can buy to offset their impact on biodiversity.

receptor site.text: Land offered by a company or individual for payment in return for creating or restoring wildlife habitat to offset damage elsewhere.

compensatory mitigation.text: Measures that restore, create, enhance or preserve wetlands to make up for damage that cannot be avoided; the US term for biodiversity offsetting.

carbon credit.text: A tradable certificate claiming that greenhouse gas emissions were avoided or that greenhouse gases were removed from the air.

conservation easement.text: A voluntary legal agreement between a landowner and a government agency or conservation group that restricts future development on a site, setting it aside permanently for conservation.

environmental crediting system.text: A system set up by a governing body that allocates debits for planned environmental damage and credits for conservation gains, so damage can be offset by buying credits.

net positive impact.text: A goal under which a project's environmental gains from mitigation outweigh its harms, leaving more biodiversity than before.

offset ratios and like-for-like rules.text: Rules that set how much habitat must be credited for each unit of damage (mitigation ratios) and require offsets to match or exceed the biodiversity lost (like-for-like).

redd+.text: A voluntary UN climate framework that pays and supports developing countries to cut emissions from deforestation and forest degradation and to conserve and build up forest carbon.

clean development mechanism.text: A UN-run offset scheme under the Kyoto Protocol that let rich countries fund emission-cutting projects in developing countries and count the savings toward their own targets.

forest degradation.text: A lasting decline in the biological richness of a forest, where the forest remains but is in worse condition.

carbon credit quality.text: How confident one can be that using a carbon credit leaves the world at least as well off as if the buyer had cut its own emissions.

criticisms of carbon offsetting.text: The case that offsets let polluters carry on with business as usual instead of cutting emissions at source.

voluntary carbon market.text: A largely unregulated market where companies, people and organisations with no legal duty to cut emissions buy offsets to meet goals they set themselves.

criticisms of redd+.text: Objections from researchers, Indigenous organisations and civil-society groups to the effectiveness, governance and fairness of REDD+.

leakage in forest carbon.text: The displacement of forest loss: protecting one area can push deforestation or degradation somewhere else, cancelling the gain.

effectiveness of redd+.text: The question of how much REDD+ and other forest-carbon schemes have actually reduced forest loss.

cancún safeguards.text: Seven social, environmental and governance safeguards for REDD+ adopted at the 2010 UN climate conference in Cancún.

verified carbon standard.text: A standard, run by the nonprofit Verra, for certifying carbon credits used to offset emissions.

carbon credit registry.text: A usually public database run by a crediting program that tracks who owns each carbon credit and when it is retired.

carbon offset project cycle.text: The steps by which an offset project is designed, financed, checked by an independent verifier and registered with a crediting program.

carbon offset project types.text: The kinds of projects that generate carbon credits, from land use and methane capture to renewable energy and energy efficiency.

land-use and forestry offsets.text: Offset projects in land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF) that protect or build natural carbon sinks such as forests and soil.

forestry offset integrity concerns.text: The criticism that forest-based carbon credits often fail to deliver the climate benefits they claim.

emissions baseline.text: An estimate of the emissions that would have occurred without a project, against which its reductions are measured.

forest reference emission level.text: A benchmark of a country's forest emissions or removals, in tonnes of CO2e per year, against which REDD+ results are judged.

forward crediting.text: Issuing carbon credits for emission cuts or removals that are only projected, so buyers can claim them before the work has happened.

gold standard.text: A certification label for emission-reduction projects in the Clean Development Mechanism and the voluntary carbon market.

market versus fund-based redd+ finance.text: The early dispute over whether REDD+ should be paid for by selling forest credits as offsets or through public funds.

redd+ eligible activities.text: The five kinds of action REDD+ counts: reducing deforestation, reducing forest degradation, conserving forest carbon, managing forests sustainably and enhancing forest carbon stocks.

redd+ phased approach.text: The UN plan for REDD+ to move in stages: readiness, then national policies and measures, then fully measured results-based actions.

forest inventory.text: The systematic collection of data about a forest, such as its trees, timber and wildlife, for assessment or analysis.

national forest monitoring system.text: A country's institutions and techniques for monitoring its forests and producing information for decisions and reporting.

hfc-23 destruction credits.text: CDM credits paid for destroying HFC-23, a super-potent by-product of refrigerant making, which became the classic case of a perverse offset incentive.

forest carbon partnership facility.text: A World Bank facility that helps developing countries prepare for and carry out REDD+.

timber cruise.text: A sample survey of a forest stand to estimate how much standing timber it holds.

safeguards information system.text: A country's system for reporting how the Cancún safeguards are addressed and respected while REDD+ is carried out.

verra rainforest credit investigations.text: Press and research investigations from 2021 onward finding that many Verra-certified forest-protection credits overstated their emission cuts.

new york declaration on forests.text: A voluntary, non-binding 2014 pledge by governments, companies and civil society to halve deforestation by 2020 and end it by 2030.

time value of carbon.text: The idea that cutting a tonne of greenhouse gas now is worth more than cutting the same tonne later, so emissions are discounted over time like money.

corresponding adjustments.text: An accounting step under the Paris Agreement that subtracts a transferred emission cut from the seller country's tally so that only the buyer counts it.

over-crediting.text: Issuing more carbon credits than the real emission cuts or removals a project achieved, sometimes producing so-called phantom credits.

debt.text: An obligation to repay money borrowed or otherwise owed to another party.

bond (finance).text: A bond is a loan in the form of a tradable security: the issuer borrows money and promises to pay the holder interest and repay the principal.

return on investment.text: Return on investment is the ratio of the profit an investment earns to what it cost.

stock.text: Stock is all the shares into which ownership of a company is divided; one share is a fraction of ownership.

conservation finance.text: Conservation finance is raising and managing money to protect land, water and natural resources.

environmental finance.text: Environmental finance is a branch of finance that uses market-based environmental policy tools, such as pricing and trading schemes, to make investment less harmful to nature.

official development assistance.text: Official development assistance is the OECD's measure of foreign aid: money that rich countries' governments give to promote poorer countries' development and welfare.

diversification (finance).text: Diversification is spreading money across different investments so that no single asset or risk can do too much harm.

economics of biodiversity.text: The economics of biodiversity studies how the variety of life supports the economy and how economic activity in turn harms it.

debt-for-nature swap.text: A debt-for-nature swap forgives part of a developing country's foreign debt in exchange for that country investing locally in conservation.

blended finance.text: Blended finance uses public development money and charitable funds strategically to draw private investment into developing countries.

trophy hunting.text: Trophy hunting is hunting for sport in which parts of the killed animal, such as the head, horns or hide, are kept and displayed.

fiduciary.text: A fiduciary is a person trusted to look after money or other assets for someone else and to act only in that person's interest.

economic drivers of biodiversity loss.text: Economic activities often harm biodiversity, and their profits mean they are usually favoured over conservation and restoration.

bond credit quality.text: Credit quality is how likely a bond's borrower is to pay the promised amounts on time rather than default.

bond yield.text: A bond's yield is the rate of return an investor earns from it.

types of bonds.text: Bonds are grouped by issuer, currency, term and the conditions attached to them.

additionality, leakage and permanence.text: Three tests of whether paid-for conservation really works: whether the result would not have happened anyway, whether harm simply moves elsewhere, and whether gains last.

divestment.text: The reduction of an asset, or the sale of a business, for financial, ethical or political objectives.

return on integration.text: Return on integration widens return on investment to count the long-term environmental and social returns of an investment alongside financial ones.

the 0.7% aid target.text: The best-known aid target says rich countries should give 0.7% of their national income as official development assistance.

tied aid.text: Tied aid is aid given on condition that the money is spent on goods from the donor country or a small group of countries.

conservation easement tax incentives.text: In the United States, donating a qualifying conservation easement can earn the landowner federal income tax deductions and other tax breaks.

purchase of conservation easements.text: Governments, nonprofits and donors often buy conservation easements outright, paying landowners directly.

criticism of debt-for-nature swaps.text: Critics argue that debt-for-nature swaps bring little real debt relief, send money to the wrong places and can harm local people.

types of debt-for-nature swaps.text: Debt-for-nature swaps come in three kinds: commercial three-party swaps run by NGOs, bilateral swaps between two governments, and multilateral swaps among several.

blended finance risk tools.text: Development funders support private investors in blended deals through technical assistance, risk underwriting and market incentives.

diversifiable and systematic risk.text: Diversifiable risk comes from a single company and can be spread away; systematic, or market, risk affects all assets and cannot.

diversification and portfolio variance.text: Mixing assets can bring a portfolio's variance, a measure of risk, below that of even its least risky asset.

agrobiodiversity and the economy.text: Agricultural biodiversity is all the parts of biodiversity that matter for food and farming, the origin of every crop and farm animal.

biodiversity and medicine.text: Biodiversity is a source of medicines and of ecosystem services that protect health.

biodiversity and nature tourism.text: Biodiversity earns money through recreation and tourism, such as hiking, fishing and wildlife watching, as a cultural ecosystem service.

biological pest control value.text: Biological pest control uses natural enemies to keep pests down, an ecosystem function that depends on biodiversity.

illegal wildlife trade economics.text: The illegal wildlife trade profits by selling products from wild animals and plants, including endangered species.

land trust.text: Land trusts are nonprofit or fiduciary arrangements that own and manage land, and sometimes water.

conservation land trust.text: A conservation land trust is a nonprofit that buys and looks after land, or holds conservation easements on it, to protect nature, farmland or recreation.

natural asset company.text: A Natural Asset Company is a corporation set up to hold and manage natural assets so that private investors can fund conservation and regenerative land use.

conservation trust fund.text: A conservation trust fund is a long-term fund that gives grants to conservation work, often set up as an endowment or a fund spent down over time.

measuring conservation finance results.text: Conservation finance deals often require reporting both how money was spent and what ecological results it achieved.

sources of conservation capital.text: Money for nature comes from domestic public spending, international public finance including aid, and private spending and investment.

sustainable finance.text: Sustainable finance covers the practices, standards, rules and products that seek financial returns while weighing environmental, social and governance concerns.

transaction costs in conservation financ.text: The costs of finding, assembling, checking, contracting and monitoring conservation projects, often cited as a barrier to scaling up.

catastrophe bond.text: A catastrophe bond moves a defined disaster risk from a sponsor, usually an insurer, to investors.

catastrophe bond triggers.text: Catastrophe bonds pay out under different triggers: the insurer's actual losses, modelled losses, industry-wide losses, or measured event parameters.

parametric insurance.text: Parametric, or index-based, insurance pays a pre-set amount when a measured trigger, such as a wind speed or rainfall level, is reached.

environmental, social, and governance.text: ESG is an investing approach that weighs a company's environmental, social and corporate governance record alongside its finances.

green bond.text: A green bond is a bond whose money is used only for projects with environmental benefits.

impact investing.text: Impact investing puts money into companies, organisations and funds meant to produce a measurable social or environmental benefit as well as a financial return.

climate, green and sustainable finance.text: UNEP separates three nested terms often used as synonyms: climate finance, green finance and sustainable finance.

sustainable finance taxonomy.text: A taxonomy is an official classification that says which economic activities count as green or sustainable for investors.

esg and financial performance.text: Economists disagree about whether attention to ESG raises or lowers a company's value and investors' returns.

responsible investment strategies.text: Responsible investors steer money using several methods: positive selection, exclusion, engagement, activism and integration of ESG factors.

eco-investing.text: Eco-investing, or green investing, is socially responsible investing focused on companies that offer environmentally friendly products and practices.

fragmented sustainability standards.text: Sustainable finance lacks a single accepted standard for measuring and reporting sustainability, so companies and funds are hard to compare.

green central banking.text: Green central banking is the idea that central banks should use monetary policy and capital rules to help cut emissions and steer money to green investment.

sustainability disclosure rules.text: Rules and standards that ask companies to report climate and other sustainability risks and impacts so investors can judge them.

sustainability bond.text: A sustainability bond is a bond whose money must fund a mix of green and social projects.

esg rating agencies.text: ESG rating agencies score companies on their ESG performance and are the main information providers for ESG investing.

equator principles.text: The Equator Principles are a framework banks use to assess and manage environmental and social risk in project finance.

principles for responsible investment.text: The Principles for Responsible Investment is a UN-backed framework, set up in 2005, to help investors analyse ESG issues and act as responsible owners.

greenium.text: The greenium is the lower yield, or pricing premium, that green bonds often carry because investors want them.

fiduciary duty and esg.text: A debate over whether investors' legal duty to beneficiaries allows, or even requires, them to weigh environmental, social and governance issues.

environmental investing.text: Environmental investing is the branch of impact investing aimed at a measurable positive environmental effect alongside financial returns.

mission investing by foundations.text: Mission investments are investments by foundations, from part or all of their endowment, that further their charitable goals while earning a return.

social finance.text: Social finance is financial services that use private capital to tackle social and environmental needs while giving investors a return.

cites.text: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, a treaty that protects endangered plants and animals from the threats of international trade.

social impact bond.text: A social impact bond is an outcomes-based contract in which private investors fund a public programme and the government repays them only if agreed goals are met.

sustainability-linked bond.text: A sustainability-linked bond is a bond whose terms, such as its interest rate, change depending on whether the issuer meets set sustainability targets.

blue bond.text: A blue bond is the ocean version of a green bond: it raises money specifically for ocean conservation and sustainable marine activity.

green bond principles.text: The Green Bond Principles are voluntary market guidance from the International Capital Market Association on how green bonds should be run.

integrated conservation and development.text: A biodiversity conservation project that also invests in rural development, so that local people gain from protecting nature.

ivory trade.text: The commercial, often illegal trade in the tusks of elephants and of other animals such as hippopotamus, walrus and narwhal.

reserve design.text: Planning a nature reserve's size, shape, location and links so that it actually achieves its goal of protecting biodiversity.

human–wildlife conflict.text: Harmful encounters between people and wild animals, with bad results both for people and their property and for wildlife and its habitat.

cites appendices.text: The three CITES lists that rank protected species by how much international trade threatens them, and set the trade controls that apply.

natural resource.text: Something drawn from nature and used with few changes, such as sunlight, air, water, land, minerals, plants and wildlife.

human–wildlife conflict mitigation.text: The methods used to reduce harmful encounters between people and wildlife, from fences and guard dogs to paying people for their losses.

conservation triage.text: The idea that not every species can be saved, so conservationists must choose which ones to spend their limited efforts on.

marxan.text: A family of software for systematic reserve design that finds networks of sites meeting biodiversity targets at low cost.

paper park.text: A protected area that exists on paper but has little real management or protection on the ground.

resource depletion.text: The using up of a natural resource faster than it can be replaced.

non-renewable resource.text: A natural resource, also called a finite resource, that nature cannot replace quickly enough to keep up with how fast people use it.

renewable resource.text: A natural resource, also called a flow resource, that replaces what is used up through natural reproduction or other recurring processes within a human time scale.

natural resource economics.text: The branch of economics that studies the supply, demand and sharing out of the Earth's natural resources.

resource curse.text: The idea that countries rich in natural resources such as oil and minerals often see slower economic growth, weaker democracy or worse development than countries with fewer resources.

exploitation of natural resources.text: Using natural resources, often non-renewable or limited ones, to drive economic growth or development.

malthusianism.text: The theory that population can grow exponentially while food and other resources grow only steadily, so living standards eventually fall until population declines.

economic rent.text: Any payment to the owner of a factor of production, such as land, beyond what is needed to bring that factor into use.

ecological yield.text: The amount of an ecosystem's growth that can be harvested while still letting it recover.

sustainable yield.text: The amount of a renewable resource people can harvest without over-harvesting or damaging it.

hubbert curve.text: A bell-shaped curve approximating how a resource's production rate rises, peaks and falls over time.

peak oil.text: The point when world petroleum production reaches its highest rate, after which it declines for good.

resource rent.text: The economic rent earned from using natural resources such as minerals, oil reserves, rivers, waterfalls, coastal space and wind.

hotelling's rule.text: A rule describing how the net price of a non-renewable resource should change over time when its owner extracts it so as to earn the most rent.

exchange rate.text: The rate at which one currency is exchanged for another.

classification of natural resources.text: Ways of sorting natural resources by origin, stage of development, renewability and ownership.

marine resources.text: Physical and biological things found in the oceans that are useful to people.

blue economy.text: Economic use of oceans, lakes, rivers and coasts, generally with an emphasis on using their resources sustainably.

dutch disease.text: The apparent link between a boom in one sector, such as natural resources, and a decline in other sectors such as manufacturing or agriculture.

law of rent.text: The principle that the rent of a piece of land equals the extra output it produces compared with the best land available rent-free, using the same labour and capital.

fixed stock versus opportunity cost para.term: Fixed stock versus opportunity cost paradigm
fixed stock versus opportunity cost para.text: A debate over whether to treat a mineral resource as a fixed physical stock, or to measure its usable amount through its price and opportunity cost.

cornucopianism.text: The view that advancing technology can keep supplying humanity's material needs, so growth is practically unlimited.

groundwater as a non-renewable resource.text: The view that much groundwater is effectively non-renewable because it refills far too slowly to be replaced within human lifetimes.

land as a fixed resource.text: The idea that land can be reused but not created on demand, so economists treat it as a fixed resource whose supply cannot respond to price.

nuclear fuel and renewability.text: The question of whether nuclear fuels should count as renewable, since mined uranium is finite but breeder reactors make more fuel than they use.

simon–ehrlich wager.text: A 1980 bet between economist Julian Simon and biologist Paul Ehrlich on whether natural resources would become scarcer, measured by metal prices up to 1990.

resource war.text: A war caused by conflict over resources, typically between whoever controls a resource and an aggressor who wants it.

malthusian checks.text: Malthus's two kinds of brake on population: preventive checks that lower birth rates and positive checks that shorten lives.

neo-malthusianism.text: The concern that overpopulation and overconsumption will deplete resources and degrade the environment until ecosystems collapse.

mineral resource classification.text: Systems for grading mineral deposits by how well they are known and whether they can be mined at a profit.

quasi-rent.text: A short-run, rent-like return earned by a factor of production, such as a machine or building, whose supply is fixed for the time being.

real exchange rate.text: The purchasing power of one currency relative to another at current exchange rates and prices, found as the nominal exchange rate times the relative price of a market basket of goods in the two countries.

oil reserve categories.text: The grouping of oil reserves by how likely they are to be produced: proven, probable and possible.

peak oil demand.text: The idea that world oil use will peak because people deliberately reduce demand, before supply runs short.

sovereign wealth fund.text: A state-owned investment fund that invests in assets such as stocks, bonds, real estate and precious metals.

unconventional oil.text: Oil that is difficult to extract, such as oil sands, as opposed to conventional oil from easy onshore and shallow offshore fields.

aid curse.text: The argument that heavy reliance on foreign aid can harm a country's development in the long run in the same way as the resource curse.
