petro-aggression.text: The tendency of a petrostate to start international conflicts or to be the target of them.

revenue volatility from resources.text: The large, sudden swings in government income that come from depending on natural resources whose prices fluctuate widely.

severance tax.text: A tax charged on removing natural resources such as oil, gas, coal, uranium or timber within a taxing jurisdiction.

perpetual resource.text: A resource so large relative to demand that it is unlikely ever to run out on a human time scale.

paleoresource.text: A resource for which there is little or no demand any more because the material taken from it has gone out of use.

blue finance.text: Finance that cuts the carbon footprint of ocean-related activities and benefits the marine environment, as part of sustainable finance.

blue justice.text: A critical approach examining how blue economy and blue growth initiatives affect coastal communities and small-scale fisheries.

conflict resources.text: Natural resources extracted in a conflict zone and sold to keep the fighting going.

corden–neary model.text: The classic 1982 economic model of Dutch disease, with a booming sector, a lagging tradable sector and a non-tradable services sector.

hotelling rent.text: The scarcity rent on a finite resource: the extra value it earns because extracting it today leaves less for the future.

resource scarcity indicators.text: Measures, such as a resource's inflation-adjusted price, used to judge whether natural resources are becoming scarcer.

resource substitution.text: Replacing a scarce material with another one in its end uses, a main way economies escape shortages of a particular resource.

critical raw materials.text: Raw materials that have no viable substitutes with current technology, that most consuming countries must import, and whose supply is dominated by one or a few producers.

stock effects in extraction.text: The tendency for extraction to become costlier as a resource stock is drawn down, pushing producers to less accessible sites and lower-grade ores.

peak minerals.text: A model of how the costs and impacts of mining change as ore quality declines before and after a region's mineral production peaks.

backstop resources.text: The theory that as a heavily used limited resource grows expensive, alternatives become cheap by comparison and so become worth using.

resource rent tax.text: A tax on the rent, or surplus profit, earned by exploiting a natural resource, which can apply to renewable and non-renewable resources.

fishery.text: A fishery is either the business of catching or raising fish and other aquatic life or, more often, the place where this happens, the fishing grounds.

overfishing.text: Overfishing is taking fish from a body of water faster than the species can naturally replace itself, so its numbers there keep falling.

aquaculture.text: Aquaculture, or aquafarming, is the controlled farming of aquatic organisms such as fish, crustaceans, molluscs, algae and aquatic plants.

fish stock.text: A fish stock is a subpopulation of one fish species whose growth, recruitment and deaths, including from fishing, are treated as the main drivers of its numbers.

fisheries management.text: Fisheries management is the set of tasks that guide users and managers toward the best use of renewable aquatic resources, mainly fish.

sustainable fishery.text: A sustainable fishery is conventionally one harvested at a rate at which the fish population does not decline over time because of fishing.

maximum sustainable yield.text: Maximum sustainable yield (MSY) is, in theory, the largest catch that can be taken from a stock year after year for an indefinite period.

marine protected area.text: A marine protected area (MPA) is a protected part of the seas, oceans or estuaries where human activity is restricted for conservation.

marine conservation.text: Marine conservation is the protection of ocean and sea ecosystems through planned management so that marine resources are not over-exploited.

population dynamics of fisheries.text: Population dynamics of fisheries is the study of how a fished population grows and shrinks over time through births, deaths and migration.

exclusive economic zone.text: An exclusive economic zone (EEZ) is a sea area, set by the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, where a coastal state has exclusive rights to explore and use marine resources.

bycatch.text: Bycatch is fish or other marine life caught unintentionally while fishing for particular species or sizes.

illegal, unreported and unregulated fish.text: Illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing covers fishing without permission or against the law, fishing that is not or wrongly reported, and fishing where no conservation rules apply.

fisheries science.text: Fisheries science is the academic discipline of understanding and managing fisheries.

wild fisheries.text: Wild fisheries, also called capture fisheries, are natural waters holding free-ranging fish or shellfish populations that are caught for commercial value.

rent dissipation in open-access fisherie.text: In an open-access fishery, competition drives fishers to invest until their costs equal their revenue, so the resource rent is wiped out.

types of overfishing.text: Biologists recognise three types of overfishing: growth overfishing, recruitment overfishing and ecosystem overfishing.

climate change and fisheries.text: Climate change affects fisheries through warming, acidifying and oxygen-poor oceans, and through altered temperatures, flows and habitats in fresh waters.

economic objective of fisheries manageme.text: In economics, the aim of fisheries management is to maximise the present value of all future profits from a fishery, which is treated as a common property resource.

ecosystem-based fisheries management.text: Ecosystem-based fisheries management manages fishing for the health and productivity of the whole ecosystem rather than for single target species.

fisheries input and output controls.text: Fisheries regulation falls into four core categories that limit either what goes into fishing (inputs such as boats and gear) or what comes out (the catch), directly or indirectly.

recreational fishing.text: Recreational fishing, also called sport or game fishing, is fishing for leisure, exercise or competition rather than for profit or survival.

optimum sustainable yield.text: Optimum sustainable yield is the level of fishing effort that maximizes the gap between total revenue and total cost, the resource's economic profit or rent.

fishing down the food web.text: Fishing down the food web is the process in which fisheries, having used up the large predatory fish, turn to ever smaller species and finally to small fish and invertebrates once ignored.

fisheries subsidy.text: A fisheries subsidy is a government action that gives fishers or fish consumers an advantage by topping up their income or lowering their costs.

regional fishery body.text: A regional fishery body is an international organization set up under a fishery agreement for countries to cooperate on conserving and sustainably using marine living resources.

plant genetic resources.text: Plant genetic resources are the variety within plants, built up by human and natural selection over millennia, that can be used for food and agriculture now or in future.

criticism of maximum sustainable yield.text: Maximum sustainable yield, though widely used by agencies managing fish, forests and wildlife, has been heavily criticised by ecologists on theoretical and practical grounds.

sustainable seafood.text: Sustainable seafood is fish and shellfish caught or farmed in ways that protect the long-term health of the species, the oceans and the communities that depend on fishing.

shifting baseline.text: A shifting baseline is when a system is judged against a reference point that itself already reflects large, forgotten changes from an earlier state.

international treaty on plant genetic re.term: International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture
international treaty on plant genetic re.text: The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture, or Plant Treaty, aims to secure food security by conserving, exchanging and sustainably using crop genetic resources and sharing their benefits fairly.

types of fisheries.text: Fisheries are divided into commercial, recreational and subsistence sectors, and can be saltwater or freshwater, wild or farmed.

fishing capacity.text: Fishing capacity is the most a fishery's boats and gear could catch, measured either by the capital fully used (input) or by the maximum catch (output).

bide model.text: The BIDE model is the basic accounting rule of population dynamics: next period's numbers equal current numbers plus births and immigrants, minus deaths and emigrants.

big old fecund female fish.text: Large, old female fish turn out to matter far more than young ones for keeping fisheries productive, contrary to traditional management.

ecopath.text: Ecopath with Ecosim is a software suite for modelling marine ecosystems, widely used in fisheries management.

integrated multi-trophic aquaculture.text: Integrated multi-trophic aquaculture recycles the wastes of one farmed species as food or fertiliser for another.

definitions of fishery sustainability.text: There are three ways to define a sustainable fishery: long-term constant yield, preserving intergenerational equity, and maintaining a whole biological, social and economic system.

huxley inexhaustible fisheries claim.text: In 1883 Thomas Huxley claimed overfishing was scientifically impossible and the great sea fisheries inexhaustible, even as fisheries were already collapsing.

overfishing versus unsustainability.text: Overfishing in the traditional sense, catching so much that yield falls below what lighter fishing would give, is not automatically unsustainable.

displaced fishing effort.text: Displaced fishing effort is the worry that closing an area to fishing just pushes the same fishing elsewhere, cancelling the reserve's benefits.

spillover effect.text: Spillover is the net movement of fish, eggs and larvae from a recovering marine protected area into the fishing grounds around it.

straddling and transboundary stocks.text: A straddling stock ranges both inside a country's exclusive economic zone and on the high seas; a transboundary stock ranges across the zones of at least two countries.

measuring fishing effort.text: Fishing effort is a measure of the human work put into catching fish, ideally roughly proportional to the amount caught.

recruitment (fisheries).text: Recruitment is the number of new young fish entering a population in a given year, usually counted from the age at which they can be caught in nets.

von bertalanffy growth model.text: The von Bertalanffy growth model, published in 1934, describes how fast individual fish grow in length toward a maximum length.

beverton–holt model.text: The Beverton–Holt model is a classic discrete-time population model that predicts next generation's numbers from this generation's, levelling off at carrying capacity.

catch per unit effort.text: Catch per unit effort (CPUE) is an indirect measure of how abundant a target species is, based on how much is caught for a given amount of fishing.

ricker model.text: The Ricker model is a classic population model that predicts the number of individuals in the next generation from the number in the current one.

fisheries monitoring, control and survei.text: Fisheries monitoring, control and surveillance (MCS) widens the enforcement of national fishing rules into support for fisheries management as a whole.

bycatch reduction devices.text: Bycatch reduction devices and other gear changes let unwanted animals escape from fishing gear.

fisheries crime.text: Fisheries crime is a wider idea than IUU fishing that takes in all criminal activity along the fishing sector's value chain.

rule of capture.text: The rule of capture means a fisher owns a fish only once it is caught, which economists see as the main driver of overfishing.

ghost nets.text: Ghost nets are fishing nets left or lost in the ocean that go on entangling fish, turtles, seabirds and other sea life.

trawling.text: Trawling is an industrial fishing method that drags a net, called a trawl, through the water behind one or more boats.

gordon-schaefer model.text: The Gordon-Schaefer model is a bioeconomic model of a fishery that combines fish population growth with the costs and revenues of fishing.

maximum economic yield.text: Maximum economic yield (MEY) is the level of catch that gives society the largest net economic benefit, or profit, from a fishery.

bottom trawling habitat damage.text: Repeatedly dragging heavy bottom trawls and dredges over the seabed flattens its habitats and radically changes the communities living there.

discards.text: Discards are the part of a catch that is not kept on board but thrown back into the sea, often dead or dying.

total allowable catch.text: A total allowable catch system caps the catch of a whole fishery: fishers may fish when and how they like until the quota is met, then fishing stops until the next season.

biological and economic overfishing.text: Biological overfishing is fishing so hard that the stock's growth slows; economic overfishing is catching more than the maximum economic yield, where resource rent is highest.

common fisheries policy.text: The Common Fisheries Policy is the European Union's fisheries policy: it sets catch quotas, gives member states access to one another's exclusive economic zones and manages sustainable fishing in the EU's zone.

territorial use rights for fishing.text: Territorial use rights for fishing (TURFs) give communities or individuals exclusive fishing privileges over a defined area to prevent overexploitation.

farming up the food web.text: Farming up the food web is the rise in the average trophic level of farmed fish while that of wild catches falls.

marine trophic index.text: The Marine Trophic Index is the average trophic level of a fishery's catch, used as a gauge of marine ecosystem health.

annual sustainable yield.text: Annual sustainable yield is the biomass that can be harvested from a fish population each year without causing it to decline.

seafood ecolabelling.text: Seafood ecolabelling has an independent third party check a fishery's or farm's production against environmental standards, licensing a label for products that pass.

seafood guides.text: Seafood guides tell shoppers which species are fine to eat and which to avoid, based on their environmental impact.

fish mortality.text: Fish mortality is a measure used in fisheries population models for the loss of fish from a stock through death.

stock assessment.text: A stock assessment gathers biological and fishery data to give fisheries managers the information they use to regulate a fish stock.

individual fishing quota.text: Individual fishing quotas, also called individual transferable quotas, are catch shares: a regulator sets a total allowable catch and hands portions of it to individual fishers.

harvest control rule.text: A harvest control rule is a set of pre-agreed tools that ties how much may be caught to the estimated state of the stock.

fisheries law.text: Fisheries law is an emerging specialist field of law that studies fisheries management approaches such as catch shares and territorial use rights.

virtual population analysis.text: Virtual population analysis is a fisheries technique that reconstructs past numbers of fish at each age from the yearly deaths in each cohort.

criticisms of individual fishing quotas.text: Critics say individual fishing quotas privatise a public resource, concentrate it in few hands and hurt fishing communities.

highgrading.text: Highgrading is catching more fish than a quota allows and dumping the less valuable ones so that the quota is filled with the best fish.

quota allocation: grants versus auctions.text: Fishing quotas can first be handed out free, usually by past catch, or sold at auction, and the choice decides who captures the resource's value.

race to fish.text: The race to fish is the scramble to catch as much as possible during short open seasons, which catch shares are designed to end.

biological reference points.text: Biological reference points are benchmarks produced by stock assessments against which fishing regulations are set.

discard ban.text: A discard ban requires fishers to land what they catch, so that dead discards are counted in the fishing mortality used for management.

fishing effort and overcapacity.text: Fishing effort is the amount of human work put into catching fish; excess effort and overcapacity in fishing fleets threaten the sustainability of fish stocks.

optimal harvesting.text: Optimal harvesting theory uses optimisation methods from economics and operations research to choose the best rate and timing of harvest, and is widely used in fisheries.

surplus production model.text: Surplus production models are the simplest of the three common kinds of fish stock assessment model, needing the least data.

density dependence.text: Density dependence is when a population's growth rate is controlled by how crowded the population is.

land use.text: A description of what happens on a piece of land: the benefits people get from it and the management actions they carry out there.

forestry.text: The science and craft of creating, managing, planting, using, conserving and repairing forests and woodlands for human and environmental benefit.

logistic harvesting model.text: The simplest harvest model subtracts a constant catch H from logistic population growth and finds where catch equals growth.

fisheries-induced evolution.text: Fisheries-induced evolution is genetic change in a fished population caused by fishing selectively removing individuals with certain traits.

international convention for the regulat.term: International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling
international convention for the regulat.text: The International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling is an international agreement to conserve whale stocks and so allow the whaling industry to develop in an orderly way.

forest management.text: The branch of forestry that handles the administrative, legal, economic and social side of running forests, along with technical work such as silviculture and forest protection.

water resources.text: Natural sources of water that are potentially useful to people, for example for drinking or irrigation.

agriculture.text: Agriculture is the cultivation of soil and the planting and harvesting of food and non-food crops, together with livestock production.

groundwater.text: Water held beneath Earth's surface in the pore spaces of soil and rock and in rock fractures.

water scarcity.text: A lack of fresh water sources, local or affordably transported, that can meet a region's normal demand for water.

water pollution.text: Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies, usually by human activity, in a way that harms how they can be used.

drainage basin.text: An area of land in which all flowing surface water drains to a single point, such as a river mouth, or into another body of water such as a lake or ocean.

urbanization.text: Urbanization is the process by which settlements grow as more people live and work in cities, shifting population from rural to urban areas.

aquifer.text: An underground layer of porous, permeable or fractured rock, or of gravel, sand or silt, that holds water.

intensive farming.text: Farming of crops or animals with high inputs and outputs per unit of land, as opposed to extensive farming.

water security.text: The goal of getting the most benefit from water for people and ecosystems while keeping the risks of floods, droughts and polluted water acceptably low.

commodity.text: A commodity is an economic good, usually a resource, whose instances the market treats as equivalent regardless of who produced them (fungibility).

land use, land-use change and forestry (.term: Land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF)
land use, land-use change and forestry (.text: A greenhouse gas inventory sector covering emissions and removals from direct human land use, land-use change and forestry.

trade.text: Trade is the exchange of something of value for something else of value, pre-agreed as a contract.

food system.text: All the connected people, institutions, policies and infrastructure involved in feeding a population.

bioenergy.text: Bioenergy is renewable energy obtained by using biomass as fuel, whether wood, energy crops, harvest residues or organic waste.

silviculture.text: The practice of controlling how forests grow, what they are made of and their quality, mainly to produce timber.

food loss and waste.text: Food that is thrown away or otherwise lost without being eaten.

pastoralism.text: A way of raising livestock by letting the animals graze on large open pastures, historically by nomadic people who moved with their herds.

shifting cultivation.text: A farming system in which a plot is cropped for a while, then left to regrow wild vegetation while the farmer moves on to another plot.

slash-and-burn agriculture.text: A form of shifting cultivation in which forest or woodland plants are cut and burned to make a field, called a swidden.

clearcutting.text: A logging practice in which most or all of the trees in an area are cut down at once.

privatization.text: Privatization most commonly means moving something from the public sector into the private sector, such as selling a state-owned enterprise to private investors.

land value tax.text: A tax on the value of land alone, ignoring buildings and other improvements on it.

groundwater depletion.text: Pumping groundwater out faster than an aquifer's equilibrium yield, also called overdrafting.

forest product.text: Any material taken from forestry for direct use or sale, such as lumber, paper or livestock fodder.

non-timber forest product.text: Useful foods, materials and other goods taken from forests other than timber.

illegal logging.text: Harvesting, transporting, buying or selling timber in breach of the law.

land use change.text: The change of a piece of land from one land-use category to another.

water right.text: A user's legal right to take and use water from a source such as a river, stream, pond or groundwater.

sustainable forest management.text: Managing forests according to the principles of sustainable development.

economic water scarcity.text: Water scarcity caused by too little investment in the infrastructure or technology needed to draw water from rivers, aquifers and other sources.

physical water scarcity.text: Water scarcity that occurs when natural water resources are not enough to meet all demands, including the water ecosystems need.

land grabbing.text: The large-scale buying or leasing of land by domestic or foreign companies, governments and individuals.

hidden costs of food.text: The environmental, social and health costs of producing and eating food that are not reflected in food prices, also called external costs.

prior-appropriation water rights.text: A rule for sharing water under which the first person to take water for a beneficial use keeps the right to go on taking that amount for that use.

riparian water rights.text: A system that shares water among the owners of land along a river, lake or other water body.

peak water.text: The idea that the availability, quality and use of fresh water face growing limits.

groundwater pollution.text: Contamination that happens when pollutants released on the ground make their way into groundwater.

land subsidence from groundwater pumping.text: Sinking or collapse of the ground when too much water is pumped out from underground.

seawater intrusion.text: The movement of dense seawater into coastal aquifers, which hold a lens of fresh water on top of salt water.

land-use regulation.text: Public rules, such as zoning, by which governments plan and control how land may be used.

land-use planning.text: The process by which a central authority regulates how land may be used.

plantation forestry.text: Growing forests planted for high-volume wood production, usually as a monoculture of one tree species.

proforestation.text: Protecting existing natural forests so they keep growing, storing carbon and gaining structural complexity without harvesting.

thermal pollution.text: Thermal pollution is the degradation of water quality by human activity that raises or lowers a water body's ambient temperature.

water pollution control.text: Water pollution is controlled by treating municipal, industrial and agricultural wastewater and by managing sediment and urban runoff at the source.

water pricing.text: The various ways of setting a price for water.

catchment factors.text: Features of a drainage basin, namely topography, shape, size, soil type and land use, that determine how likely it is to flood.

endorheic basin.text: An inland drainage basin whose water never reaches the ocean.

confined and unconfined aquifers.text: A classification of aquifers by whether an impermeable layer lies above them.

forest genetic diversity.text: The DNA differences among forest trees, which keep forests healthy and able to adapt.

forestry law.text: Laws that govern activities on designated forest land, mainly forest management and timber harvesting.

concentrated animal feeding operations.text: Raising livestock in confinement at high density, often called factory farming.

water conflict.text: Violence or disputes over access to or control of water, or the use of water and water systems as weapons or targets in conflicts.

water risk.text: The possibility of water-related problems such as scarcity, stress, flooding, drought or decaying infrastructure.

water use by sector.text: How water is divided among uses such as irrigated farming, industry and households, some needing water only at times and others continuously.

water resource management.text: Planning, developing, distributing and managing the best use of water resources.

integrated water resources management.text: A process that coordinates the development and management of water, land and related resources to maximize economic and social welfare fairly without harming vital ecosystems.

virtual water.text: The water hidden in food and other goods, which in effect moves from place to place when those goods are traded.

environmental flow.text: The amount, timing and quality of river flow needed to sustain freshwater and estuarine ecosystems and the people who depend on them.

water stress indicators.text: Simple measures of how scarce water is, such as the ratio of water use to water available or the water available per person each year.

reduced-impact logging.text: A set of carefully planned and controlled timber-harvesting practices, carried out by trained workers, that make selective logging of tropical forests less damaging.

faustmann's formula.text: A formula giving the present value of the income from repeatedly growing and harvesting a forest, used to find the best age to cut it.

dublin principles.text: Four principles for water management set out in the 1992 Dublin Statement.

commodity super cycle.text: A commodity super cycle is a period of about a decade when commodities as a whole trade above their long-term moving average.

free trade.text: Free trade is a policy by which a government does not discriminate against imports or exports through tariffs or subsidies.

protectionism.text: Protectionism is the policy of restraining and discouraging trade between states, often through tariffs and restrictive quotas.

trade sanctions.text: Trade sanctions are restrictions imposed on a country to punish it for an action, the severest being an embargo, a blockade of all trade.

alternative food systems.text: Initiatives that organize food production, distribution and eating differently from conventional industrial systems.

sustainable food system.text: A food system that provides healthy food while sustaining the environmental, economic and social systems around food.

biofuel generations.text: Biofuels are classed as first-generation, made from food crops on arable land, or second-generation, made from non-food biomass.

surface power density.text: Surface power density is the power a generation source delivers per square metre of land, which fixes how much land a given supply needs.

precision agriculture.text: A farm management strategy that collects and analyzes data on fields, plants and animals to tailor decisions to local variation and use resources more efficiently.

coppicing.text: A way of regrowing a forest that relies on cut trees sending up new shoots from their stumps.

even-aged and uneven-aged forest managem.text: The two broad families of methods that combine harvesting timber with re-establishing the forest, differing in how much of the stand is cut at once.

forest thinning.text: Cutting out some of the trees in a stand so that the remaining ones grow faster.

net animal losses.text: A measure of food waste: the calories in human-edible crops fed to animals minus the calories returned as meat, dairy and fish.

pastoral commons and hardin's critique.text: The dispute over whether shared grazing lands are bound to be overused, as Garrett Hardin argued in 1968, or can be governed well by communities, as Elinor Ostrom showed.

forms of privatization.text: Privatization takes several main forms: share issue, asset sale, voucher privatization, privatization from below and management buyout.

agricultural economics.text: A branch of applied economics that uses economic theory to improve how food and fibre are produced and distributed.

multiple use and sustained yield.text: A forest management principle, written into a 1960 United States law, of using a forest's timber, range, water, recreation and wildlife together while keeping their output going indefinitely.

commodification of water.text: The process of turning water, especially fresh water, from a public good into a commodity that can be bought and sold.

socio-economic effects of groundwater ov.text: The unequal economic burden created as falling water tables force users to dig deeper wells.

urban economics.text: Urban economics is a branch of microeconomics that studies urban spatial structure and the location of households and firms.

tropical rainforest conservation.text: Efforts to protect and restore tropical rainforests, ranging from strict preservation to sustainable management by people living in them.

water bankruptcy.text: A state in which long overuse of a water system has caused damage so lasting that it can no longer return to its former supply and ecosystem services.

water privatization.text: The involvement of private companies in providing water supply and sanitation services.

first-in-time rights beyond water.text: The use of the first in time, first in right principle for resources other than water, such as mineral deposits, farmland and pollution rights.

backstop water sources.text: Water sources, such as desalinated seawater, that can replace unsustainable or non-renewable water use, usually at a higher cost.

criteria and indicators of sustainable f.term: Criteria and indicators of sustainable forest management
criteria and indicators of sustainable f.text: Policy tools for evaluating and reporting how sustainably forests are managed in a country or region.

water resource policy.text: The policy-making and laws that govern how water is collected, treated, used, disposed of and protected.

water abstraction charges.text: Fees some countries levy for taking water directly from rivers, lakes and aquifers, which in most countries is free.

restoration hotspots.text: Areas where restoring rainforest gives the highest social and economic benefits and is most feasible.

human right to water and sanitation.term: Human right to water and sanitation
human right to water and sanitation.text: The principle that clean drinking water and sanitation are a universal human right because every life depends on them.

transboundary water agreements.text: Treaties and other agreements between countries on how to share and manage water that crosses their borders.

natural resource management.text: Natural resource management is the managing of land, water, soil, plants and animals with attention to how it affects life for people now and in the future.

commons.text: The commons are the cultural and natural resources open to all members of a society, such as air, water and a habitable Earth.

property regimes for natural resources.text: Resource management approaches can be grouped by who holds rights over a resource: the state, a private owner, a group, no one, or a mix.

von thünen model.text: Johann Heinrich von Thünen's model of farmland use, set out in The Isolated State (1826), in which the cost of transporting goods eats into the rent land can earn.

water-energy nexus.text: The two-way link between the water used to produce energy and the energy used to extract, treat, move, heat and dispose of water.

enclosure.text: Enclosure was the English practice of fencing off 'waste' or common land and taking it over, which stripped commoners of their traditional rights to use it.

community-based natural resource managem.text: Community-based natural resource management combines conservation goals with economic benefits for rural communities.

community forestry.text: Community forestry is a participatory approach, prominent since the 1970s, in which local communities take an active part in managing forests and deciding land use.

ostrom's design principles.text: A set of rules Elinor Ostrom found in commons that are governed successfully, such as clear boundaries, monitoring and graduated sanctions.

global commons.text: The global commons are shared resource areas, such as the high seas, the atmosphere, outer space and Antarctica, that lie beyond the political reach of any single nation.

customary land.text: Customary land is land held and used under unwritten local custom rather than written, codified law.

common ownership.text: Common ownership means holding an organization's or community's assets as one undivided whole, not in the names of individual members.

integrated natural resource management.text: Integrated natural resource management manages resources systematically, balancing biophysical, political and economic aspects to meet both users' production goals and wider community goals.

stakeholder analysis in resource managem.text: Stakeholder analysis identifies the different interest groups affected by how natural resources are used and conserved.

commoning.text: Commoning treats the commons as an ongoing practice, the process of people coming together to manage shared resources, rather than as a thing.

urban commons.text: Urban commons are city resources managed by citizens themselves, valued by their use and upkeep costs rather than their market price.

joint forest management.text: Joint Forest Management is India's term for partnerships in which state forest departments and local communities share forest protection and development.

open-field system.text: Before enclosure, English common land lay under the manorial lord, with a manor made up of peasant tenants' holdings and the lord's own demesne farm.

institutional analysis and development f.text: The IAD framework is Elinor Ostrom's theoretical tool for studying how people, called actors, interact with common-pool resources.

joint ownership in contract theory.text: In the incomplete-contracts approach of Oliver Hart and colleagues, ownership matters because the owner holds residual control rights: the say over an asset in any situation a contract does not cover.

international association for the study.term: International Association for the Study of the Commons
international association for the study.text: A non-profit association founded in 1989 to advance understanding of institutions for managing resources held or used in common.

governing the commons.text: Governing the Commons (1990) is Elinor Ostrom's best-known book, showing that communities worldwide have managed shared resources successfully through local rules.

nature-based solutions.text: Nature-based solutions (NBS) are actions that protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle social challenges while benefiting both people and biodiversity.

ecosystem-based adaptation.text: Ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA) is the use of biodiversity and ecosystem services to help people adapt to the harmful effects of climate change.

ecological engineering.text: Ecological engineering uses ecology and engineering to design, build or restore, and manage ecosystems that benefit both human society and nature.

phytoremediation.text: The use of living plants to clean up soil, air and water contaminated with pollutants.

monitoring and evaluation.text: Management processes that organizations use to improve their outputs, outcomes and impact.

criticism of nature-based solutions.text: Critics argue nature-based solutions can serve as greenwashing and distract from cutting emissions, and that their evidence base is uneven.

hybrid green–grey infrastructure.text: Hybrid green–grey infrastructure combines nature-based solutions with conventional built ('grey') infrastructure, which studies find works better than either alone.

types of nature-based solutions.text: A scientific typology sorts nature-based solutions by how much they engineer ecosystems and how many services and stakeholder groups they target.

barriers to ecosystem-based adaptation.text: Although case studies show EbA can be effective and cost-effective, several recognised challenges slow its adoption.

ecological engineering functional classe.text: Mitsch and Jorgensen sort ecological engineering designs into five functional classes by how the ecosystem is used.

ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction.text: Ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction (Eco-DRR) uses ecosystems to prevent and reduce disasters.

phytoextraction.text: A phytoremediation process in which plants take up contaminants from soil or water and concentrate them in above-ground biomass.

phytoscreening.text: Using plants as biosensors of subsurface contamination to delineate contaminant plumes.

phytostabilization.text: A phytoremediation process that lowers the mobility of pollutants by holding them in the soil near the roots rather than in plant tissue.

phytostimulation.text: Enhancement of soil microbial activity near roots to degrade organic contaminants, also called rhizodegradation.

phytovolatilization.text: Removal of substances from soil or water by plants, with release into the air as more volatile or less polluting forms.

rhizofiltration.text: A process that filters water through a mass of roots to remove toxic substances or excess nutrients.

natural climate solutions.text: Natural climate solutions are conservation, restoration and improved land-management actions that increase carbon storage or avoid greenhouse-gas emissions.

stormwater.text: Water that comes from precipitation, including heavy rain and melted hail and snow.

green infrastructure.text: A network of natural or nature-like features, also called blue-green infrastructure, used to solve urban and climate problems by building with nature.

flood management.text: The methods, also called flood control, used to reduce or prevent the harm done by flood waters.

flood.text: An overflow of water that submerges land that is usually dry.

drinking water.text: Water that is safe to ingest, whether drunk directly or used in food preparation.

dam.text: A structure that impounds water or restricts its flow.

urban flooding.text: Flooding of land or property in a built-up area when rain or coastal storm surges overwhelm drainage systems such as storm sewers.

constructed wetland.text: An artificial wetland built to clean sewage, greywater, stormwater runoff or industrial wastewater.

levee.text: An elevated ridge alongside a river, often built to protect the adjoining area from flooding.

sustainable drainage system.text: A set of water management practices, also called SuDS, that make modern drainage work with natural water processes as part of a wider green infrastructure strategy.

bioswale.text: A channel, usually planted or mulched, that gathers and carries stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution.

water-sensitive urban design.text: A planning and engineering approach, called WSUD, that builds the whole urban water cycle (stormwater, groundwater, wastewater and supply) into city design to limit environmental harm and improve amenity.

bioretention.text: The removal of pollutants and sediment from stormwater runoff by a planted soil area.

rain garden.text: A shallow planted hollow, also called a bioretention facility, that helps rain runoff soak back into the soil.

detention basin.text: An excavated area on or near a waterway that protects against flooding, and sometimes downstream erosion, by temporarily storing water.

low-impact development.text: A North American land planning and engineering approach, called LID, that manages stormwater runoff as part of green infrastructure.

permeable paving.text: Paving made of porous material, or of solid blocks with gaps, that lets stormwater pass through into the ground below.

combined sewer.text: A gravity sewer system that carries sewage and urban stormwater runoff together to a treatment plant or disposal site.

stormwater management.text: Managing the quantity and quality of stormwater, using both engineered controls and everyday practices known as best management practices.

structural flood control.text: Reducing flood effects with physical works such as reservoirs, levees, dredging and diversion channels.

non-structural flood management.text: Ways of reducing flood risk that do not physically hold back water, such as zoning, mapping, modelling and planning.

economics of green versus grey infrastru.term: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure
economics of green versus grey infrastru.text: The comparison of costs and benefits between green infrastructure and conventional 'grey' infrastructure such as concrete pipes and tunnels.

green gentrification.text: The displacement of lower-income residents when new green spaces raise property values and attract wealthier people.

sponge city.text: A nature-based urban planning model from China that uses green infrastructure, not just drains, to manage urban water and floods.

beaver dam.text: A dam built by beavers, creating a pond that protects them from predators and stores food for winter.

combined sewer overflow.text: A relief structure, and the discharge event it causes, diverting flow beyond a combined sewer's treatment capacity into waterways.

flood peak attenuation.text: Slowing runoff so that a flood's short, steep peak is spread out over time and lowered.

flood risk mapping.text: Drawing maps of where floods may reach, so policy makers can make informed decisions about flood hazards.

managed retreat from floodplains.text: Removing buildings from flood-prone areas and leaving the land as parks or wilderness.

storm surge barrier.text: A floodgate built to stop a storm surge or spring tide from flooding the area behind it.

point-of-use water treatment.text: Household-scale or community-scale treatment of drinking water at the point where it is used.

water fluoridation.text: The controlled addition of fluoride to public water supplies to reduce tooth decay.

barriers to green infrastructure.text: The obstacles, above all a lack of funding, that slow the building of green infrastructure.

blue infrastructure.text: City infrastructure that involves water, such as rivers, ponds, lakes and harbours.

constructed floating wetland.text: A planted structure that floats on a lake, river, estuary or coastal water and supports wetland vegetation.

downspout disconnection.text: Cutting a roof's downspout off from the sewer and sending the roof water onto ground that can soak it up.

green and blue roofs.text: Roofs covered with plants and soil (green roofs) or built to collect and hold rainfall (blue roofs).

green infrastructure planning.text: A planning approach that maps what the natural environment does and then protects key natural areas through regulation or planning policy.

floodplain restoration.text: Returning all or part of a river's floodplain to its condition before levees were built and wetlands drained.

stream restoration.text: Work to improve the environmental health of a river or stream, for biodiversity, recreation, flood management or landscape.

stormwater basin.text: A planted hollow in the ground that collects rainwater to cut runoff to sewers, reduce erosion, filter water and prevent flooding.

dam spillways and outlets.text: Auxiliary structures that release water from a reservoir: spillways pass excess flow and outlets permit partial drawdown.

dam types.text: Human-made dams are grouped by structure as embankment, gravity, buttress, arch or composite.

dam removal.text: Demolishing a dam to return natural water flow to a river.

economic impacts of urban flooding.text: The financial costs urban floods impose on property owners, businesses and cities.

grey infrastructure.text: Conventional infrastructure such as dams, seawalls, pipes and channels, built of concrete or other impervious materials to control water.

integrated urban water management.text: Managing a city's freshwater, wastewater and stormwater together as parts of one river-basin plan.

types of urban flooding.text: The three kinds of urban flood planners distinguish: pluvial (from heavy rain), fluvial (from a river overflowing) and coastal (often from storm surges).

subsurface flow constructed wetland.text: A constructed wetland in which the wastewater flows among plant roots below a gravel surface, so no water shows at the top.

surface flow constructed wetland.text: A constructed wetland with open water flowing horizontally across plant roots, also called a free water surface wetland.

environmental impacts of levees.text: Levees cut rivers off from their floodplains and change sediment and habitat.

levee failure.text: The ways a natural or artificial levee can fail and let water onto the land it protects.

natural levee.text: A ridge of mud and silt that forms on a floodplain beside a river channel without human intervention.

retention basin.text: An artificial pond, also called a wet pond, with plants around its edge and a permanent pool of water, used to manage stormwater.

infiltration trench.text: A shallow trench filled with gravel or rock that holds stormwater underground and lets it seep slowly into the soil and groundwater.

sedimentation basin.text: A basin that holds stormwater briefly and slows it so coarse and medium sediments settle out.

types of permeable pavement.text: The families of porous paving materials, each with its own advantages for particular uses.

combined sewer overflow mitigation.text: Measures to cut untreated overflows, including sewer separation, storage, more treatment capacity and green infrastructure.

beaver dam analog.text: A human-built structure that imitates a beaver dam, to gain its benefits or to attract beavers to settle.

room for the river.text: A Dutch government plan, run from 2006 to 2015, that protects against floods by giving the country's rivers more space while improving landscape and environment.

flood pulse concept.text: The idea that a river's regular cycle of flooding and drying controls the exchange of water, nutrients and organisms between the channel and its floodplain.

alternatives to dam removal.text: Ways of reducing a dam's harm without removing it, such as better equipment, environmental flows and fish ladders.

dam removal methods.text: The four common ways of removing a dam, chosen mainly by how the sediment behind it is handled.

active and passive riparian revegetation.text: Bringing back riparian plants either by planting them (active) or by removing the disturbance and letting them return (passive).

engineered log jam.text: Placing large wood in a stream to recreate the natural log jams that channelization and beaver removal took away.

form-based stream restoration.text: Restoration that changes a stream channel's physical shape to improve its condition.

natural channel design.text: A US method from the 1990s that classifies a stream by its shape, slope and bed and then redesigns the channel to a target form.

process-based stream restoration.text: Restoration that rebuilds the water and sediment processes that shape a stream, rather than its form.

stream corridor (freedom space).text: A band of land, set by a stream's hydrology and geomorphology, within which the stream is left free to move with minimal intervention.

streambank bioengineering.text: Stabilizing stream banks with live plants rather than only with hard structures such as riprap and gabions.

blue carbon.text: Carbon taken up and stored by living marine systems, especially coastal ones, in ways that people can manage.

coastal erosion.text: The loss of land, or long-term removal of sediment and rock, along a coastline by waves, currents, tides, wind-driven water, ice or storms.

first flush.text: The first runoff of a rainstorm, which washes off pollution that has built up on hard surfaces.

source water protection.text: Planning by water utilities and governments to protect drinking water sources from overuse and contamination.

coastal management.text: Defending coasts against flooding and erosion, including techniques that stop erosion to claim land.

managed retreat.text: The planned, coordinated movement of people, buildings and infrastructure away from places at risk.

seawall.text: A hard coastal defence built where the sea acts directly on the land, to protect people, property and activities from tides, waves or tsunamis.

longshore drift.text: Longshore drift is the transport of sediment (clay, silt, pebbles, sand, shingle, shells) along a coast parallel to the shoreline, depending on the angle of incoming waves.

beach nourishment.text: Replacing sand lost from a beach through erosion or longshore drift with sediment brought from elsewhere.

oyster reef.text: A dense colony of oysters that builds up into a large reef, also called an oyster bed, bank or bar.

coastal defence strategies.text: The broad choices for responding to coastal change: abandon, retreat, armour, build seaward, or raise land and buildings.

soft engineering.text: A shoreline management practice that uses ecological principles and natural materials to stabilize shorelines and protect waterside habitats.

managed realignment.text: Deliberately removing or breaching coastal flood defences so the sea can reclaim land and form natural soft landforms such as salt marsh.

sand dune stabilization.text: A coastal management practice that keeps sand dunes from eroding.

oyster reef restoration.text: Repairing and rebuilding degraded oyster reefs.

deep blue carbon.text: Carbon stored in deep ocean waters and the sea floor of the high seas, beyond national jurisdictions.

coral reef restoration.text: Natural and human-led processes for restoring damaged coral reefs.

seagrass meadow carbon storage.text: Seagrass meadows bury a large share of ocean carbon in their sediments despite covering a tiny part of the sea floor.

seaweed as blue carbon.text: The open question of whether seaweed (macroalgae) forests should count as blue carbon ecosystems.

tidal marsh carbon storage.text: Tidal marshes are intertidal ecosystems of non-woody plants that act as important carbon sinks.

shoreline mapping.text: Recording where the shoreline is and how it moves over time, a basic need for coastal scientists, engineers and managers.

buyout programs.text: Programs in which government buys at-risk properties and relocates or demolishes them, a form of managed retreat.

natural coastal barriers.text: Coastal ecosystems such as mangroves, coral reefs and coastal vegetation that blunt tsunamis and storm surges like a living seawall.

mangrove loss and degradation.text: The rapid worldwide decline of mangrove forests, driven by clearing for development, aquaculture and farming and by climate change.

mangrove restoration.text: Rehabilitating degraded or destroyed mangrove forests so they return to a state like their condition before disturbance.

hard engineering.text: Protecting shorelines with non-living reinforcing materials such as concrete, steel and rock to stop erosion and flooding.

redd+ and mangroves.text: Using the UN REDD+ mechanism, which pays developing-country stakeholders to avoid deforestation, to protect and restore mangroves.

stakeholder engagement in mangrove resto.text: Involving local communities in planning, doing and maintaining mangrove restoration.

living shoreline.text: A way of protecting shorelines and marshes from erosion that uses as many natural elements as possible instead of walls.

coastal erosion control methods.text: The three common ways to deal with coastal erosion: soft controls, hard controls, and relocation.

groyne.text: A wall or barrier built at right angles to the coast to trap sand carried along the shore and so build up a beach.

hold the line.text: A coastal strategy that keeps the shoreline where it is, usually by hardening it with permanent concrete and rock structures.

detached breakwater.text: A detached breakwater is a shore protection structure built to build up sandy material between it and the coast.

ports and harbours effect on drift.term: Ports and harbours effect on drift
ports and harbours effect on drift.text: Ports and harbours can seriously disrupt natural longshore drift by altering sedimentation patterns.

sediment budget.text: A sediment budget accounts for the sediment sources and sinks within a coastal system.

spits and barriers.text: Spits and barriers are landforms built where longshore drift deposits sediment, a spit being attached to land at one end and a barrier at both.

integrated mangrove-shrimp aquaculture.text: A farming system, also called silvofishery, that grows shrimp in ponds alongside planted mangrove trees as a way to rehabilitate mangroves.

dune plant zones.text: The bands of plants across a beach dune, from the sea-facing foredune through the backdune to a later shrub stage.

cultching.text: Laying down cultch, such as old shell or similar hard material, to give young oysters surfaces to settle on and rebuild a reef.

climate-driven community relocation.text: Whole or partial abandonment of places, or plans to move their people, because of human-caused climate change.

coral gardening.text: Cultivating coral by growing small fragments in nurseries until mature, then moving them to damaged reefs.

microfragmentation.text: A coral-growing technique that cuts live coral into very small pieces which, fixed to plugs in tanks, grow much faster.

coastal squeeze.text: The loss of coastal habitat when rising seas push zones such as salt marsh landward and they run up against seawalls or other solid structures.

community based mangrove management.text: Management and rehabilitation of mangrove forests led by local communities, with resource users directly involved.

sea rewilding.text: Restoring marine organisms and ecosystems to their natural state so that damaged seas can recover and thrive on their own.

urban heat island.text: The urban heat island effect is the way cities become noticeably warmer than the countryside around them.

urban green space.text: In town planning, urban green spaces are open areas set aside for parks and other greenery.

green roof.text: A building roof partly or fully covered with plants and a growing medium, laid over a waterproof membrane.

urban park.text: An urban or city park is a park or garden in a town or suburb that gives residents and visitors green space and places to relax and play.

urban agriculture.text: Urban agriculture covers the growing, processing and distribution of food in towns and cities.

green wall.text: A green wall, living wall or vertical garden is an upright built structure deliberately covered with plants.

green belt.text: A green belt is a planning policy and zone that keeps mostly undeveloped, wild or farmed land around or beside towns and cities.

urban forestry.text: The care and management of individual trees and groups of trees in towns and cities to improve the urban environment.

urban forest.text: An urban forest is a forest or grove of trees growing inside a city, town or suburb.

green space and health.text: The World Health Organization treats urban green space as important to people's mental and physical health.

green space inequality.text: The uneven sharing of parks, trees and other green space, with poorer and minority neighbourhoods often having less access.

urban ecology.text: Urban ecology is the scientific study of how living things relate to each other and to their surroundings in cities.

urban resilience.text: Urban resilience is a city's or urban community's ability to withstand, recover from or adapt to human-made and natural disasters.

brown roof.text: A brown or biodiverse roof covers the flat roof of a new building with locally sourced material to replace wildlife habitat lost to development.

intensive and extensive green roofs.text: Green roofs are grouped as intensive, semi-intensive or extensive according to how deep their planting medium is and how much upkeep they need.

cool roof.text: Painting rooftops white has become a common way to reduce the heat island effect.

biophilic design.text: Biophilic design tries to connect people more closely with nature, and with nature-like design, to improve their health and well-being.

urban heat inequity.text: Urban heat inequity, or thermal inequity, is the uneven spread of heat across a city that hits some communities harder than others.

blue roof.text: A blue roof is designed to store rainwater for a while and then release it slowly.

blue-green roof.text: A roof that combines a blue roof's water storage with a green roof's plants, holding stormwater beneath layers of soil and vegetation.

urban biodiversity.text: The variety of plant and animal life found in cities, which planners can sustain by enlarging green areas and linking them with green corridors.

active and passive recreation.text: Park space is split into active recreation areas, built up for sports and play, and passive recreation areas that keep open space and natural habitat.

linear park.text: A linear park is a park much longer than it is wide.

community garden.text: A community garden is public space where residents grow plants for food, recreation and learning.

food desert.text: Low-income and minority neighbourhoods with poor access to healthy food, a pattern the USDA found well supported in 2009.

street tree.text: A street tree is any tree growing along a city street, such as between the sidewalk and the curb.

urban rewilding.text: Urban rewilding is a form of rewilding that tries to bring working ecosystems, from plants to animals, into cities.

biophilic city.text: A biophilic city, in Timothy Beatley's view, is one whose residents want to take part in, protect and connect with the nature around them.

pocket forest.text: A small forest made by planting many different native trees and shrubs close together, usually to restore native plants quickly in damaged places.

green urbanism.text: Green urbanism is the practice of building communities that are good for both people and the environment.

reforestation.text: Reforestation is restoring forests and woodlands that once stood on a site but were destroyed or damaged.

afforestation.text: Afforestation is creating a forest or stand of trees on land that has had no recent tree cover.

ecological restoration.text: Ecological restoration is helping an ecosystem recover after it has been degraded, damaged, destroyed or transformed.

rewilding.text: Rewilding is a kind of ecological restoration that aims to raise biodiversity and restore natural processes while reducing human influence.

financial incentives for reforestation.text: Payments, credits and tax breaks that reward landowners or countries for replanting forests or for not cutting them down.

plantation forests.text: Plantation forests are intensively managed stands of one or two tree species of the same age, planted in regular rows mainly to produce wood.

un decade on ecosystem restoration.text: The UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration is a United Nations campaign running from 2021 to 2030 to promote the repair of degraded ecosystems worldwide.

restoration versus emission cuts.text: The debate over relying on nature restoration to fight climate change instead of quickly cutting fossil fuel emissions.

great green wall (africa).text: The Great Green Wall is an African Union project, adopted in 2007, first meant to stop desertification in the Sahel by planting a belt of trees from Djibouti to Senegal.

species reintroduction.text: Species reintroduction is deliberately releasing a species into the wild, from captivity or from other places, where it can survive.

novel ecosystem.text: A novel ecosystem is one that human activity, land use and climate change have pushed into a mix of species and conditions never seen before.

land restoration.text: Land restoration, which may include rewilding, is returning land to a different or earlier state for a chosen purpose.

land rehabilitation.text: Land rehabilitation is returning damaged land, for example after industry or natural disasters, to some degree of its former state.

land competition in reforestation.text: The problem that reforestation can take land and water needed for food, grazing and housing, and may push out people who use that land.

permanence of forest carbon.text: The risk that carbon stored by reforestation returns to the air, for example through fire, insect outbreaks or harvesting.

afforestation and surface albedo.text: New forest canopy can darken Earth's surface, lowering its albedo so it absorbs more heat and may warm the planet.

afforestation of grasslands and savannas.text: A criticism of tree-planting campaigns that put forests where they would not grow naturally, such as grasslands and savannas.

monoculture tree plantations.text: A criticism of planting forests of a single tree species, often conifers: tree cover rises but the varied habitat wildlife needs is missing.

ecological succession in restoration.text: Ecological succession is the way a community of living things changes over time, especially after a disturbance.

forest restoration.text: Forest restoration is action that speeds the return of a forest's structure, ecological workings and biodiversity toward those of a climax forest, the end stage of natural succession.

secondary forest.text: A secondary forest is woodland that has grown back largely by natural processes after logging, clearing for farming or a similar natural disturbance.

forest landscape restoration.text: Forest landscape restoration (FLR) is a planned process to regain ecological integrity and improve human well-being across deforested or degraded landscapes.

bonn challenge.text: The Bonn Challenge is a global goal to restore 150 million hectares of degraded and deforested land by 2020 and 350 million hectares by 2030.

assisted natural regeneration.text: Assisted natural regeneration (ANR), or managed regrowth, is protecting and caring for tree seedlings that sprout naturally so a forest regrows.

passive rewilding.text: Passive rewilding is letting land, usually after it has been abandoned, return to nature with little or no human management.

international standards for ecological r.text: Guidance from the Society for Ecological Restoration that sets out principles and standards for planning, doing and monitoring restoration projects.

restoration ecology and conservation bio.text: Two related sciences that both value protecting and restoring habitat, but conservation biology studies species populations while restoration ecology works at the community level.

mine reclamation.text: Mine reclamation is reshaping mined land so it again works as an ecosystem or can be used economically.

science–practice gap in restoration.text: The divide between restoration ecology research and the people who carry out restoration on the ground.

traditional ecological knowledge in rest.text: Knowledge Indigenous peoples have built up by observing and managing their environment, which shows restoration has been practised for thousands of years.

active rewilding.text: Active rewilding covers rewilding approaches that involve human intervention.

criticism of rewilding.text: Objections to rewilding from governments, farmers, conservationists and others, about livelihoods, evidence and conflicts with people.

ecosystem engineers.text: Ecosystem engineers are living things that clearly reshape the structure of their habitats.

pleistocene rewilding.text: Pleistocene rewilding is bringing back surviving Ice Age megafauna, or close stand-ins for extinct ones, to restore how ecosystems work.

trophic rewilding.text: Trophic rewilding restores food-web interactions, especially top predators controlling plant-eaters, by (re)introducing species so ecosystems regulate themselves.

trillion tree campaign.text: The Trillion Tree Campaign is a project to plant one trillion trees worldwide to fight climate change.

cost-effectiveness of restoration.text: The comparison of what restoring ecosystems costs with the benefits it returns, and with the cost of doing nothing.

restoration economy.text: The restoration economy is the economic activity that comes from repairing land and nature, such as ecological restoration work.

financing forest landscape restoration.text: The range of money sources, from loans to grants and public spending, used to plan and carry out forest and landscape restoration.

post-fire forest regeneration.text: Restoring forest after fire, a heavy cause of forest loss in many parts of the world.

protecting regrowth from browsing animal.text: Shielding young, regrowing forest from deer and other browsing animals that can over-graze seedlings.

anthromes.text: Anthromes are the land's biomes in their modern, human-altered form, mapped by patterns of lasting human land use.

managing novel ecosystems.text: The choices for handling novel ecosystems: tolerating them, managing against them back toward history, or managing for them as new systems.

restoring desert land.text: Restoring land lost to desertification, done in phases that first fix the soil and then enrich it.

mine rehabilitation bonds.text: A rehabilitation security bond is money a mining company must put up before mining begins to guarantee it will repair the land afterwards.

exclosure.text: An exclosure is a fenced-off patch of grazing land that keeps out cattle, deer or other browsing animals.

forestry reclamation approach.text: The Forestry Reclamation Approach (FRA) is a set of guidelines for regrowing forest on land mined for coal.

african forest landscape restoration ini.text: AFR100, the African Forest Landscape Restoration Initiative, aims to bring 100 million hectares of degraded land in Africa under restoration by 2030.

peatland rewetting.text: Rewetting returns a drained peatland to its original waterlogged state so peat-forming plants can recover.

economic value of peatland restoration.text: Estimates of the money value society gains from restoring peatlands, compared with what restoration costs.

paludiculture.text: Paludiculture is farming on drained peatlands after they have been rewetted.

ecology.text: The natural science that studies the interactions between organisms and their environments.

sustainable agriculture.text: Farming that reduces harm to the environment, maintains and builds up natural resources, and uses non-renewable resources productively.

soil health.text: The state of a soil that performs the full range of ecosystem functions suited to its environment.

agricultural pollution.text: Contamination or damage to the environment, people or their livelihoods from the by-products of farming.

carbon farming.text: A set of farming and forestry methods meant to store carbon from the air in soil and living plant material.

crop rotation.text: Growing a sequence of different crops on the same land over successive seasons.

tillage.text: The agricultural preparation of soil by mechanical agitation such as digging, stirring and overturning.

regenerative agriculture.text: An approach to farming that aims to restore rather than just sustain, rebuilding topsoil, biodiversity and ecosystem services.

permaculture.text: An approach to designing land use and settlements that copies the arrangements found in thriving natural ecosystems.

no-till farming.text: Growing crops or pasture without disturbing the soil by tillage, also called zero tillage or direct drilling.

soil conservation.text: Preventing the loss of topsoil to erosion and the loss of fertility from overuse, acidification, salinization or contamination.

cover crop.text: A plant grown to cover the soil rather than to be harvested.

agroecology.text: The study and practice of applying ecological processes to farming systems, looking at links between plants, animals, people and the environment.

agroforestry.text: A way of managing land that grows trees together with crops or pasture on the same ground.

landscape-scale conservation.text: An approach that manages a whole landscape to balance nature conservation against farming, forestry and other economic uses of the same land.

hedge.text: A line of shrubs, sometimes with trees, planted and trained as a barrier or boundary; old field-boundary hedges are called hedgerows.

riparian buffer.text: A strip of vegetation, usually trees, along a stream that shades it and shields it from the effects of nearby land use.

rotational grazing.text: Moving livestock between sections of pasture, called paddocks, so that the rest of the pasture can recover.

silvopasture.text: Combining trees, forage plants and grazing livestock on the same land so each benefits the others.

land sharing.text: A strategy, also called wildlife-friendly agriculture, that makes room for biodiversity inside farmed areas by farming less intensively.

land sparing.text: A strategy that keeps farmland and nature strictly apart, farming some land intensively for high yields so that other land can stay wild.

land sparing versus land sharing.text: The long scientific argument over whether nature is better protected by separating farms from wild land or by mixing them.

sustainable intensification.text: Farming methods that raise production while also improving environmental outcomes, without clearing more land.

conservation agriculture.text: A farming system, defined by the FAO, that protects farmland from loss and restores degraded land through minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and a variety of crops.

levels of ecological organization.text: Ecology structures the biological world as a hierarchy from organisms to populations, guilds, communities, ecosystems, biomes and the biosphere.

fertilizer runoff.text: The loss of nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilized fields into water and air, where they cause pollution.

greenhouse gas emissions from agricultur.text: The heat-trapping gases released by farming, both directly from crops and livestock and indirectly from clearing land for farms.

climate-smart agriculture.text: A set of farming methods that try at once to adapt farming to climate change, raise yields for food security, and cut farm greenhouse gas emissions.

biodiversity in agriculture.text: The variety of living things found on farmland.

niche construction.text: Organisms not only face environmental pressures but also modify their habitats.

ecological farming.text: Farming focused on the environmental side of sustainable agriculture, using methods that rebuild ecosystem services.

land blending.text: An in-between strategy that mixes land sparing and land sharing to suit each landscape.

multifunctional agriculture.text: The view that farming does more than produce food and fibre, also managing renewable resources, conserving landscapes and supporting biodiversity.

rotation effect.text: The yield gain that rotated crops show compared with crops grown alone year after year.

three-field system.text: A medieval European rotation dividing land into autumn crops, spring crops and a fallow field, rotated each year.

four-field crop rotation.text: An 18th-century rotation of wheat, turnips, barley and clover that let livestock be kept all year.

forest site preparation.text: Treatments applied to a forest site to ready it for seeding or planting and ease regeneration.

primary and secondary tillage.text: Primary tillage is deeper and more thorough, while secondary tillage is shallower and prepares the seedbed.

tillage residue cover classes.text: Tillage types are classed by how much crop residue they leave on the soil surface.

zone tillage.text: A modified deep tillage that tills only narrow strips, leaving the soil between rows untilled.

alley cropping.text: Growing strips of crops between rows of closely spaced trees or hedges.

forest farming.text: Growing high-value specialty crops under a forest canopy that is managed to give the right shade and habitat.

forest gardening.text: A low-maintenance way of producing food modelled on woodland, with layers of fruit and nut trees, shrubs, herbs, vines and perennial vegetables.

shade-grown crops.text: Crops deliberately grown in the shade beneath a canopy of trees.

urban agroforestry.text: Applying agroforestry in towns, combining trees, shrubs and crops in gardens, parks and streets.

windbreak.text: Rows of trees or shrubs planted to slow the wind over and around crops.

soil health testing.text: Measuring a soil's physical, chemical and biological condition against benchmarks of healthy function.

holistic planned grazing.text: Moving livestock herds constantly between fields to imitate how wild herds graze.

hügelkultur.text: Burying wood in mounds or beds so that it soaks up water and keeps the soil moist.

permaculture ethics.text: The three core ethics of permaculture: care of the Earth, care of people, and setting limits to consumption and sharing the surplus.

permaculture zones.text: A layout that places parts of a design by how often people use them, numbered 0 to 5 outward from the house.

plant guild.text: A mutually beneficial group of species that each provide different services within a larger ecosystem.

rainwater harvesting.text: Collecting and storing rainwater for later use before it runs off or soaks into the ground.

sheet mulching.text: Layering materials such as leaves, cardboard and wood chips over soil to imitate a forest floor.

conservation tillage.text: A group of practices that reduce how much the soil is tilled.

contour ploughing.text: Ploughing furrows along a slope's contour lines so they stay level, which slows runoff.

organic farming.text: A farming system that relies on natural inputs such as compost, manure and green manure and on methods like crop rotation, and largely bans synthetic pesticides and fertilizers.

keyline design.text: An extension of contour farming that shapes contour lines around the whole watershed.

soil salinity management.text: Preventing and reducing the build-up of salt in soil, which mainly comes from irrigating with salty water.

terrace farming.text: Cutting a hillside into a series of nearly level steps for growing crops.

green manure.text: A cover crop grown to raise soil fertility, usually ploughed in before it matures.

syntropic agroforestry.text: An organic agroforestry system, developed by Ernst Götsch in Brazil, that copies natural forest succession to build productive food forests.

organic certification.text: Rules, voluntary or set by law, that define how organic food must be produced and allow it to be labelled organic.

organic price premium.text: The higher price organic food fetches over conventional food, which is key to whether organic farming pays.

organic yield gap.text: The difference between organic and conventional crop yields and whether organic farming could feed the world.

trap crop.text: A crop grown to lure pests away from the valuable crop.

agricultural plastic pollution.text: Plastic from greenhouse sheeting, storage bags, silage wrap and mulch film that ends up in farmed land.

biological pest control risks.text: The debate over releasing predators, parasites or pathogens to control farm pests in place of pesticides.

livestock greenhouse gas estimates.text: The dispute over how large a share of human greenhouse gas emissions comes from livestock.

manure management.text: Handling and treating animal waste to limit air, soil and water pollution.

pesticide persistence.text: The tendency of some pesticides to stay in the environment for many years after use.

bamboo farming for carbon.text: Growing bamboo plantations as a way to store carbon on farmland.

climate-resilient agriculture index.text: A scoring tool that measures how resilient farming systems are to climate change.

gender-responsive climate-smart agricult.text: Designing climate-smart farming programmes to address the different constraints and abilities of women and men farmers.

inga alley cropping.text: Growing crops between rows of nitrogen-fixing Inga trees, whose pruned leaves form a thick mulch.

wood pasture.text: A traditional European system in which open woodland gave grazing animals shelter and forage while also yielding timber and fuel.

integrated landscape management.text: A way of managing a landscape sustainably by bringing together stakeholders who want different things from the land.

agri-environment schemes.text: Programmes, compulsory for EU member states, that pay farmers to adopt environmentally friendlier methods to make up for the cost of changing.

hedge laying.text: Restoring a hedge by cutting most of the way through each stem near the base, bending it over and weaving it between stakes.

hooper's rule.text: A rule of thumb that estimates a hedge's age as the number of woody species in a thirty-yard stretch times 110 years.

hydrologically adapted buffer.text: A riparian buffer whose width follows local groundwater flow instead of a fixed distance.

riparian buffer zones.text: The usual three-zone layout of a riparian buffer, from stream-side trees to outer grass strips.

polyculture.text: Growing more than one crop species together in the same place at the same time, in contrast to monoculture.

intercropping.text: Growing two or more crops at the same time in the same field, a form of polyculture.

landscape heterogeneity.text: The variety of habitats and features across a farmed landscape, which supports a variety of species.

regenerative economics.text: An economic approach that aims to renew capital assets, treating the Earth as the original capital asset, instead of using them up.

regenerative finance.text: Investing that builds on sustainable finance to support ecological health, social well-being and economic resilience.

living mulch.text: A second crop sown beneath a main crop to cover the soil and reduce erosion.

mixed cropping.text: A polyculture in which all the seeds are mixed and sown together.
