rice polyculture.text: Systems that raise fish, ducks or both with rice on the same paddy.

relay cropping.text: Sowing a second crop while the first is still growing, so the first is harvested to make room for the second.

integrated pest management.text: A pest control approach that combines non-chemical and chemical methods to control pests economically while relying less on pesticides.

economic injury level.text: The pest population at which the crop damage would cost more than treating the pest.

push-pull cropping.text: Pest control that pairs an attractive trap crop pulling pests in with a repellent crop pushing them away from the main crop.

greenwashing.text: Advertising or public relations meant to mislead people into believing an organization's products, goals or policies are good for the environment.

monoculture.text: Growing a single crop species in a field at a time.

albedo.text: The share of incoming sunlight that a surface reflects.

introduced species.text: A species living outside its native range after being brought there by human action, also called alien, exotic or non-native.

tree plantation.text: A forest planted to produce large volumes of wood, usually as a single-species monoculture.

tree planting.text: Transplanting young tree seedlings into the ground, usually for forestry, land reclamation or landscaping.

forest monoculture.text: Plantations made up of a single tree species, often grown for timber.

regulation of green claims.text: Laws, codes and guidelines that govern what businesses may say about the environmental benefits of their products, aimed at curbing greenwashing.

forest albedo trade-off.text: The way dark forest canopies absorb more sunlight, partly cancelling the cooling gained when new trees store carbon.

tree planting for climate mitigation.text: Using new trees to pull carbon dioxide from the air and store it, as a way to limit climate change.

food sovereignty.text: The idea that people should control their own food systems, including how food is produced, distributed and consumed.

agro-extractivism.text: Foreign control over farming driven by large-scale production of agricultural commodities for export, often grown as monocultures.

genetic monoculture.text: Planting crops, or raising animals, with little or no genetic variation across a whole region.

mixed-species plantation.text: A tree plantation that grows several species together instead of one.

greenscamming.text: Giving an organization or product a name that falsely suggests it is environmentally friendly.

seven sins of greenwashing.text: A list of seven kinds of misleading environmental claims, set out by the consultancy TerraChoice in 2007 to help shoppers spot them.

types of greenwashing.text: Ways of sorting greenwashing by where the misleading claim or misconduct arises: in a firm itself, in its suppliers, in a product, or across the whole organization.

human-caused albedo change.text: Changes in how much sunlight the land reflects caused by human land use such as cities, farms and deforestation.

ice–albedo feedback.text: A self-reinforcing loop in which melting snow or ice exposes darker surfaces that absorb more heat and cause more melting.

limitations of systematic reviews.text: The ways systematic reviews can mislead, through biased inputs, outdated searches or poor reporting, despite being treated as the strongest evidence.

economic analysis of climate change.text: The use of economic tools and models to estimate how large climate change damages are and who bears them.

scoping review.text: A review that maps the concepts, language and data around a topic, refining its search as it goes, to gauge how much evidence an area holds.

introduced species in plantations.text: Planting tree species far outside their natural range because they grow fast and suit industrial use.

plantations and natural forest loss.text: The argument over whether high-yield plantations spare natural forests from logging or instead replace them.

bluewashing.text: False or misleading claims about how an action affects water and ocean environments, by analogy with greenwashing.

climate risk.text: The chance that the impacts of climate change will cause harm to societies or ecosystems.

social cost of carbon.text: An estimate, usually in dollars, of the economic damage caused by emitting one more ton of carbon dioxide.

carbon accounting.text: A set of methods for measuring and tracking how much greenhouse gas an organization emits.

stern review.text: A 700-page review of the economics of climate change released for the UK government in October 2006 by economist Nicholas Stern.

climate change scenario.text: A plausible picture of how the future might unfold, built on a set of assumptions about the main forces driving climate change.

integrated assessment modelling.text: A kind of scientific modelling that links the main features of society and the economy with the biosphere and atmosphere in one framework.

shared socioeconomic pathways.text: Scenarios of how global society and economy might change up to 2100, used in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report.

marginal abatement cost.text: The cost of reducing pollution by one more unit.

cumulative emissions.text: Emissions added up over long periods, which indicate who is responsible for the build-up of greenhouse gases in the air.

costs of climate change adaptation.text: The costs of planning, preparing for, enabling and carrying out adaptation to climate change.

costs of climate change mitigation.text: The economic cost of actions that cut greenhouse gas emissions or enlarge the carbon sinks that absorb them.

emissions by economic sector.text: The division of global greenhouse gas emissions among the sectors of the economy that cause them.

emissions inequality.text: The large gap in greenhouse gas emissions between rich and poor people, driven by a strong link between income and per capita emissions.

airborne fraction and atmospheric lifeti.text: Measures of how much of an emitted greenhouse gas stays in the air and for how long, set by the balance between its sources and sinks.

cost–benefit analysis of climate change.text: Applying standard cost-benefit analysis to climate change by turning the good and bad effects of an action into money values.

global economic costs of climate change.term: Global economic costs of climate change
global economic costs of climate change.text: The total predicted impacts of climate change across all market sectors, plus non-market impacts on ecosystems and health.

hazard, exposure and vulnerability.text: The IPCC framework in which climate risk arises from the interaction of three factors: hazards, vulnerability and exposure.

dice model.text: William Nordhaus's integrated assessment model that combines economics, the carbon cycle, climate science and impacts to weigh the costs and benefits of slowing climate change.

kaya identity.text: An equation that breaks total CO2 emissions into four factors multiplied together: population, GDP per person, energy per unit of GDP, and emissions per unit of energy.

carbon lock-in.text: The self-reinforcing inertia of large fossil-fuel energy systems that holds back efforts to bring in alternative energy technologies.

ancillary benefits of mitigation.text: The side effects of mitigation policies, beyond their effect on the climate, which can raise or lower estimated costs.

cost-effectiveness analysis in climate p.text: A method that ranks policy options by their cost per unit of a set goal, used when benefits are hard to put in money terms.

equity in climate economics.text: The debate over who should bear the costs of adaptation and mitigation, on which there is no consensus.

sequential decision making on climate.text: Handling climate uncertainty by making a series of decisions that are revised as better information arrives.

ethics of climate change.text: The study of the moral questions that climate change raises.

carbon bubble.text: A suspected overvaluation of fossil fuel companies, because reserves that cannot be burned within carbon budgets are still counted as valuable.

sharing the costs of mitigation.text: The competing proposals for deciding which countries should bear how much of the job of cutting emissions.

underestimation of climate damages.text: The argument that economic estimates of climate damages are too low because models leave out tipping points, tail risks and knock-on effects.

climate risks to ecosystems.text: The ways climate change threatens ecosystems and the services they provide.

fat-tailed distribution.text: A probability distribution in which extreme outcomes are much more likely than in a normal or exponential distribution.

calculating the social cost of carbon.term: Calculating the social cost of carbon
calculating the social cost of carbon.text: The chain of steps used to estimate the social cost of carbon, from projecting emissions to discounting future damages.

dice, fund and page models.text: The three main integrated assessment models that have historically underpinned social cost of carbon estimates.

tipping points in the social cost of car.term: Tipping points in the social cost of carbon
tipping points in the social cost of car.text: Extensions to climate-economy models that add abrupt, irreversible damages when warming crosses critical thresholds.

climate change mitigation scenario.text: A possible future in which global warming is reduced by deliberate actions, such as a broad switch away from fossil fuels.

representative concentration pathway.text: IPCC scenarios that project future greenhouse gas concentrations, not emissions.

process-based integrated assessment mode.text: Integrated assessment models that map detailed sector-by-sector pathways, used by the IPCC to quantify mitigation scenarios.

transient and equilibrium climate sensit.text: The two main measures of climate sensitivity: the short-term transient climate response and the long-term equilibrium climate sensitivity.

intergenerational climate ethics.text: The duty of people alive now to use resources sustainably and protect the interests of future generations from climate change.

deep uncertainty.text: Uncertainty so great that decision-makers do not know or agree on how actions lead to outcomes or on the probabilities of key inputs.

robust decision-making.text: An iterative framework for finding strategies that hold up across many possible futures, exposing their weak points and the trade-offs among them.

fund model.text: An integrated assessment model that estimates climate damages region by region and sector by sector, used for the social cost of carbon.

page model.text: A probabilistic integrated assessment model, one of the three main models behind estimates of the social cost of carbon.

green paradox.text: Hans-Werner Sinn's argument that climate policy expected to tighten over time pushes fossil fuel owners to extract faster, speeding up global warming.

efficient energy use.text: Reducing the amount of energy needed to provide the same products and services.

energy economics.text: The study of how societies supply and use energy, and of the costs and value of energy services.

electricity generation.text: The process of producing electric power from primary energy sources, carried out in power stations before delivery or storage.

energy security.text: The link between a nation's security and the reliable availability of energy resources.

price of oil.text: The spot price of a barrel of benchmark crude oil, such as Brent or West Texas Intermediate, used as a reference by buyers and sellers.

energy intensity.text: The amount of energy an economy uses per unit of GDP or other economic output.

demand response.text: Changes in how much electricity customers use, made to better match demand to the available supply.

energy poverty.text: Lack of access to modern energy services, such as electricity and clean cooking fuel, in the home.

rebound effect in energy efficiency.text: The tendency for efficiency gains to save less energy than expected because they make energy services cheaper, so people use more of them.

capacity factor.text: The ratio of the electricity a power plant actually produces over a period to what it would produce running at full rated power the whole time.

variable renewable energy.text: Renewable power sources such as wind and solar whose output rises and falls with the weather and cannot be adjusted on demand.

grid energy storage.text: Technologies connected to the power grid that store electricity for later use.

levelized cost of electricity.text: The average cost of electricity from a generator over its lifetime, expressed in today's money per unit of energy produced.

distributed generation.text: Small, grid-connected devices that generate and store electricity close to the load they serve, called distributed energy resources.

smart grid.text: An upgrade of the 20th-century electrical grid that uses two-way communications and distributed intelligent devices.

experience curve effect.text: The pattern in which the cost of making something falls by a steady share each time the total amount ever produced doubles.

merit order.text: The ranking of power sources from cheapest to most expensive to run, which sets the order in which they are switched on to meet demand.

energy conservation.text: Actively using less energy, through changes in behaviour as well as through more efficient technology.

energy resilience.text: The ability of an energy system to adjust to and withstand interruptions in supply.

strategic petroleum reserve.text: A government stockpile of oil held as a buffer against the economic and political shocks of an energy crisis.

operating reserve.text: Spare generating capacity a grid keeps ready to follow changes in demand or replace generation that is suddenly lost.

sector coupling.text: Linking the power system with transport, heating and gas so that demand and generation can be better matched.

1970s oil crises.text: The 1973 and 1979 oil supply shocks that sharply raised world oil prices and reshaped energy policy.

oil futures and speculation.text: Contracts to buy or sell oil at a set future date, through which investors bet on oil prices and firms hedge against price swings.

economics of energy storage.text: How storage earns money and what it costs, measured over its lifetime and against the services it provides to the grid.

pumped-storage hydroelectricity.text: Storing electricity by pumping water uphill to a reservoir when demand is low and releasing it through turbines when demand peaks.

peak demand.text: The highest level of electricity use on a grid, which sets how much generating capacity must be built.

load shedding.text: Deliberately cutting power to some users when generating capacity falls below demand.

microgrid.text: A localized grouping of generation, storage and loads that normally runs connected to the main grid but can disconnect and operate autonomously.

green nudges.text: Government interventions, such as feedback on energy bills, that steer energy users toward greener choices without forcing them.

multidimensional energy poverty index.text: A composite index that classes people as energy poor according to how many kinds of energy deprivation they face.

levelized avoided cost of energy.text: The discounted costs a new generator would avoid, divided by its discounted lifetime output, used as a measure of its value to the grid.

base load and peaking power plants.term: Base load and peaking power plants
base load and peaking power plants.text: The split between power plants run continuously at high output and plants switched on only when demand is high.

wright's law.text: A power-law formula in which unit cost falls by a fixed proportion, the learning rate, with each doubling of cumulative production.

economic dispatch.text: The short-term choice of how much each power plant should produce to meet load at the lowest possible cost within grid and operating limits.

merit order effect.text: The lowering of wholesale electricity prices when wind and solar, which have near-zero fuel costs, push expensive plants out of the merit order.

climate change mitigation.text: Action to limit the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere that cause climate change; also called decarbonisation.

carbon sequestration.text: The storing of carbon in a carbon pool, a place in the Earth system where carbon stays for a period of time.

carbon budget.text: The largest total amount of carbon dioxide humanity can still emit, added up over time, while keeping global warming below a chosen limit.

biomass.text: Material produced by the growth of microorganisms, plants or animals.

low-carbon economy.text: An economy that absorbs as much greenhouse gas as it emits, or more broadly one whose activities produce far lower emissions.

carbon capture and storage.text: Separating carbon dioxide from industrial sources before it reaches the air and moving it to long-term storage, usually deep underground; known as CCS.

weathering.text: The deterioration of rocks, soils and minerals through contact with water, atmospheric gases, sunlight and living organisms.

biochar.text: A charcoal made by heating biomass with little oxygen, intended for use in soil and other organic uses.

co-benefits of climate mitigation.text: Side benefits of cutting emissions beyond slowing climate change, such as cleaner air, better health, jobs and energy security; also called ancillary benefits.

demand-side mitigation.text: Cutting emissions by reducing demand for the goods and services that cause them, through behaviour, infrastructure and end-use technology.

mitigation by economic sector.text: The grouping of emission cuts by the part of the economy where they happen: buildings, transport, industry, and agriculture, forestry and land use.

preserving and enhancing carbon sinks.text: Managing Earth's natural carbon sinks so they keep or increase their ability to take CO2 from the air and store it durably.

biological carbon sequestration.text: Capturing and storing atmospheric carbon dioxide through living processes, mainly plant growth, that people keep up and enhance.

geological carbon sequestration.text: Storing carbon dioxide deep underground in depleted oil and gas fields, saline formations or coal beds that cannot be mined.

greenhouse gas inventory.text: A record of the greenhouse gases emitted, and removed by carbon sinks, in a country, region or organisation.

stranded asset.text: An asset that has suffered an unexpected or early write-down, loss of value, or conversion into a liability.

pyrolysis.text: Thermal decomposition of organic matter in an inert, oxygen-free environment, breaking its covalent bonds.

low-carbon electricity.text: Electricity produced with far lower lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions than fossil fuel power.

barriers to climate mitigation.text: The individual, institutional and market obstacles that hold back cutting emissions.

climate pledges and warming outlook.text: Countries' announced emission targets and how much warming they would lead to if carried out.

coal-to-gas switching.text: Replacing coal with natural gas to cut emissions in the short term.

low-carbon diet.text: Eating fewer animal products and more plant-based food to cut the greenhouse gas emissions caused by food.

allocating national carbon budgets.text: The question of how to split the world's carbon budget among countries, which requires value judgments about fairness.

negative side effects of mitigation.text: Harms and risks that some mitigation measures can cause, such as damage to biodiversity or mining pressure on conservation areas.

sharing the costs of emissions cuts.term: Sharing the costs of emissions cuts
sharing the costs of emissions cuts.text: The question of how responsibility for cutting emissions, and its costs, should be divided among regions, income groups and sectors.

biomass burial.text: Storing carbon by burying wood or other plant matter where it cannot rot, mimicking how fossil fuels formed.

direct deep-sea co2 injection.text: An abandoned idea of storing carbon dioxide by injecting it directly into the deep ocean for some centuries.

learning-by-doing.text: The economic idea that productivity rises through practice, self-improvement and small innovations.

production- and consumption-based emissi.text: The two main ways to count a country's emissions: production-based counts emissions made on its territory, consumption-based counts those caused by what it consumes, including imports.

mineral carbonation.text: Locking carbon dioxide into solid carbonate minerals by reacting it with metal oxides such as magnesium or calcium oxide.

nuclear power in decarbonisation.text: The disagreement over whether expanding nuclear power is needed to reach a low-carbon economy.

carbon capture and utilization.text: Using captured CO2 as a raw material for products instead of storing it.

energy penalty of ccs.text: The extra energy a facility uses to capture, compress and store its CO2.

enhanced oil recovery with captured co2.term: Enhanced oil recovery with captured CO2
enhanced oil recovery with captured co2.text: Injecting captured CO2 into old oil fields to push out more oil, and the dispute over whether this helps or harms the climate.

chemical weathering.text: Weathering in which water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances react with rock to change its composition.

physical weathering.text: Weathering that breaks rock into smaller fragments without chemical change, also called mechanical weathering.

slash-and-char.text: A tropical farming method that chars cleared vegetation into biochar instead of burning it, as an alternative to slash-and-burn.

carbon capture technologies.text: The three main ways to capture CO2 from burning fuel: post-combustion, pre-combustion and oxy-fuel combustion.

emissions embodied in trade.text: Greenhouse gases released making goods in one country that are consumed in another.

shared emissions responsibility.text: The proposal that emissions be split between importing and exporting countries at each stage of the supply chain.

net-zero emissions.text: The state in which greenhouse gas emissions from human activity are balanced by human removals; often shortened to net zero.

carbon dioxide removal.text: Deliberate human activity that takes carbon dioxide out of the air and stores it durably on land, underground, in the ocean or in products.

supply-side environmental policy.text: Rules that limit or discourage the extraction of natural resources such as fossil fuels, rather than only their use.

emissions gap.text: The difference between the emission cuts countries have pledged and the cuts needed to meet a temperature goal, tracked in UNEP's annual Emissions Gap Report.

direct air capture.text: Using chemical or physical processes to pull carbon dioxide straight out of the surrounding air; with long-term storage it is called DACCS.

bioenergy with carbon capture and storag.term: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage
bioenergy with carbon capture and storag.text: Getting energy from biomass and capturing and storing the carbon dioxide this produces; known as BECCS.

geoengineering.text: Deliberate large-scale intervention in Earth's climate system to counteract human-caused climate change; also called climate engineering.

solar radiation modification.text: Large-scale methods to limit global warming by reflecting more sunlight away from Earth back to space; also called solar geoengineering.

credibility of net-zero pledges.text: The debate over whether net-zero targets are trustworthy, given that most are voluntary and lack enforcement.

costs of carbon dioxide removal.text: What it costs per tonne to remove carbon dioxide, which varies with how mature each method is and with the markets for removals and by-products.

enhanced weathering.text: Speeding up natural rock weathering by spreading finely ground silicate rock, such as basalt, so it reacts with water and air and removes carbon dioxide.

biochar carbon removal.text: A negative emissions method that turns leftover biomass into biochar by pyrolysis and stores it in soil or durable materials; also called pyrogenic carbon capture and storage.

net zero for short-lived gases.text: The point that short-lived gases such as methane need not reach zero to halt warming, because cutting them lowers their warming effect at once.

carbon removal as moral hazard.text: The worry that promises of future carbon removal could weaken efforts to cut emissions now.

marine carbon dioxide removal.text: Methods that remove carbon dioxide through the ocean, whose dissolved carbon stays in balance with CO2 in the air.

permanence of carbon removal.text: How long carbon taken from the air stays stored before it might return to the atmosphere.

residual emissions and like-for-like rem.text: Residual emissions are those not practical to cut for technical reasons; robust net zero rules say they must be balanced by removals that store carbon as long as the gas would last.

glacial geoengineering.text: Proposed interventions to slow the loss of glaciers, ice sheets and sea ice.

governance of geoengineering.text: The international rules and agreements that address geoengineering, mostly specific to each method.

marine cloud brightening.text: Spraying tiny sea-water droplets into low ocean clouds to make them reflect more sunlight.

energy transition.text: A major structural change in how energy is supplied and used; today, the shift from fossil fuels to renewable and low-carbon energy.

stratospheric aerosol injection.text: Putting small reflective particles into the upper atmosphere to reflect sunlight and cool the planet.

termination shock.text: The rapid warming that would follow if solar radiation modification masking much warming were stopped suddenly.

biomass carbon removal and storage.text: A family of carbon removal methods that collect biomass, such as farm waste, and store its carbon permanently or semi-permanently; known as BiCRS.

biochar carbon credits.text: Carbon credits earned by certified biochar carbon removal and sold in carbon markets.

sustainable energy.text: Energy that meets present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs, judged by its effects on environment, economy and society.

just transition.text: The principle that the shift to a low-carbon economy should treat people fairly and leave no workers, places or countries behind.

fossil fuel phase-out.text: The proposed gradual reduction of fossil fuel use and production to zero, to cut air pollution, limit climate change and gain energy independence.

electrification.text: Switching to electricity as the power source; in sustainable energy, moving end uses like transport and heating onto clean electricity.

energy justice.text: The aim that communities gain affordable, safe and sustainable energy and take part in decisions about it.

falling cost of renewables.text: The steep drop in the cost of wind, solar and batteries that has made them the cheapest new power in many regions.

coal phase-out.text: Stopping the burning of coal in power plants and elsewhere, as part of the fossil fuel phase-out.

renewable energy sources.text: Energy sources that are naturally replenished, such as solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, bioenergy and marine energy.

climate-related asset stranding.text: The loss of value of assets such as fossil fuel reserves and carbon-intensive plants as climate policy, technology and markets shift.

100% renewable energy.text: The goal of meeting all energy use from renewable resources.

critical minerals for the energy transit.term: Critical minerals for the energy transition
critical minerals for the energy transit.text: Minerals needed for clean energy technologies, whose demand is set to rise steeply with the transition.

energy additions.text: The view that humanity has never truly switched energy sources but has kept adding new ones on top of old ones.

geopolitics of the energy transition.text: How shifting energy sources changes the relations, dependencies and fortunes of countries and companies.

clean cooking.text: Replacing polluting cooking fuels such as wood and dung with clean facilities.

financing the energy transition.text: Raising the money for innovation and investment that the energy transition needs.

hydrogen as a clean fuel.text: Using cleanly produced hydrogen gas as a fuel where cheaper low-carbon options are scarce, such as heavy industry and long-distance transport.

sustainability of bioenergy.text: The question of whether energy from plant and animal material really cuts emissions, given how biomass is grown and sourced.

unabated fossil fuels.text: Fossil fuels burned without measures, such as carbon capture, that substantially cut their emissions.

heating electrification.text: Switching space, water and industrial heating from burning fuels to electricity, mainly heat pumps.

transport electrification.text: Replacing fuel-burning vehicles with electric ones to make transport more sustainable.

phase-out of fossil fuel vehicles.text: Bans on selling new petrol and diesel vehicles, requiring new cars to be electric or otherwise zero-emission.

peak coal.text: The point of highest coal consumption, after which use is expected to decline.

climate change adaptation.text: The process of adjusting to current and expected effects of climate change, to reduce harm and take advantage of opportunities.

sea level rise.text: The rise in average ocean level, which has sped up sharply as human-caused warming expands seawater and melts land ice.

climate resilience.text: How well people or ecosystems can cope with, and bounce back from, climate hazards such as floods and droughts.

vulnerability.text: The state of being open to harm; for hazards, the features of a community, system or asset that make it susceptible to damage.

adaptive capacity.text: The ability of people, institutions, ecosystems and other organisms to adjust to potential harm, seize opportunities or cope with consequences.

adaptation costs and the adaptation gap.term: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap
adaptation costs and the adaptation gap.text: The cost of adapting to climate change, and the shortfall between that cost and the money available, known as the adaptation gap.

barriers to private adaptation investmen.text: The reasons private investors find adaptation harder to fund than mitigation, chiefly the lack of a clear income stream.

climate risk factors.text: The three interacting ingredients of climate risk: the hazard, the exposure of people and assets, and their vulnerability.

climate change vulnerability.text: How strongly people or ecosystems are likely to be harmed by climate change; formally, their propensity to be adversely affected.

disaster risk reduction.text: Actions that make disasters less likely and less damaging, by preventing new risk, reducing existing risk and managing what remains.

international adaptation finance.text: Money from richer countries and international funds that helps developing countries adapt to climate change.

limits to adaptation.text: The points beyond which adaptation can no longer protect people or ecosystems from climate risks.

loss and damage.text: The harms from climate change that mitigation and adaptation fail to prevent, and the question of how to deal with them.

maladaptation.text: An adaptation action that ends up increasing vulnerability to climate change or reducing the ability to adapt sustainably later.

sea level rise adaptation.text: The ways societies respond to rising seas: retreating, accommodating coastal change, or protecting coasts with hard or soft defences.

climate risk insurance.text: Insurance designed to cover the financial risks of climate change, especially extreme weather.

early warning system.text: A chain of sensors, detection and communication that spots hazards early and gives people time to prepare and limit harm.

the adaptation fund.text: An international fund under the Kyoto Protocol that pays for projects helping developing countries adapt to climate change.

adaptation–mitigation synergies and trad.text: The ways actions to adapt to climate change and actions to limit it can reinforce or work against each other.

additionality in adaptation finance.text: The principle that adaptation money should be extra to existing development aid rather than redirected from it.

economics of disaster risk reduction.text: The costs of disasters and the case for spending on prevention rather than only on response and recovery.

climate services.text: Systems that deliver usable climate information to people and organisations to support adaptation, mitigation and risk decisions.

types of adaptation options.text: The four kinds of adaptation action: infrastructural, institutional, behavioural and nature-based.

climate resilient development.text: Development that pursues adaptation, mitigation and sustainable development together, using their synergies and reducing trade-offs.

resilience measurement.text: Tools and indicators for tracking the climate resilience of households, communities or nations to guide spending on resilience.

climate risk management.text: Strategies for reducing climate risk that draw on adaptation, disaster management and sustainable development.

ecological anthropology.text: The branch of anthropology that studies how human cultures adapt to and shape their environments.

sendai framework for disaster risk reduc.term: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction
sendai framework for disaster risk reduc.text: The international framework adopted on March 18, 2015, setting seven targets for reducing disaster risk to 2030.

social vulnerability.text: The inability of people, organisations and societies to withstand harm from multiple stresses such as social exclusion and natural hazards.

types of climate vulnerability.text: The main split between biophysical vulnerability, the effects of physical hazards, and social vulnerability, shaped by political, economic and social structures.

climate vulnerability assessment.text: Tools that measure climate vulnerability, from global indices to local models and participatory methods, to guide responses.

loss and damage fund.text: A climate finance fund agreed at COP27 in Egypt in 2022 to support communities where adaptation is inadequate or comes too late.

warsaw international mechanism.text: The UN body created in 2013 to address loss and damage in highly vulnerable countries through research and dialogue.

crop insurance.text: Government-subsidised insurance bought by farmers against crop losses from disasters such as hail, drought and floods, or against lost revenue.

index-based insurance.text: Insurance, mainly for farming, that pays out when an index closely tied to losses, such as rainfall or yield, crosses a set trigger.

flood insurance.text: Insurance against losses from flooding, one of the most widely used forms of climate risk insurance.

base flood.text: A flood with a one percent chance of being equalled or exceeded in any year, also called the 100-year flood, used to define floodplains.

basis risk.text: The mismatch in index insurance between what the index pays and the losses a particular farmer actually suffers.

united nations framework convention on c.term: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
united nations framework convention on c.text: The international treaty, and the UN process built on it, through which countries negotiate how to limit dangerous climate change.

climate finance.text: Money, such as loans, grants or government budget spending, used to cut greenhouse gas emissions, adapt to climate change or build resilience.

ozone depletion.text: Ozone depletion is a lowered total amount of ozone in the upper stratosphere plus a much larger springtime decrease over the polar regions, observed since the late 1970s.

montreal protocol.text: An international treaty that protects the ozone layer by phasing out the production of substances that deplete it.

kyoto protocol.text: An international treaty extending the UNFCCC that committed its parties to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

paris agreement.text: An international climate treaty, negotiated in 2015 and signed in 2016, covering mitigation, adaptation and finance.

fossil fuel divestment.text: Pressuring institutions to sell off stocks, bonds and other investments in fossil fuel extraction companies, as a way to fight climate change.

united nations climate change conference.text: The yearly conferences, known as COPs, at which the parties to the UN climate convention meet to assess and negotiate climate action.

annex i and non-annex i countries.term: Annex I and non-Annex I countries
annex i and non-annex i countries.text: The UNFCCC's grouping of countries into industrialised and transition economies (Annex I), richer donor countries (Annex II) and mostly developing countries (non-Annex I), each with different duties.

nationally determined contribution.text: A country's own pledge, under the Paris Agreement, of how it will cut greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to climate change.

article 6 cooperative mechanisms.text: The part of the 2015 Paris Agreement that sets out how countries may cooperate voluntarily to carry out their nationally determined contributions.

ultimate objective of the unfccc.text: The UNFCCC's Article 2 goal of stabilising greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate.

climate target.text: A measurable long-term commitment in climate and energy policy, also called a climate goal or pledge, aimed at limiting climate change.

common but differentiated responsibiliti.text: The principle, set in the 1992 UN climate convention, that all countries share a duty to tackle environmental damage but not to the same degree.

adaptation finance.text: Climate finance that pays for responding to the consequences of climate change.

mitigation finance.text: Investment that aims to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions.

global stocktake.text: The Paris Agreement's five-yearly review of how far the world as a whole has got toward the agreement's goals.

climate debt.text: The debt said to be owed by developed countries to developing ones for the damage caused by their far larger share of climate-changing emissions.

enhanced transparency framework.text: The Paris Agreement's common system, under Article 13, for monitoring, reporting and verifying what countries do on climate and the support they give or receive.

action for climate empowerment.text: The UNFCCC's name, adopted in 2015, for its work on climate education, training, public awareness, participation, access to information and cooperation on these.

criticism of the unfccc process.text: The argument that the UNFCCC and Kyoto Protocol have failed to cut greenhouse gas emissions as intended.

2 degree climate target.text: The international policy goal of keeping global warming below two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial (1850–1900) levels.

national communication (unfccc).text: A report that each country party to the UNFCCC submits on its climate measures and vulnerabilities.

doha amendment.text: The 2012 extension of the Kyoto Protocol that set a second commitment period running to 2020.

hot air (surplus kyoto allowances).text: The large surplus of Kyoto emission allowances held by former Soviet-bloc economies, whose sale would not actually cut emissions.

kyoto compliance mechanism.text: The Kyoto Protocol's system for monitoring whether parties meet their commitments and penalising those that do not.

effectiveness of the paris agreement.text: The debate over whether the Paris Agreement can achieve its temperature goals.

antarctic ozone hole.text: The Antarctic ozone hole is an area of the Antarctic stratosphere where ozone has dropped to as low as 33 percent of pre-1975 values.

ozone-depleting substances.text: Ozone-depleting substances are halogenated chemicals, chiefly CFCs, that are mainly responsible for man-made ozone depletion.

intended nationally determined contribut.text: The initial, voluntary and non-binding climate pledges countries made before the 2015 Paris Agreement, which became their first NDCs.

ratchet mechanism.text: The Paris Agreement's five-yearly cycle of reporting, review and new pledges, designed to raise countries' climate ambition over time.

pledge and review.text: A way of organising international climate action in which each country makes its own pledge, others review its progress, and stronger pledges follow.

glasgow climate pact.text: The agreement reached at the 2021 UN climate conference (COP26) in Glasgow.

adaptation finance gap.text: The difference between the estimated cost of adapting to climate change and the money available for adaptation.

climate finance gap.text: The shortfall between the climate investment that is needed and what is actually provided.

green climate fund.text: A climate finance fund set up under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change to help developing countries with mitigation and adaptation.

global environment facility.text: The Global Environment Facility is a multilateral environmental fund giving grants and blended finance to developing countries for biodiversity, climate change, international waters, land degradation, pollutants and forests.

debt-for-climate swap.text: A deal in which a country's debt is repaid on new discounted terms and the repayments, in local currency, are redirected to domestic climate projects.

multilateral climate funds.text: Funds governed by several national governments together that pay out money for climate action.

private climate finance.text: Climate investment from private sources such as banks, pension funds, insurers, asset managers, companies and households.

climate club.text: A voluntary coalition of countries that agree on a common climate standard, such as a carbon price, and penalise non-members.

kigali amendment.text: A 2016 amendment to the Montreal Protocol under which countries promised to cut their use of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) by more than 80% over 30 years.

multilateral fund (montreal protocol).text: The fund that helps developing countries with low use of ozone-depleting substances comply with the Montreal Protocol.

additionality of climate finance.text: The rule that climate finance given to developing countries should be new money, additional to existing development aid.

green bank.text: A usually public or quasi-public financial institution that works with private investors to speed up the spread of clean energy technologies.

climate reparations.text: Requested loss-and-damage payments for harm caused by climate change, framed as compensation owed for historical emissions and possibly including debt cancellation.

gef governance structure.text: The GEF is governed through an Assembly, a Council, a Secretariat, agencies, a scientific panel and an Independent Evaluation Office.

incremental cost principle.text: The GEF funds the incremental or additional costs of turning a project with national benefits into one with global environmental benefits.

bali action plan.text: The 2007 decision at COP 13 in Bali that set a timeline and structure for negotiating a climate framework for after 2012.

internationally transferred mitigation o.text: Measured emission reductions or removals that one country transfers to another under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement and that count toward the buyer's NDC.

corresponding adjustment.text: The accounting step that makes sure an emission reduction transferred between countries is counted in only one country's NDC.

non-market approaches (article 6.8).text: Voluntary cooperation between countries under Article 6.8 of the Paris Agreement that involves no international transfer of emission reductions.

paris agreement crediting mechanism.text: A UN-supervised scheme set up under Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement that registers emission-cutting activities and issues credits for verified reductions or removals.

global climate regime.text: The worldwide framework of rules for regulating how human activity affects the climate system, in order to limit climate change.

soft loan.text: A loan with an interest rate below the market rate.

new collective quantified goal on climat.term: New Collective Quantified Goal on climate finance
new collective quantified goal on climat.text: The new climate finance target, negotiated at COP29 in 2024, for supporting developing countries after 2025, building on the earlier $100 billion a year goal.

history of climate change policy.text: The history of political actions, policies, controversies and activism concerning climate change.

contraction and convergence.text: A proposed global framework that shrinks total greenhouse gas emissions to a safe level while bringing every country's emissions per person to the same level.

icj advisory opinion on climate obligati.term: ICJ advisory opinion on climate obligations
icj advisory opinion on climate obligati.text: A 2025 advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice on what international law requires states to do to protect the climate, requested by the UN General Assembly in 2023.

first global stocktake (2023).text: The first Paris Agreement stocktake, concluded at COP 28 in Dubai in December 2023 as part of the UAE Consensus.

adaptation debt.text: The compensation developing countries claim they are owed for climate damage caused by the developed world's emissions.

emissions debt.text: The part of climate debt said to be owed by developed countries for having used more than their fair share of the atmosphere's capacity to absorb emissions.

criticism of the kyoto protocol.text: The debate over whether the Kyoto Protocol's commitments were too weak, too costly, or wrongly designed.

cancún agreements.text: Decisions taken at the 2010 UN climate conference in Cancún, including national mitigation pledges and the creation of the Green Climate Fund.

copenhagen accord.text: A 2009 agreement produced by a group of countries at the Copenhagen climate conference, which the conference only 'took note of'.

ecological economics.text: A field of research, drawing on many disciplines, that studies how human economies and natural ecosystems depend on each other and change together over time and space.

energy.text: The quantitative property transferred to a body or system, seen in the capacity to do work and in heat and light.

renewable energy.text: Energy made from renewable natural resources that are replenished on a human timescale.

money.text: Any item or verifiable record generally accepted as payment for goods and services and repayment of debts in a given country or context.

mathematical model.text: An abstract description of a concrete system using mathematical concepts and language.

energy storage.text: Capturing energy produced at one time so it can be used later, which reduces imbalances between energy demand and supply.

heterodox economics.text: A broad term for schools of economic thought that are not generally seen as part of mainstream economics.

systems ecology.text: A holistic, interdisciplinary branch of ecology that studies ecosystems as complex systems, applying general systems theory to ecology.

cost shifting.text: The ecological-economics view that environmental and social harms are not occasional side effects ('externalities') but costs that businesses routinely shift onto others.

critique of ecosystem service valuation.text: The argument, made by Douglas McCauley among others, that putting money values on nature and its services can harm conservation.

growth versus development.text: The distinction ecological economics draws between growth, a quantitative rise in economic output, and development, a qualitative improvement in quality of life.

history of ecological economics.text: How ecological economics grew from 19th-century and early 20th-century ideas into a discipline with its own society and journal by 1989.

laws of thermodynamics.text: The basic physical laws governing energy, heat, work, temperature and entropy, which rule out things such as perpetual motion machines.

entropy.text: A physical quantity often described as a measure of how spread out, or dispersed, energy is in a system; loosely, its degree of disorder.

first law of thermodynamics.text: The law of conservation of energy applied to heat and work: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.

embodied energy.text: The total energy needed to produce a good or service, counted as if it were stored inside the product.

green building.text: Both a structure and the processes that make it environmentally responsible and resource-efficient across its life cycle, from planning to demolition.

exergy.text: The maximum useful work that can be obtained from a system as it comes into balance with its surroundings; often called 'available energy'.

energy return on investment.text: The ratio of usable energy delivered by an energy source to the energy spent to obtain it.

uneconomic growth.text: Economic growth that reflects or causes a fall in quality of life.

spaceship earth.text: A worldview that sees Earth as a spaceship with limited supplies, whose passengers must act as one crew for the common good.

stationary state in classical economics.text: The classical economists' idea that an economy would eventually stop growing and settle with a constant population and stock of capital.

buddhist economics.text: A spiritual and philosophical approach to economics that aims for the most well-being with the least use of resources.

thermoeconomics.text: A school of heterodox economics, also called biophysical economics, that applies the laws of thermodynamics to economic theory.

social metabolism.text: The flows of materials and energy between nature and society, between societies, and within them.

post-keynesian economics.text: A heterodox, non-equilibrium school of economics that grew out of Keynes's General Theory and was developed by Kalecki, Robinson, Kaldor, Weintraub and others.

costanza's valuation of the global ecosy.term: Costanza's valuation of the global ecosystem
costanza's valuation of the global ecosy.text: A 1997 study led by Robert Costanza that tried to put a total money value on the services the world's ecosystems provide.

ecological-economic modeling.text: The use of mathematical models to analyse how economies and ecosystems interact.

energy accounting.text: Tracking energy into and out of a system, the useful work done and the energy lost, to judge resource use and environmental impact.

green economy.text: An economy that is low-carbon, efficient in its use of resources and socially inclusive; green economics is a more politically applied relative of ecological economics.

conservation of mass.text: The physical law that in a system closed to matter flowing in or out, total mass stays constant: matter is neither created nor destroyed, only rearranged.

second law of thermodynamics.text: The law that natural processes are irreversible: the total entropy of interacting systems never decreases, so heat never flows by itself from cold to hot.

monetary theory in ecological economics.text: Ecological economics' work on money and monetary policy, aimed at sustainable scale, just distribution and efficient allocation.

non-western approaches to ecological eco.text: Cultural and traditional economic outlooks, such as Buen Vivir and Ecological Swaraj, that stress harmony with nature and are now counted as ecological economic practice.

schools of ecological economics.text: The competing camps within ecological economics, from those close to mainstream resource economics to far more heterodox ones.

metabolic rift.text: A theory, credited by sociologist John Bellamy Foster to Karl Marx, that capitalism breaks the natural exchange of materials between society and nature, producing ecological crisis.

entropy pessimism.text: The view that technology cannot escape the laws of physics, since every technology turns valuable resources into waste and so raises entropy.

resource decoupling.text: Economic activity becoming less demanding on nature, so fewer natural resources are needed per unit of output.

seminal works of 1966-1972.text: Four works published between 1966 and 1972 on the importance of natural resources and the environment that led to ecological economics.

ecologically unequal exchange.text: The idea that world trade hides an unfair flow of materials, energy and environmental damage, not just labour, from poorer to richer countries.

space colonisation and limits to growth.term: Space colonisation and limits to growth
space colonisation and limits to growth.text: The proposal that settling outer space could ease overpopulation and resource limits on Earth.

types of money.text: Money can be commodity, representative, fiat, demurrage, commercial bank or digital money.

stock-flow consistent model.text: A family of non-equilibrium macroeconomic models built on strict accounting so that every flow and stock in an economy is included and adds up.

sustainability science.text: An applied academic discipline, emerging in the 1980s, that studies sustainability and sustainable development and links knowledge to action.

unequal exchange.text: The hidden transfer of labour and ecological value from poor countries, mainly in the Global South, to rich countries and corporations, mainly in the North, through structurally unequal trade.

heterodox critique of homo economicus.text: The objection, shared by many heterodox schools, to the neoclassical picture of people as rational agents who maximise their own utility or profit.

heterodox critique of market equilibrium.text: The objection that neoclassical models of markets settling at efficient equilibrium prices rarely capture real markets.

ecological energetics.text: The quantitative study of how energy flows through ecological systems.

deliberative democracy.text: A form of democracy in which deliberation is central to decision-making and the source of legitimacy for law.

urban metabolism.text: A model for describing and analysing the flows of materials and energy through cities, as in a city-level material flow analysis.

embodied energy data methods.text: The ways databases estimate embodied energy: bottom-up process data, top-down input-output data, or a hybrid of both.

embodied energy in transport.text: The energy used to make, maintain and recycle vehicles and to build transport networks, beyond the fuel burned.

embodied energy of buildings.text: The energy used to extract, process, transport, assemble, maintain and finally dispose of a building's materials.

energy quality.text: How much of a form of energy can be turned into useful work, measured as the ratio of its exergy to its energy.

emergy.text: The total energy of one kind, usually sunlight, used directly and indirectly to make a product or service; a way of expressing differences in energy quality.

exergy destruction.text: The work potential lost, or wasted, in a real process; also called irreversibility.

exergy in environmental policy.text: Proposals to use exergy analysis to make environmental policy fairer and more effective.

eroi of energy sources.text: Estimates of energy return on investment for particular technologies, from oil shale to hydropower.

energy cannibalism.text: The effect where rapid growth of an energy industry consumes the energy of existing plants to build new ones, limiting how fast it can grow.

energy stored on energy invested.text: For a storage device, the ratio of electricity stored over its lifetime to the embodied electricity needed to build it.

expanded eroi calculations.text: Three wider ways of counting EROI: point of use, extended and societal.

falling eroi and civilisational collapse.text: The argument that a declining energy return on investment helps explain why complex societies collapse.

steady-state economy.text: An economy with a constant stock of physical wealth (capital) and a constant population, so that it does not grow over time.

throughput.text: The flow of matter and energy that enters the economy from nature as resources and leaves it again as waste and pollution.

net energy and payback time.text: Net energy is the amount of energy gained from a source after subtracting what was invested, while EROI expresses the same thing as a ratio.

jevons paradox.text: The proposition that technology which makes resource use more efficient tends to increase, not reduce, total use of that resource.

declining-state economy.text: The argument, from Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen and degrowth thinkers, that a shrinking economy is better than a steady one for stretching finite minerals.

capitalism without growth.text: The question, raised by radical critics, of whether a steady or shrinking economy can be imposed on top of capitalism.

daly's institutions for a steady state.term: Daly's institutions for a steady state
daly's institutions for a steady state.text: Herman Daly's proposal to create a steady-state economy by policy, through three state institutions limiting inequality, population and resource use.

degrowth as a path to the steady state.term: Degrowth as a path to the steady state
degrowth as a path to the steady state.text: Christian Kerschner's view that rich countries should shrink their economies as a route to a fair world steady-state economy.

post-normal science.text: A problem-solving approach for science used in policy when 'facts are uncertain, values in dispute, stakes high and decisions urgent', developed by Silvio Funtowicz and Jerome Ravetz in the 1990s.

great stagnation critique of degrowth.text: Wim Naudé's criticism that Western economies already resemble degrowth, in a 'Great Stagnation' of falling innovation and entrepreneurship.

overdevelopment.text: The idea that rich countries of the global north are too developed, increasing humanity's ecological impact and causing problems for both rich and poor countries.

solar-income budget.text: Daly's term for the limit humans lived within before industrialisation, relying on the steady flow of sunlight rather than the stock of minerals.

emergy performance indicators.text: Ratios from emergy accounting that judge how a process uses local, renewable and purchased resources.

transformity.text: The emergy needed per unit of available energy produced; a measure of an energy form's quality.

social metabolism accounting schools.text: The two main ways of measuring social metabolism: the Vienna school's Material and Energy Flow Analysis (MEFA) and the Barcelona school's MuSIASEM.

musiasem.text: Multi-Scale Integrated Analysis of Societal and Ecosystem Metabolism: an accounting method for analysing social-ecological systems and simulating possible development paths.

sociometabolic regimes.text: Rolf Sieferle's classification of human history into hunter-gatherer, agrarian and industrial regimes according to their main energy source and conversion technology.

eco-urbanism and the metabolic rift.text: Efforts in city planning to close loops by bringing a city's energy, water, food and waste flows back within its own systems.

moore's reading of the metabolic rift.term: Moore's reading of the metabolic rift
moore's reading of the metabolic rift.text: Jason W. Moore's view that metabolic rifts began with capitalism in the 'long' 16th century and recur in each phase of capitalist development.

declining terms of trade.text: Raúl Prebisch's finding that prices of raw materials exported by poorer countries fall over time relative to the manufactured goods they import.

coevolutionary economics.text: An approach in ecological economics that studies change as mutual feedback and selection between social, environmental and economic systems.

materials balance principle.text: The application of conservation of mass to the economy: tracking the mass of materials through a system so that everything that goes in is accounted for as product, stock or waste.

maximum power principle.text: Howard T. Odum's principle that organisms, ecosystems and societies organise themselves to maximise their use of available energy for survival.

optimal scale of the economy.text: The ecological-economics question of how large the economy should be relative to the ecosystems it depends on, alongside fair distribution and efficient allocation.

extended peer community.text: In post-normal science, the wider group of stakeholders, beyond scientists, who share in checking the quality of scientific inputs to a decision.

green logistics.text: Efforts to measure and reduce the environmental impact of moving and storing goods, information and services.

quantitative methods of post-normal scie.text: Quantitative techniques linked to post-normal science: NUSAP for numbers, sensitivity auditing for indicators and models, quantitative storytelling and MuSIASEM.

sustainability.text: Sustainability is the ability to keep going over a long time; today it usually means a state in which environment, economy and society all continue to exist long into the future.

weak and strong sustainability.text: Weak and strong sustainability are two opposing approaches from environmental economics that differ on whether natural capital can be replaced by human-made capital.

three dimensions of sustainability.text: The three dimensions of sustainability are the environmental, social and economic areas that scholars usually distinguish within the concept.

robert solow.text: An American economist who developed the Solow–Swan growth model and won the 1987 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.

sustainable development.text: Sustainable development is an approach to growth and human development that aims to meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

economic dimension of sustainability.text: The economic dimension of sustainability concerns how economic development fits with protecting the environment and meeting basic needs, and it is controversial.

nested model of sustainability.text: The nested model ranks the three dimensions of sustainability, drawing the economy inside society and society inside the environment.

sustainability barriers.text: Sustainability barriers are the reasons sustainability is so hard to achieve.

sustainability transition.text: A sustainability transition (or transformation) is a deep, system-wide change in technology, economy, society, values and goals towards sustainability.

brundtland commission.text: The Brundtland Commission, formally the World Commission on Environment and Development, was a UN body set up to unite countries in pursuit of sustainable development.

intergenerational equity.text: Intergenerational equity is the idea of fairness or justice between generations, including between people alive now and future generations.

capital approach to sustainability.text: The capital approach judges sustainability by the stock of capital (human, natural and other) that each generation passes on.

daly's operational principles of sustain.text: Daly's operational principles are three rules for sustainable development published by Herman Daly in 1990.

strong sustainability.text: Strong sustainability is the view that natural and human-made capital are complementary but not interchangeable, so certain natural capital must be preserved.

weak sustainability.text: Weak sustainability is the view that natural capital may decline as long as human-made capital grows enough to keep the total capital stock from falling.

hartwick's rule.text: Hartwick's rule states how much a society must invest in produced capital to exactly offset the decline of its non-renewable resources, so living standards do not fall.

overlapping generations model.text: The overlapping generations (OLG) model is a leading framework in macroeconomic dynamics in which people live for a finite time, long enough to overlap with other generations.

cobb–douglas production function.text: The Cobb–Douglas production function is a widely used mathematical form linking the amounts of inputs, especially labour and capital, to the output they can produce.

genuine savings.text: Genuine savings is a monetary measure of a nation's net change in produced, natural and human capital stocks.

social bequest approach.text: The social bequest approach reframes sustainability around what specific rights and opportunities we leave to future generations, rather than how much.

critical natural capital.text: Critical natural capital is natural capital such as air, water and land whose ecological functions cannot be replaced by human-made alternatives, as opposed to non-critical capital such as minerals.

constant elasticity of substitution.text: Constant elasticity of substitution (CES) is a common form for production and utility functions in which the ease of substituting one input or good for another stays the same at all levels of output or utility.

elasticity of substitution.text: The elasticity of substitution measures how easily one input or good can be swapped for another: the percentage change in their ratio of use for a percentage change in their relative marginal values or prices.

substitutability of natural capital.text: Substitutability of natural capital is the question of how far human-made capital (buildings, machinery, technology) can replace natural capital (forests, water, clean air).

marginal rate of technical substitution.text: The amount by which one input must be reduced when one more unit of another input is used so that output stays constant.

solow–swan model.text: An economic model that explains long-run growth through capital accumulation, labour or population growth, and rising productivity from technological progress.

population growth.text: The increase in the number of people in a population.

logistic growth and carrying capacity.text: A model in which a population's growth slows as it nears the carrying capacity, the largest population its environment can sustain.

golden rule savings rate.text: The share of income saved that gives the highest level of consumption per person that can be kept up forever, as in the Solow–Swan model.

mankiw–romer–weil model.text: A 1992 version of the Solow–Swan model that adds human capital, such as education, as a factor of production.

conditional convergence.text: The prediction that poor countries' incomes catch up with rich countries' if they save similar shares of output in physical and human capital.

solow residual.text: The part of output growth left unexplained after accounting for capital accumulation, taken as a measure of total factor productivity growth.

ak model.text: The simplest endogenous growth model, in which output is a linear function of capital, Y = AK.

overconsumption.text: Using goods, services or natural resources faster than they can be replenished or reused.

human overpopulation.text: The idea that human populations may grow too large to be supported by their environment or resources over the long term.

the limits to growth.text: A 1972 report that used computer simulation to explore what happens when the economy and population grow exponentially on a planet with finite resources.

rebound effect.text: The loss of part of the expected savings from a more efficient technology, because people and the economy respond by using more.

economic inequality.text: An umbrella term for income inequality, wealth inequality and consumption inequality, measurable between or within nations and sub-populations.

i = pat.text: A formula stating that human impact on the environment (I) is the product of population (P), affluence (A) and technology (T).

eco-economic decoupling.text: The idea that an economy could grow without a matching rise in pressure on the environment.

degrowth.text: An academic and social movement, mainly in Europe, that calls for planned, democratic reduction of production and consumption to tackle social and ecological crises.

global north and global south.text: A way of grouping countries by socioeconomic characteristics, roughly developed and developing or least developed countries.

green growth.text: Paths of economic growth that are environmentally sustainable, a term used in economic theory and policymaking.

demographic transition.text: The historical shift from high to low birth and death rates as societies gain technology, education (especially for women) and economic development.

resource efficiency.text: Using the Earth's limited resources sustainably so that the same output or consumption is achieved with fewer resources and less environmental impact.

sustainable consumption.text: Using products and services in ways that keep their harm to the environment as small as possible.

kuznets curve.text: Simon Kuznets's hypothesis that, as an economy develops, market forces first raise and then lower economic inequality, tracing an inverted U.

environmental kuznets curve.text: The hypothesis that environmental damage gets worse as an economy grows until average income reaches a certain level, after which it improves.

universal basic income.text: A welfare proposal in which all members of a population regularly receive a minimum income as an unconditional transfer, with no means test or work requirement.

doughnut economics.text: A doughnut-shaped picture of sustainable development that joins planetary boundaries (an outer ecological ceiling) with a social foundation of basic human needs (an inner ring).

resource intensity.text: The amount of a resource, such as water, energy or materials, needed to produce, process and dispose of one unit of a good or service.

planned obsolescence.text: Designing a product with an artificially short useful life or a deliberately weak design so that it stops working, or looks out of date, after a set time.

appropriate technology.text: A movement and set of technology choices that are small-scale, affordable to users, labor-intensive, energy-efficient, environmentally sustainable and locally autonomous.

world3.text: A system dynamics computer model simulating how population, industrial growth, food production and Earth's ecosystem limits interact.

ecological overshoot.text: What happens when the demands placed on an ecosystem exceed its ability to regenerate.

agrowth.text: The policy stance of being indifferent to GDP growth when designing policies for economic and social progress.

ecomodernism.text: An environmental philosophy holding that technology can protect nature and improve human wellbeing by decoupling economic growth from environmental impact.

green new deal.text: A movement calling for public policy that tackles climate change while also creating jobs, supporting economic growth and reducing inequality.

eco-sufficiency.text: A strategy of shrinking a society's environmental footprint by moderating its demand for energy, carbon and material-based goods and services.

sustainability strategies.text: Established ways of moving toward sustainability, classically the three strategies of sufficiency, efficiency and consistency.

post-growth.text: An umbrella term for economic, ecological and political views that accept endless economic growth cannot last on a finite planet.

growth imperative.text: The idea that an economy may be forced to grow, because firms, households or governments face serious harm without growth.

consumerism.text: A socio-cultural and economic phenomenon in which many people aspire to acquire goods and services beyond what is needed for survival or traditional displays.

simple living.text: Practices that promote simplicity in one's lifestyle, such as owning fewer possessions, using less technology and spending less money.

types of rebound effect.text: The three ways the economy can take back efficiency savings: the direct, indirect and economy-wide rebound effects.

relative and absolute decoupling.text: Relative decoupling means environmental impact per unit of output falls while total impact may still rise; absolute decoupling means total impact falls while output grows.

decoupling evidence debate.text: The dispute over whether growth has been, or can be, decoupled from environmental pressure fast enough to avoid serious damage.

affluence and overconsumption.text: The argument that the richest consumers drive a disproportionate share of overconsumption and its environmental harm.

green economics.text: Any economic theory that treats the economy as a part of the ecosystem it sits within.

green economy indices.text: Indicators built to measure how green an economy is, from human ecological impact to efficiency and green investment flows.

overpopulation.text: The state in which a species' population is larger than the carrying capacity of its environment.

resource productivity.text: The amount of a good or service obtained for each unit of resource used.

degrowth policy proposals.text: The concrete measures degrowth writers propose for shrinking production and consumption fairly.

human population planning.text: Proposals to stabilize and then gradually reduce human numbers as a response to overpopulation.

bariloche model.text: A world model built by Latin American scientists in answer to The Limits to Growth, arguing that the real limits to development were social and political, not physical.

exponential reserve index.text: A way of estimating how long a resource will last when yearly use keeps growing, instead of simply dividing reserves by current use.

limits to growth compared with data.term: Limits to Growth compared with data
limits to growth compared with data.text: Later studies that check The Limits to Growth scenarios against what actually happened.

second demographic transition.text: A framework formulated in 1986 by Lesthaeghe and van de Kaa on changes in sexual and reproductive behavior in North America and Western Europe since about 1963.

limits to green growth.text: The barriers that may make green growth wishful thinking, as listed by the European Environmental Bureau.

conviviality.text: In political and degrowth thought, the ability of people to act creatively and independently with others and their environment to meet their own needs.

policies against the rebound effect.text: Measures that keep efficiency gains from being eaten up by extra use, usually by holding the cost of use steady or higher.

time rebound effect.text: Extra resource use that follows when a technology saves people time, which they then spend on more of the service or other activities.

strong and weak sustainable consumption.text: A distinction between consumption that actively cuts environmental impact (strong) and consumption that fails to (weak).

material kuznets curve.text: The finding that a country's use of steel and other metals rises and then falls over its course of development, like a Kuznets curve.

bright green environmentalism.text: An environmental philosophy that relies on advanced technology, social innovation, eco-innovation and sustainable design to solve environmental problems.

five axes of decoupling.text: A set of at least five dimensions for judging whether a claimed case of decoupling is real and enough.

resource and impact decoupling.text: Resource decoupling cuts the resources used per unit of economic activity; impact decoupling cuts the environmental harm caused while output grows.

perceived obsolescence.text: When products still work but seem out of date because styles change, so buyers replace them.

growth versus environment debate.text: The dispute over whether economic growth can be made compatible with environmental sustainability, with positions ranging from green growth through agrowth to degrowth.

variants of planned obsolescence.text: The different ways products are made to become obsolete, from built-in short lifetimes to deliberate disabling.

monetary growth imperative.text: The claim that money created as interest-bearing debt forces the economy to keep growing.

ten sustainability strategies framework.text: Eric Hartmann's framework of ten sustainability strategies, five for future generations and five for people living today.

environmental space.text: The amount of a resource a country can use without endangering its continued availability, assuming everyone in the world has an equal share.

waste.text: Unwanted or unusable materials, any substance discarded after primary use or judged worthless or defective.

khazzoom–brookes postulate.text: The claim that energy-efficiency improvements that make sense for individual users lead to higher total energy use across the economy.

factor 10.text: A policy goal of a tenfold cut in resource use per unit of output, so that economies stay within the planet's carrying capacity.

dark, light and bright greens.text: Alex Steffen's three-way split of environmentalists into dark, light and bright greens.

degrowth in the global south.text: The study of whether and how degrowth ideas apply to the countries of the Global South.

recycling.text: Turning waste materials into new materials and objects.

circular economy.text: An economic system that tries to keep products, parts and materials in use at their highest value for as long as possible.

plastic pollution.text: The build-up in the environment of plastic objects and particles, such as bottles, bags and microbeads, that harms people, wildlife and habitats.

industrial ecology.text: The study of how materials and energy flow through industrial systems.

waste hierarchy.text: A ranking of ways to deal with waste, from the most to the least environmentally preferable, usually drawn as a pyramid.

electronic waste.text: Discarded electrical or electronic devices, also called WEEE, end-of-life electronics or e-waste.

waste minimisation.text: A set of processes and practices intended to reduce the amount of waste produced.

resource recovery.text: Using wastes as raw material to make valuable new products.

zero waste.text: A set of principles focused on preventing waste by redesigning how resources flow so that all products are reused or repurposed.

economics of recycling.text: The dispute over whether recycling's economic and environmental benefits outweigh its costs.

dematerialization.text: Making more goods, or serving the same economic needs, with less material.

cradle-to-cradle design.text: A nature-inspired way of designing products and systems in which materials are treated as nutrients that circulate safely and endlessly.

sharing economy.text: An economic system in which people share in making, distributing, trading and using goods and services, often through online platforms.

circular business models.text: Ways of running a firm, such as product-as-a-service, sharing platforms and life-extension services, that make money while keeping resources in use.

critiques of the circular economy.text: Objections that the circular economy keeps growth unquestioned, ignores economics and thermodynamics, and neglects social justice.

r-hierarchies of circularity.text: Ranked lists of 're-' actions (refuse, reduce, reuse, repair, recycle and so on) that order circular strategies by how much value they keep or waste they avoid.

material flow analysis.text: A method for measuring the flows and stocks of materials or substances within a clearly defined system.
