remanufacturing.text: Rebuilding a used product to the original maker's specifications from a mix of reused, repaired and new parts.

waste valorization.text: Giving economic value to waste or residues by reusing or recycling them into useful materials.

upcycling.text: Turning waste or unwanted products into new materials or products seen as having greater quality or value, such as artistic or environmental value.

bioeconomy.text: The part of the economy that uses renewable biological resources and biotechnology to produce food, materials, products and energy.

pay as you throw.text: Charging households for rubbish collection according to how much waste they put out, instead of a flat fee.

recycling collection systems.text: The ways recyclables are gathered from the waste stream: drop-off centres, buy-back centres and curbside collection.

recycling supply and demand policies.text: Laws that secure a steady supply of recyclable material and a market for recycled products.

types of recycling.text: The main ways of recycling, grouped by process and by what the material becomes.

biomimetics.text: The replication of models, systems and elements of nature to solve complex human problems.

product-service system.text: A business model in which a firm sells a combined package of products and services that together meet a customer's need.

biorefinery.text: A facility that converts biomass into energy and other useful products such as chemicals.

circular bioeconomy.text: A bioeconomy run on circular principles, producing food, materials and energy from renewable biological resources while reducing dependence on natural resources.

circular economy standards.text: Formal standards that guide organisations in applying circular economy principles.

eu circular economy action plan.text: The European Union's policy programme for moving its economy toward circularity.

right to repair.text: The legal right of owners to maintain, repair or modify their own devices and equipment, such as cars, electronics and farm machinery.

industrial symbiosis.text: A part of industrial ecology in which separate firms exchange materials, energy, water and by-products so that one firm's waste becomes another's input.

waste management.text: The processes and actions that manage waste from its inception to its final disposal.

repurposing.text: Using an item for a purpose other than the one it was made for, usually something considered junk.

microplastics.text: Tiny insoluble plastic particles, from 1 micrometre to 5 mm across, that pollute water, soil and air.

weee and rohs directives.text: EU legislation of 2003 that set up e-waste collection and restricted hazardous substances in electronics.

composting and anaerobic digestion.text: Biological processes that break down organic waste such as food scraps and garden material into compost, fertiliser and energy.

resource recovery from wastewater.text: Recovering water, energy, nutrients and other materials from wastewater, sewage sludge and human excreta.

zero waste hierarchy.text: A ranking of policies and strategies for a zero-waste system, from the highest and best use of materials to the lowest.

eco-industrial park.text: A group of businesses on shared land that work together on environmental and resource issues to improve their environmental, economic and social performance.

life cycle thinking.text: An approach that looks at and reduces a product's environmental impacts at every stage of its life, from raw materials to disposal.

ecological sanitation.text: Sanitation systems that allow safe recycling of nutrients to crop production while minimizing use of non-renewable resources.

cradle to cradle certification.text: A product certification run by the Cradle to Cradle Products Innovation Institute that scores products against cradle-to-cradle criteria.

downcycling.text: Reusing materials to make products of lower quality or value than the original.

technical and biological nutrients.text: The cradle-to-cradle split of all materials into technical nutrients, which cycle in industry, and biological nutrients, which return safely to nature.

eco-efficiency.text: Providing goods and services that meet human needs while steadily cutting their environmental impact and resource use over their whole life cycle.

product stewardship.text: An approach in which everyone who makes, sells, buys, uses or disposes of a product shares responsibility for reducing its environmental and health impacts over its life.

container deposit scheme.text: A system in which buyers pay a refundable fee on a bottle or container, which they get back when they return it.

food waste valorisation.text: Turning food waste into food or feed products, or extracting food or feed ingredients from it.

bioplastics.text: A family of plastics made from biological rather than fossil sources, with different properties and uses.

cascading use of biomass.text: Processing biomass in an ordered pattern so that it yields the highest-value products before lower-value ones.

source reduction.text: Cutting hazardous and other waste before it arises, by changing how things are produced.

servitization.text: Meeting customer needs by selling a product's function or output, or a product-service package, rather than the product itself.

sustainable materials management.text: A systemic approach to using and reusing materials more productively across their whole life cycle.

linear economy.text: The conventional 'take-make-waste' economy in which resources are extracted, made into products, used and thrown away.

integrated product policy.text: A policy approach that reduces product-related environmental damage by acting at whichever life-cycle stage is most effective.

life cycle costing.text: Adding up all the costs a product or system incurs over its whole life to find the cheapest way of providing it.

circular fashion.text: Applying the circular economy to clothing so that fashion products last longer and are reused, recycled or repurposed instead of discarded.

circular procurement.text: Buying goods and services that follow circular economy principles, favouring reuse, durability and recycling to extend product lives and cut waste.

urban mining.text: Recovering rare metals from a society's stockpile of discarded electronic waste, its 'urban mine', by mechanical and chemical treatment.

environmental resource management.text: The management of how human societies interact with and affect the environment, rather than management of the environment itself.

adaptive management.text: A structured, repeated process for making decisions under uncertainty that uses monitoring to learn and reduce that uncertainty over time.

environmental governance.text: The ways decisions are made about controlling and managing the environment and natural resources, involving government, business and civil society.

international environmental agreement.text: A treaty among countries, meant to be legally binding, whose main purpose is to prevent or manage human impacts on natural resources.

national park.text: A government-owned and protected area of natural, semi-natural or developed land set aside for conservation because of its outstanding national natural, historic or cultural value.

european green deal.text: A set of European Commission policies, approved in 2020, whose overarching aim is to make the European Union climate neutral by 2050.

agenda 21.text: A non-binding United Nations action plan for sustainable development, produced by the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.

rio declaration on environment and devel.term: Rio Declaration on Environment and Development
rio declaration on environment and devel.text: A short document of 27 principles, produced at the 1992 Earth Summit, to guide countries in future sustainable development.

marine pollution.text: Harmful effects in the ocean from substances humans use or spread, such as waste, particles, noise, light, excess carbon dioxide or invasive organisms.

ecosystem management.text: An approach to natural resource management that aims to keep an ecosystem's functions and services going over the long term while meeting people's social, economic, political and cultural needs.

basel convention.text: An international treaty that limits the movement of hazardous waste between countries, especially from developed to less developed countries.

ecosystem-based management.text: An environmental management approach that considers all the interactions within an ecosystem, humans included, instead of single issues, species or ecosystem services in isolation.

ecosystem approach.text: A framework under the Convention on Biological Diversity for the integrated management of land, water and living resources that promotes conservation and fair, sustainable use.

public participation.text: Involving the public, especially those affected by or interested in a decision, in the activities and decisions of an organisation or project.

climate governance.text: The diplomacy, mechanisms and responses aimed at steering societies to prevent, mitigate or adapt to the risks of climate change.

climate change litigation.text: The use of lawsuits to set legal precedents that push governments and companies to act on climate change.

aarhus convention.text: A 1998 UNECE treaty, signed in Aarhus, Denmark, that gives the public rights to environmental information, participation in decisions and access to justice.

global governance.text: The institutions that coordinate the behaviour of actors across borders, help them cooperate, settle disputes and ease collective-action problems.

collective action.text: Action taken together by a group of people to improve their condition and reach a common objective.

multi-level governance.text: The way power is spread vertically across levels of government and horizontally across many non-state and quasi-state organisations.

race to the bottom.text: A situation in which governments, firms or individuals compete by steadily lowering standards or regulations to cut costs and attract economic activity.

law of the sea.text: The body of international law setting out the rights and duties of states at sea, from navigation to seabed minerals and coastal waters.

spatial planning.text: Managing space and resources by making and carrying out plans that limit how land and space can be used and developed.

global environmental governance.text: The worldwide system of institutions and agreements that tackles transboundary environmental problems such as climate change, biodiversity loss and land degradation.

earth system governance.text: A field of research that places environmental policy and conservation in the wider context of human-caused change to the whole Earth system.

stewardship.text: An ethical practice of responsibly planning and managing resources, which can be applied to the environment, economics, property and more.

citizen science.text: Research conducted with the participation of the general public or amateur and nonprofessional researchers.

bloomington school.text: A research tradition in political economy, built around Elinor and Vincent Ostrom at Indiana University Bloomington, that studies how institutions and communities govern shared problems.

vienna convention for the protection of.term: Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer
vienna convention for the protection of.text: A 1985 multilateral agreement that set the framework for international cuts in chlorofluorocarbons, which destroy the ozone layer.

london convention on marine dumping.text: A 1972 treaty to control pollution of the sea from the deliberate dumping of wastes from ships, aircraft and platforms.

forest principles.text: A non-binding 1992 Earth Summit document setting out recommendations for conserving and sustainably developing all types of forests.

local agenda 21.text: Local programmes in which towns and cities carry out Agenda 21's sustainable development plan, as its Chapter 28 recommends.

fisheries co-management.text: A flexible, cooperative way of managing aquatic resources in which fishing communities and government share responsibility.

convention on long-range transboundary a.term: Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution
convention on long-range transboundary a.text: A UNECE treaty that commits its parties to limit, gradually reduce and prevent air pollution, including pollution that travels long distances across borders.

integrated coastal zone management.text: A process for managing coasts sustainably that works across geographic and political boundaries and weighs natural, social and economic systems together.

rio conventions.text: The three conventions agreed at the June 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro: on climate change (UNFCCC), biological diversity (CBD) and desertification (UNCCD).

institutional fit.text: The match, or mismatch, between the scale of an environmental problem and the level at which policy tackles it.

polycentric governance.text: Governance by many overlapping, independent decision-making centres operating at different scales, rather than by one central authority.

marine spatial planning.text: A public process of mapping and allocating where and when human activities take place at sea to meet ecological, economic and social goals set through politics.

global goal-setting.text: A way of governing globally through goals that are not legally binding, leave each country flexibility and come without strong institutions.

orchestration (global governance).text: A soft, indirect form of global steering in which an actor such as an international organisation recruits voluntary intermediaries to influence a target group.

basel ban amendment.text: A 1995 amendment to the Basel Convention that bans exports of hazardous waste from mostly OECD developed countries to developing countries, for any reason including recycling.

transnational environmental policy.text: Environmental policy that tackles global problems such as climate change, ozone depletion or marine pollution and involves actors from at least two sovereign states.

earth system law.text: A young legal field, part of earth system governance, that imagines law rooted in the planetary scale of the Anthropocene and its socio-ecological crisis.

planetary justice.text: A view of justice that extends environmental justice to the whole human and non-human world, covering fairness among people and between people and nature.

lisbon principles.text: Six principles set out in 1997 by ecological economist Robert Costanza for the sustainable governance of the oceans and other shared resources.

freedom of the seas.text: The principle that the open sea is international territory that every nation may use but none may own.

international water law.text: The rules and agreements that govern how states share transboundary waters, meaning rivers, lakes, seas or groundwater bordered by two or more states.

science–policy interface.text: The meeting ground where scientists and policy-makers work together so that research can inform, and be guided by, decisions.

collaborative environmental governance.text: An approach to environmental governance that builds cooperation among actors across scales and jurisdictions to deal with mismatches of scale in linked human and natural systems.

transition management.text: A governance approach that tries to speed up sustainability transitions through a participatory process of shared visions, learning and experiments.

multi-level perspective on transitions.text: A framework that sees change in socio-technical systems as playing out across three levels: the broad landscape, the dominant regime and innovative niches.

sustainable development goals.text: Seventeen global goals that all UN members adopted in 2015 as part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

convention on biological diversity.text: A multilateral treaty, known informally as the Biodiversity Convention, for conserving the variety of life on Earth.

protected area.text: A place that is protected because of its recognised natural or cultural value, where human use of resources is limited.

united nations convention on the law of.term: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
united nations convention on the law of.text: An international treaty, known as UNCLOS, that sets the legal framework for all marine and maritime activities.

genetic resources.text: Genetic material from plants, animals, microbes or other sources that has actual or potential value.

sustainable development goal 14.text: The UN goal 'Life below water': to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources.

sustainable development goal 13.text: The UN goal 'Climate action': to take urgent action to limit climate change and adapt to its impacts.

ipbes.text: An independent intergovernmental body, set up by governments in 2012, that links biodiversity science to policy-making.

united nations convention to combat dese.term: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
united nations convention to combat dese.text: A UN treaty to combat desertification and ease the effects of drought through long-term national action programmes backed by international cooperation.

biodiversity action plan.text: A national or local program for protecting and restoring threatened species and habitats, prepared under the Biodiversity Convention.

sustainable development goal 15.text: The UN goal 'Life on land': to protect, restore and sustainably use land ecosystems, manage forests, combat desertification and halt biodiversity loss.

world heritage site.text: A landmark or area protected under a UNESCO-run treaty because of its outstanding cultural, historical or natural value to humanity.

ramsar convention.text: An international treaty, signed at Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, for the conservation and wise use of wetlands of international importance.

aichi biodiversity targets.text: Twenty international targets for 2011–2020, set under the Biodiversity Convention, to protect biodiversity, species and sustainable use of resources.

nagoya protocol.text: A 2010 supplementary agreement to the Biodiversity Convention on access to genetic resources and fair sharing of the benefits from their use.

high seas treaty.text: A legally binding agreement under the Law of the Sea convention to conserve and sustainably use marine life in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

other effective area-based conservation.text: Sites outside formal protected areas that are governed and managed in ways that conserve biodiversity in place over the long term.

financing the sdgs.text: Estimates of how much money reaching the SDGs would take, and where it might come from.

sdg targets and indicators.text: Indicators are the measures decision-makers use to track progress towards each SDG target.

sdgs weak on environmental sustainabilit.text: The criticism that the SDGs treat economic growth as foundational and do not make protecting the Earth system an end in itself.

trade-offs among the sdgs.text: The concern that pursuing some SDGs can work against others, so that not all 17 can be reached together.

cbd conference of the parties.text: The governing body of the Biodiversity Convention, made up of all governments that have ratified it.

kunming-montreal global biodiversity fra.text: The global plan for nature adopted at the 2022 UN Biodiversity Conference (COP15) under the Biodiversity Convention.

30 by 30.text: A global initiative for governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and ocean area by 2030.

criticism of the biodiversity convention.text: Arguments that the Biodiversity Convention has been weakly enforced and unfair to biodiversity-rich poorer countries.

ecologically or biologically significant.term: Ecologically or Biologically Significant Marine Areas
ecologically or biologically significant.text: Ocean areas identified under the Biodiversity Convention, using scientific criteria, as especially important for marine life.

world charter for nature.text: A UN declaration adopted on 28 October 1982 setting out five principles of conservation to guide all human conduct affecting nature.

iucn protected area categories.text: Six categories, set by the IUCN's World Commission on Protected Areas, that classify protected areas by their management objectives.

protected area effectiveness.text: How well protected areas actually prevent biodiversity loss, judged for example by comparing populations inside and outside them.

digital sequence information.text: A placeholder policy term, used especially in the Biodiversity Convention, for data such as DNA sequences derived from genetic resources.

harmful fisheries subsidies.text: Government payments to fishing fleets that encourage overcapacity, overfishing or illegal fishing, which SDG Target 14.6 aims to end.

large-scale marine protected areas.text: Marine protected areas of at least 100,000 square km, set up to cut overfishing and human disturbance of ocean ecosystems.

cartagena protocol on biosafety.text: A supplement to the Biodiversity Convention that governs the movement of genetically modified organisms between countries to protect biodiversity.

convention on migratory species.text: An international agreement, also called the Bonn Convention, to conserve migratory animals throughout their ranges.

biodiversity and climate change nexus.text: The idea, set out in a joint IPBES–IPCC report, that climate change and biodiversity loss are linked and must be tackled together.

ipbes nexus assessment.text: An IPBES report, approved on 17 December 2024, on how biodiversity, water, food and health are connected.

ipbes transformative change assessment.text: An IPBES report, approved on 18 December 2024, on the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and how to bring about transformative change.

illegal wildlife trade targets.text: SDG targets 15.7 and 15.c to end poaching and trafficking of protected species and tackle both demand and supply of illegal wildlife products.

gbf implications for business and financ.term: GBF implications for business and finance
gbf implications for business and financ.text: Expected effects of the global biodiversity framework on companies, banks and central banks, according to the UNEP Finance Initiative.

eu biodiversity strategy for 2030.text: The European Commission's 2020 plan for biodiversity, offered as the EU's contribution to the post-2020 global framework.

nature restoration law.text: A 2024 European Union regulation that makes binding targets for restoring damaged nature across the EU.

paper parks.text: Protected areas that exist in law but lack the funding, staff or enforcement to stop poaching, logging or development inside them.

national biodiversity strategy and actio.term: National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan
national biodiversity strategy and actio.text: A country's main plan for carrying out the Biodiversity Convention at home, known as an NBSAP.

criticism of the nagoya protocol.text: Concerns that the Nagoya Protocol's bureaucracy harms biodiversity research, conservation and disease response.

half-earth proposal.text: E. O. Wilson's 2016 proposal that half of the Earth's surface be set aside as a human-free natural reserve to preserve biodiversity.

common heritage of mankind.text: The principle that certain resources, such as the deep seabed, belong to all humanity rather than to any one nation.

2010 biodiversity target.text: A global conservation target to halt, or significantly slow, the decline of biodiversity by the end of 2010.

indigenous peoples.text: Peoples marked by self-identification, cultural difference from others in their state, a special bond with their traditional territory, and a history of domination and discrimination; no single definition is generally accepted.

environmental justice.text: A social movement against the harm done to poor or marginalized communities by hazardous waste, resource extraction and other land uses they do not benefit from.

traditional ecological knowledge.text: Knowledge, practices and beliefs about how living things, including people, relate to each other and their surroundings, built up over generations and passed on through culture.

wildfire.text: An unplanned and uncontrolled fire in an area of combustible vegetation.

political economy.text: An interdisciplinary field of political science and economics that studies how political and economic systems relate to and influence each other.

political ecology.text: The study of how political, economic and social factors relate to environmental issues and climate change.

extractivism.text: The removal of large amounts of natural resources, mainly for export, with little or no processing.

land law.text: The branch of law that deals with the rights to use land, transfer it, or keep others off it.

ecological debt.text: The debt some campaigners say the Global North owes the Global South for historical environmental injustice, such as resource exploitation, habitat damage and pollution.

environmental racism.text: The disproportionate burden of environmental hazards, pollution and ecological damage on marginalized communities and people of colour.

biopiracy.text: Taking the genetic resources and knowledge of farming and Indigenous communities without permission, to gain monopoly control through patents.

environmental conflict.text: A social conflict caused by environmental damage or by unequal sharing of environmental resources; also called an ecological distribution conflict.

indigenous land stewardship.text: The care of land by Indigenous peoples with secure tenure, which yields environmental and economic benefits for everyone.

climate justice.text: A form of environmental justice concerned with how unequally climate change harms marginalized and vulnerable people.

climate change and indigenous peoples.text: The disproportionate impact of climate change on Indigenous peoples worldwide compared with non-Indigenous peoples.

ecocide.text: The destruction of the environment by humans; the word joins Greek oikos, 'home', and Latin caedere, 'to kill'.

procedural justice.text: The idea of fairness in the processes used to settle disputes and share out resources.

climate change and poverty.text: The close link between climate change and poverty, since climate change hits poor people and developing countries hardest.

human rights and climate change.text: A conceptual and legal framework for studying and addressing how global warming affects international human rights.

indigenous land rights.text: The rights of Indigenous peoples, individually or collectively, to land and the natural resources on it, mostly in colonised countries.

right to a healthy environment.text: The human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, seen as necessary for enjoying rights such as life, health, food and water.

access and benefit sharing agreement.text: An agreement that sets out how the benefits from using genetic resources are shared fairly and equitably.

fortress conservation.text: A conservation approach that tries to protect nature by creating protected areas cut off from people.

green grabbing.text: Taking land and resources, often by foreign actors, in the name of environmental goals, in a way that produces unjust development; also called green colonialism.

environmental gentrification.text: A process in which cleaning up pollution or adding green amenities raises local property values and draws wealthier residents into a formerly polluted or neglected neighbourhood.

environmental defender.text: A person or group that protects the environment from harms such as resource extraction, hazardous waste dumping, infrastructure projects or land seizure.

free, prior and informed consent.text: The principle that an Indigenous people must be consulted, bottom-up, before development starts on its ancestral land or uses resources in its territory.

critical environmental justice.text: An approach created by David Pellow that questions the assumptions and gaps of earlier environmental justice studies.

dimensions of environmental justice.text: The main kinds of fairness environmental justice asks for: fair sharing of environmental benefits and burdens, a real say in decisions, and recognition of marginalized groups.

hazardous waste exports to the global so.term: Hazardous waste exports to the Global South
hazardous waste exports to the global so.text: The shifting of toxic waste from rich countries to the Global South, where weaker rules make disposal cheaper.

indigenous environmental justice.text: Environmental justice as understood by Indigenous peoples, framed by their colonial situation and possibly aiming at decolonization.

community-based conservation.text: A conservation movement from the 1980s that involves local communities in protecting nature, in reaction to top-down conservation that ignored them.

green imperialism.text: A critical label for what is seen as a Western strategy of influencing the internal affairs of developing nations in the name of environmentalism.

burden-sharing principles in climate jus.text: Three rules for deciding who should carry the larger costs of climate change: those who caused most of it, those most able to pay, and those who benefited most.

intergenerational climate equity.text: The fairness question raised because the generations mainly responsible for climate change are not the ones who will bear most of its damage.

nimby.text: Opposition by residents to proposed development or infrastructure in their local area, with support for strict land use regulation.

indigenous and community conserved area.text: Territories and areas governed, managed and conserved in practice by Indigenous peoples or local communities, with clear benefits for biological and cultural diversity.

harmony with nature.text: A principle of friendly, holistic coexistence between humanity and nature.

wipo treaty on genetic resources and tra.term: WIPO treaty on genetic resources and traditional knowledge
wipo treaty on genetic resources and tra.text: A 2024 international treaty, known as GRATK, that requires patent applicants to disclose when inventions are based on genetic resources or associated traditional knowledge.

facets of traditional ecological knowled.text: Nicholas Houde's six-part breakdown of TEK: factual observations, management systems, past and current uses, ethics and values, culture and identity, and cosmology.

indigenous cultural burning.text: Traditional controlled burning used by Indigenous peoples as a land management tool and spiritual practice.

neo-extractivism.text: A development model in which governments take greater control of resource extraction and its revenue in order to fund social programmes.

land rights.text: The ability to freely obtain, use and possess land, as long as doing so does not infringe on others' rights.

measuring ecological debt.text: Attempts to put numbers on ecological debt, mostly by comparing each country's emissions with its fair per-person share.

environmental reparations.text: Payments or investments made to people judged to be harmed by the presence of industry.

hoodia benefit-sharing case.text: A dispute over a patented weight-loss compound from the Hoodia plant, long used by the San people, that ended in a benefit-sharing deal.

neem patent dispute.text: A challenge to US and European patents on pesticide and antifungal products from the neem tree, used by Indian farmers for around 2,000 years.

conservation refugee.text: A person, usually Indigenous, displaced from their homeland when a park or other protected area is created.

sacrifice zone.text: A geographic area permanently damaged by heavy environmental change or economic neglect, often through locally unwanted land uses.

locally unwanted land use.text: A facility or project, such as a landfill, power plant or prison, that a local community opposes because of the harms it expects from it.

seven generation sustainability.text: The principle that people today should live and work for the benefit of the seventh generation to come.

ecological distribution conflict.text: A concept coined in 1995 by Joan Martínez-Alier and Martin O'Connor for conflicts over unfair access to natural resources and unequal pollution burdens.

environmentalism of the poor.text: Social movements that arise when poor people fight powerful state or private interests threatening their livelihood, health, sovereignty and culture.

ethnoecology.text: The scientific study of how different groups of people understand the ecosystems around them and their relationships with their environments.

atmospheric colonization.text: The idea that rich Global North countries have taken over most of the atmosphere's capacity to absorb greenhouse gases, leaving the Global South to bear the consequences.

climate apartheid.text: A situation in which only the rich can escape the consequences of climate change.

distributional effects of environmental.text: How the costs and benefits of an environmental policy fall on different groups, and whether it widens or narrows environmental and social injustice.

un declaration on the rights of indigeno.term: UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
un declaration on the rights of indigeno.text: A declaration adopted by the UN in 2007 that sets out the collective rights of Indigenous peoples, including self-determination.

environmental personhood.text: A legal idea that gives certain natural entities, such as rivers or forests, the status of a legal person.

rawls's kinds of procedural justice.text: John Rawls's division of procedural justice into perfect, imperfect and pure forms, set out in A Theory of Justice.

climate refugees and human rights.text: People forced to move by climate change who fall into a legal gap because such migration is not yet covered by international law.

climate migration.text: Movement of people driven by sudden or gradual climate-exacerbated disasters such as heavy rains, drought, desertification, environmental degradation, sea-level rise and cyclones.

environmental migrant.text: A person forced to leave their home by sudden or long-term changes in the local or regional environment that compromise well-being or livelihood.

aboriginal title.text: A common-law doctrine holding that Indigenous peoples' customary land rights survive after a settler state takes sovereignty.

varieties of environmentalism.text: Martinez-Alier's division of environmentalism into three currents: the cult of the wilderness, the gospel of eco-efficiency, and environmental justice or the environmentalism of the poor.

ancestral domain.text: The lands, territories and resources of Indigenous peoples, a term used especially in the Asia-Pacific region.

feminist political ecology.text: A feminist approach within political ecology that studies how gender shapes people's access to, control over and knowledge of natural resources.

rights of nature law.text: The writing of the rights-of-nature theory into constitutions, statutes, treaties, local laws and court rulings.

gender and environment.text: The study of how relations between women, men and the environment shape resource use, the sharing of responsibilities and people's well-being.

poverty.text: A condition in which a person lacks the money and essentials needed for a basic standard of living.

ilo convention 169.text: An international treaty on Indigenous and tribal peoples adopted by the International Labour Organization in 1989.

indigenous fpic protocols.text: Rules written by Indigenous peoples themselves, since the early 2000s, for how consent processes must be carried out.

cycle of poverty.text: A situation, also called a poverty trap, in which poverty seems to be passed down, so that later generations cannot escape it.

poverty and environmental degradation.text: The two-way link between poverty and damage to nature: the poor suffer most from degradation, and some argue poverty itself drives it.

land degradation and poverty.text: The way degraded land and human deprivation reinforce each other, as falling land productivity cuts food, income and security.

sustainable livelihood.text: An idea from development and environmental studies about how people, especially vulnerable groups, can support themselves in ways that last and can recover from shocks.

water subsidies and the poor.text: The pattern in which subsidies that make piped water cheap mostly help richer connected households, while many poor people go unserved.

energy poverty and development.text: The link between lack of modern energy and lack of development, since businesses, public services and households all depend on energy.

poverty traps in developing countries.text: The ways whole poor countries stay stuck in poverty, through causes such as lack of credit, environmental degradation, corruption, disease, war and poor infrastructure.

livelihood capitals framework.text: The United Nations Development Programme's way of assessing livelihoods by the five kinds of capital people can draw on: human, social, natural, physical and financial.

sustainable business.text: Running a business so that it makes money while keeping its harm to the environment, local communities and society as small as possible.

nature-positive.text: A goal to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030 and to achieve its full recovery by 2050.

fossil fuel.text: A flammable carbon or hydrocarbon material formed naturally in the Earth's crust from the buried remains of prehistoric organisms.

fossil fuel formation.text: The geological process by which buried dead organisms become coal, oil and gas.

eu taxonomy for sustainable activities.text: A European Union classification system that defines which economic activities count as environmentally sustainable, created under the European Green Deal.

environmental management system.text: A system of policies, procedures and processes that a firm uses to train staff and to monitor, summarize and report its environmental performance to people inside and outside the firm.

environmental audit.text: An evaluation that finds gaps in an organization's compliance with environmental rules and in its environmental management system, and sets out corrective actions.

fossilflation.text: The impact of fossil fuel prices on inflation.

health effects of fossil fuel pollution.term: Health effects of fossil fuel pollution
health effects of fossil fuel pollution.text: The illness and premature death caused by inhaling particulates and other air pollution from burning fossil fuels.

corporate social responsibility.text: Companies running their main business responsibly and sustainably so that their overall effect on society is positive.

greenhouse gas protocol.text: A set of standards that organizations use to measure and track their greenhouse gas emissions, the most common in greenhouse gas accounting.

stakeholder theory.text: The view that a firm is answerable not only to its shareholders but to every group with a relationship to it, such as workers, customers, suppliers and communities.

design for the environment.text: A design approach that cuts a product's or service's harm to health and the environment, counting impacts across its whole life cycle.

corporate sustainability strategies.text: Plans a company uses to win new revenue from sustainability while guarding against rising energy, regulation and resource costs and shifting customer views.

sustainability reporting.text: The disclosure, voluntary or required, of a company's non-financial performance information to people outside the organization.

ethical consumerism.text: Choosing what to buy, and what to boycott, according to how products affect people, animals and the environment.

shareholder value versus social responsi.text: The argument over whether a company exists only to earn returns for its owners within the law, or also owes duties to society and the environment.

social license to operate.text: The ongoing support and approval that local communities and other stakeholders give to a company's activities.

corporate sustainability.text: A business approach that aims to create long-term value for stakeholders by building ethical, social, environmental, cultural and economic concerns into company strategy.

task force on climate-related financial.term: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
task force on climate-related financial.text: An international task force whose recommendations tell investors how companies are managing the risks of climate change and how they are governed.

creating shared value.text: A business strategy in which a company seeks profit by solving social problems linked to its own operations, improving its competitiveness and the conditions of its communities at once.

supply chain sustainability.text: Managing the environmental, social and economic effects of goods and services, and encouraging good governance, across their whole life cycle from suppliers to customers.

csr as misdirection.text: The criticism that companies use social responsibility programs to draw attention away from harmful parts of their business.

csr-consumer paradox.text: The gap between consumers saying they will buy only from responsible companies and what they actually buy.

carroll's pyramid of csr.text: Archie Carroll's four-part framework of what society expects of business: economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities.

resource-based view of csr.text: A way of judging the costs and benefits of CSR by asking whether it gives a firm a competitive advantage that rivals cannot copy.

corporate environmental responsibility.text: A company's duty to avoid damaging the natural environment.

social accounting.text: Reporting the social and environmental effects of a company's economic activity to interest groups and to society at large.

socially responsible investing.text: Investors using where they put their money to encourage company behaviour they consider responsible.

types of corporate social initiatives.text: Six kinds of activity through which companies practise CSR, from donations to behaviour-change campaigns.

business action on climate change.text: What businesses do about climate change, from cutting their own emissions to trying to influence climate regulation such as the Kyoto Protocol.

sustainable sourcing.text: Obtaining the materials, products and services a company needs from suppliers in a way that is socially and environmentally responsible while still economically sound.

scope 3 emissions.text: The indirect greenhouse gas emissions in a company's value chain, such as those of its suppliers and from the use of its products.

social sustainability in business.text: A business's responsibility for the well-being of its employees, customers and community.

science-based emissions targets.text: Company targets for cutting greenhouse gas emissions that are set in line with climate science and the Paris Agreement goals.

sustainability and financial performance.text: The debate over whether a company's environmental and social efforts raise or lower its profits.

insetting.text: A business-coined way for a company to claim it has met emission targets by means other than cutting its own emissions.

do no significant harm.text: The rule that an activity counts as sustainable under the EU taxonomy only if it contributes substantially to one environmental objective without seriously harming any of the other five.

eco-efficiency and socio-efficiency.text: Eco-efficiency compares the economic value a firm adds with its total ecological impact; socio-efficiency compares that value with the firm's social impact.

natural gas and nuclear in the eu taxono.term: Natural gas and nuclear in the EU taxonomy
natural gas and nuclear in the eu taxono.text: The dispute over whether fossil gas and nuclear power should be labelled as environmentally sustainable investments under the EU taxonomy.

material flow cost accounting.text: A management tool that traces the physical flows of materials and energy through a company or supply chain and assigns costs to them, to reveal and reduce their environmental and financial costs.

bottom of the pyramid and inclusive busi.term: Bottom of the pyramid and inclusive business
bottom of the pyramid and inclusive busi.text: Inclusive business models create value by selling products and services to the poor or buying from them, bringing poor people directly into companies' value chains.

supplier audits.text: Visits to supplier sites to check that they meet social and environmental standards.

carbon bomb.text: A new fossil fuel extraction project whose potential emissions exceed 1 billion tonnes of CO2.

strategic support for environmental regu.text: A firm backing new environmental rules because they will hurt its competitors more than itself.

voluntary sustainability standards.text: Requirements on matters such as human rights, worker safety and environmental impact that producers, traders and retailers may be asked to meet, adopted voluntarily along the value chain.

multi-stakeholder sustainability initiat.text: Partnerships of NGOs, companies, suppliers and governments that use voluntary, market-based approaches to make production of a particular product or sector more sustainable.

double materiality.text: The principle that a company should report both how sustainability issues affect its finances and how it affects society and the environment.

corporate sustainability reporting direc.text: The European Union law that sets uniform sustainability reporting rules for companies, replacing the earlier Non-Financial Reporting Directive.

mainstreaming nature in business.text: Building nature into a company's decision-making, governance, strategy and risk management rather than leaving it to site ecologists.

physical and transition risk.text: The two kinds of climate risk: physical risks from climate impacts such as extreme weather, and transition risks from the costs of moving to a lower-carbon society.

supply chain transparency.text: Making it possible to see and trace where goods come from and how they were made along the supply chain.

stockholm conference of 1972.text: The United Nations Conference on the Human Environment, held in Stockholm from 5 to 16 June 1972, was the first global conference on environmental issues.

earth summit.text: The Earth Summit was the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, held in Rio de Janeiro from 3 to 14 June 1992.

classical economics.text: Classical economics is the school of economic thought that flourished mainly in Britain from the late 18th to the mid-19th century, led by Adam Smith, David Ricardo, Thomas Malthus and John Stuart Mill.

our common future.text: Our Common Future, or the Brundtland Report, is the 1987 report of the UN's World Commission on Environment and Development that set out the best-known definition of sustainable development.

conservation movement.text: The conservation movement is an environmental, social and political movement that seeks to manage and protect natural resources, wild species and their habitats for the future.

silent spring.text: Silent Spring is Rachel Carson's 1962 environmental science book documenting the harm done by indiscriminate use of the pesticide DDT.

rio+20.text: Rio+20, the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development, was a 2012 summit in Rio de Janeiro that sought to reconcile the world's economic and environmental goals.

club of rome.text: An informal non-profit group of intellectuals and business leaders, founded in Rome in 1968, that critically discusses pressing global problems.

earth day.text: Earth Day is an annual event held on April 22 to show support for environmental protection, first held in 1970.

physiocracy.text: Physiocracy, from the Greek for 'government of nature', was an 18th-century French economic theory holding that a nation's wealth comes solely from its land and farming.

small is beautiful.text: Small Is Beautiful: A Study of Economics As If People Mattered is a 1973 essay collection by the economist E. F. Schumacher that criticizes mainstream economics for ignoring nature's limits.

the economics of ecosystems and biodiver.term: The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity
the economics of ecosystems and biodiver.text: TEEB was an international study, led by Pavan Sukhdev from 2007 to 2011, that set out to show the global economic benefits of biodiversity and the rising cost of losing it.

an essay on the principle of population.term: An Essay on the Principle of Population
an essay on the principle of population.text: An Essay on the Principle of Population is Thomas Robert Malthus's 1798 book arguing that population tends to grow until it outruns the supply of food and other basic resources.

earth summit 2002.text: The World Summit on Sustainable Development, nicknamed Rio+10, was held in Johannesburg, South Africa, from 26 August to 4 September 2002.

the population bomb.text: The Population Bomb is a 1968 book by Paul and Anne Ehrlich that predicted worldwide famines from overpopulation and called for immediate limits on population growth.

a sand county almanac.text: A Sand County Almanac is a 1949 book of essays by the American ecologist and forester Aldo Leopold that argues for a 'land ethic', a responsible relationship between people and the land.

stockholm declaration.text: The Stockholm Declaration of 1972 was the first United Nations declaration on the global environment, a set of 26 principles agreed at the Stockholm Conference.

history of economic thought.text: The history of economic thought is the study of the thinkers and theories behind political economy and economics, from the ancient world to today.

mercantilism.text: Mercantilism is a nationalist economic policy that aims to maximize a country's exports and minimize its imports.

the dasgupta review.text: A 2021 report on the economics of biodiversity, led by economist Partha Dasgupta and commissioned by the UK government.

the economics of welfare.text: The Economics of Welfare is Arthur Cecil Pigou's 1920 book that introduced the idea of the externality and proposed correcting it with a tax.

classical theory of value.text: The classical theory of value explained prices by a 'natural price' set by lasting forces, toward which day-to-day market prices tend to move.

tableau économique.text: The Tableau économique is an economic model François Quesnay described in 1759 that traced how production and money flow between social classes.

conservation reconsidered.text: Conservation Reconsidered is John V. Krutilla's 1967 paper describing the economic value of undisturbed natural places such as rivers and forests.

pesticide.text: Pesticides are substances used to control pests, including herbicides, insecticides, nematicides and fungicides.

herman daly.text: Herman Daly (1938–2022) was an American ecological economist, best known as a senior economist at the World Bank and for the idea of a steady-state economy.

william stanley jevons.text: William Stanley Jevons (1835–1882) was an English economist and logician, a leader of the marginal revolution and author of The Coal Question.

ronald coase.text: Ronald Coase (1910–2013) was a British economist whose work on transaction costs and property rights reshaped how economists think about externalities.

garrett hardin.text: Garrett Hardin (1915–2003) was an American ecologist and microbiologist, best known for his 1968 paper "The Tragedy of the Commons".

elinor ostrom.text: Elinor Ostrom (1933–2012) was an American political scientist and political economist who showed how communities can manage shared resources themselves.

arthur cecil pigou.text: Arthur Cecil Pigou (1877–1959) was an English economist, best known for the idea of taxing activities that cause negative externalities.

robert costanza.text: Robert Costanza (born 1950) is an American/Australian ecological economist at University College London's Institute for Global Prosperity.

nicholas georgescu-roegen.text: Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen (1906–1994) was a Romanian mathematician, statistician and economist whose work on entropy and natural resources helped found ecological economics.

william nordhaus.text: William Nordhaus (1941–2026) was an American economist at Yale, best known for economic modelling of climate change.

howard t. odum.text: Howard T. Odum (1924–2002) was an American ecologist known for pioneering ecosystem ecology and for linking ecological energy flows to economics.

harold hotelling.text: Harold Hotelling (1895–1973) was an American mathematical statistician and economic theorist, known for Hotelling's law, Hotelling's lemma and Hotelling's rule.

e. f. schumacher.text: E. F. Schumacher (1911–1977) was a German-born British economist best known for proposing human-scale, decentralised and appropriate technologies.

william e. rees.text: William E. Rees is a Canadian human ecologist and ecological economist, best known for co-developing the ecological footprint with his graduate students.

c. s. holling.text: C. S. 'Buzz' Holling (1930–2019) was a Canadian ecologist and one of the conceptual founders of ecological economics.

joan martinez alier.text: Joan Martinez Alier (born 1939) is a Spanish economist whose work in ecological economics and political ecology is summed up in the idea of the environmentalism of the poor.

donella meadows.text: Donella Meadows (1941–2001) was an American environmental scientist and writer, best known as lead author of The Limits to Growth and Thinking in Systems.

nicholas stern.text: Nicholas Stern (born 1946) is a British economist, banker and academic who led the Stern Review on the economics of climate change.

mathis wackernagel.text: Mathis Wackernagel is a Swiss-born sustainability advocate who co-created the ecological footprint and heads the Global Footprint Network.

william forster lloyd.text: William Forster Lloyd (1794–1852) was an English writer on economics, best known for an 1833 lecture that first set out the tragedy of the commons.

partha dasgupta.text: Sir Partha Dasgupta (born 1942) is an Indian-British economist at the University of Cambridge whose long-standing interest is ecological economics.

robert ayres.text: Robert Ayres (1932–2023) was an American-born physicist and economist who applied the laws of thermodynamics to economics and originated the idea of industrial metabolism.

aldo leopold.text: Aldo Leopold (1887–1948) was an American forester, ecologist, writer and conservationist, known for his land ethic.

ecological economics (journal).text: Ecological Economics is a peer-reviewed journal published by Elsevier for the International Society for Ecological Economics, covering research on ecological economics.

john muir.text: John Muir was a Scottish-born American naturalist and writer, called the Father of the National Parks, who championed the preservation of wilderness.

kenneth e. boulding.text: Kenneth Boulding (1910–1993) was an English-born American economist, educator, peace activist and interdisciplinary thinker.

gifford pinchot.text: Gifford Pinchot (1865–1946) was an American forester and politician, a key figure in the history of conservation and natural resource management in the United States.

alternatives to pesticides.text: Alternatives to pesticides include cultivation practices, biological pest control, sterile insect release and genetic engineering of crops.

gretchen daily.text: Gretchen Daily (born 1964) is an American environmental scientist and tropical ecologist who advanced the science of ecosystem services and ways to value nature in decisions.

costs and benefits of pesticide use.term: Costs and benefits of pesticide use
costs and benefits of pesticide use.text: Pesticides raise crop yields and farm incomes but impose costs on health and the environment that the user does not bear.

pesticide regulation.text: In many countries a government agency must approve pesticides for sale and use, and international codes seek common standards.

william baumol.text: William Baumol (1922–2017) was an American economist, among the world's most influential, whose work included environmental economics.

dennis meadows.text: Dennis Meadows (born 1942) is an American systems scientist best known as a co-author of The Limits to Growth.

martin weitzman.text: An American economist at Harvard whose research centred on environmental economics, especially climate change and catastrophes.

allen v. kneese.text: Allen V. Kneese (1930–2001) was an American economist and a pioneer of environmental economics.

david pearce.text: David Pearce (1941–2005) was a British pioneer of environmental economics and professor at University College London.

kate raworth.text: Kate Raworth (born 1970) is an English economist known for doughnut economics, a model balancing essential human needs against planetary boundaries.

serge latouche.text: Serge Latouche (born 1940) is a French emeritus professor of economics and one of the best-known advocates of degrowth.

milner baily schaefer.text: Milner Baily Schaefer (1912–1970) was an American fisheries scientist notable for his work on the population dynamics of fisheries.

richard b. norgaard.text: Richard B. Norgaard (born 1943) is an American professor emeritus of ecological economics at the University of California, Berkeley, considered one of the field's founders.

karl-göran mäler.text: Karl-Göran Mäler (1939–2020) was a Swedish economist known for his work in economics and ecological economics.

annmari jansson.text: AnnMari Jansson (1934–2007) was a Swedish systems ecologist who helped pioneer research joining ecology and economics.

john v. krutilla.text: John V. Krutilla (1922–2003) was an American environmental economist who invented the concept of existence value, the economic value of undisturbed wilderness.

karl william kapp.text: Karl William Kapp (1910–1976) was a German-American economist whose theory of social costs makes him a foundational thinker of social ecological economics.

serhiy podolynsky.text: Serhiy Podolynsky (1850–1891) was a Ukrainian socialist, physician and sociologist, an early pioneer of ecological economics.

journal of environmental economics and m.term: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
journal of environmental economics and m.text: The Journal of Environmental Economics and Management is a peer-reviewed environmental economics journal published six times a year.

pavan sukhdev.text: Pavan Sukhdev (born 1960) is an Indian environmental economist working on the green economy, biodiversity, natural capital and sustainable finance.

martin faustmann.text: A German forester regarded as the father of forest economics.

united nations environment programme.text: The body that coordinates responses to environmental issues within the United Nations system.

international union for conservation of.term: International Union for Conservation of Nature
international union for conservation of.text: An international organization of governments and conservation groups working on nature conservation and the sustainable use of natural resources.

international society for ecological eco.text: The main international scholarly society for ecological economics, founded in 1989 largely on Herman Daly's work.

world resources institute.text: A global non-profit research organization, founded in 1982, that studies sustainable practices for business, economics, finance and governance.

integrity council for the voluntary carb.term: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market
integrity council for the voluntary carb.text: An independent governance body that publishes the Core Carbon Principles, criteria meant to define high-integrity carbon credits in the voluntary carbon market.

psychological impact of climate change.text: The effects climate change can have on people's mental and emotional well-being.

global forest watch.text: An open-source web application that monitors the world's forests in near real-time.

national adaptation programme of action.text: A plan in which a least developed country tells the UN climate convention its most urgent and immediate needs for adapting to climate change.

core carbon principles.text: The ten principles the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market uses as a threshold benchmark for carbon credit quality.
